title: Repo Board
pitch: A real-time GitHub task board where humans set the work and agents with WebMCP support claim, plan, execute, and follow it safely through pull requests.
about_excerpt: A real-time GitHub task board where humans set the work and agents with WebMCP support claim, plan, execute, and follow it safely through pull requests. Like Comment Story Updates A real-time GitHub task board where humans set the work and agents with WebMCP support claim, plan, execute, and follow it safely through pull requests. Problem Coding agents can work quickly, but teams of people still need a reliable way to decide what someone's agent may do, prevent two agents from taking the same task, review a plan before implementation, and see what happened after the agent stops. Issue trackers record work for people. Agent transcripts record work inside one conversation. Neither gives people and browser agents a shared, live workflow with explicit ownership and bounded actions. Solution Repo Board is a real-time task board for one GitHub repository. Humans create and groom tasks in a five-column workflow: Todo -> Ready -> In Progress -> In PR -> Done The page exposes WebMCP tools for the actions that are allowed in the current context. A Codex agent can inspect tasks, claim one, attach or revise a plan, start work, report progress, link a pull request, read review state, and check CI. Humans retain authority over sensitive actions such as replacing an active owner, canceling work, and archiving a completed task. The first valid claim wins. Ownership is bound to the signed-in GitHub user and the browser tab, backed by an unguessable per-tab capability. It does not expire because a timer ran out or a WebSocket disconnected. Another agent can take over only after the person using the page confirms it. Why This Matters Agent coordination fails in ordinary, expensive ways: two agents edit the same work, a plan gets separated from its implementation, a stale browser tab continues mutating state, or a human cannot tell whether a status report came from the repository or from the agent itself. Repo Board makes those boundaries visible and enforceable. The person and the agent work against the same task, plan revision, board revision, pull request snapshot, and activity history. The app treats task text, plans, progress reports, and GitHub content as untrusted data. That content cannot select tools, authorize a mutation, choose a repository, or supply secrets. How We Used AI Repo Board does not embed a model or require an OpenAI API key. It gives an AI agent a precise interface to a live product through browser-native WebMCP. The agent discovers only the tools that are valid for the current user, selected task, assignment, and workflow state. For example, an unassigned Ready task exposes claim_task . After the current tab claims it, the registry replaces that tool with read_plan , update_plan , report_progress , start_work , and release_task . After the task reaches In PR, the agent can read review and check state. Aborting the active registration removes stale tools when context changes. This makes the agent useful without giving it hidden authority. Read operations are bounded. Mutations carry an idempotency key and expected board revision. The Durable Object independently checks authorization and state transitions instead of trusting the browser tool layer. How We Used Codex Codex helped turn the product plan into a working system. It traced and implemented the React client, Cloudflare Worker, SQLite-backed Durable Object, D1 directory, GitHub App integration, WebSocket updates, and dynamic WebMCP profiles. It also wrote and ran focused tests for task transitions, validation, authorization, session isolation, concurrent claims, reconnect behavior, pull request state, and tool registration. The build process used Codex to pressure-test product decisions instead of only generating code. One important revision replaced timer-based leases with durable per-tab ownership after the failure modes of expiring work were examined. Codex then added explicit, human-confirmed takeover and server-side fencing for the former owner. A later pass added archive_task with the same rule in both the WebMCP layer and the Durable Object: only completed, unarchived Done work can be archived, and the page must ask the human first. Repo Board was also used for real work. In Codex's in-app browser, the airy-pond ticket for a private GitHub repository was inspected, claimed for planning, and given an approved plan. Repo Board moved it from Todo to Ready and closed the planning assignment. That exercise also caught a stale tool handle; fetching the current WebMCP registry resolved it, which validated the context-replacement design. Key Features Dynamic WebMCP tool profiles based on authentication, permissions, route, selection, assignment, and task state Atomic task claims with structured conflict results when another agent wins Durable ownership bound to a GitHub user and browser tab, with explicit human-confirmed takeover Immutable ticket and plan revisions plus an append-only activity log Typed workflow transitions instead of arbitrary drag-and-drop state changes Real-time board updates through hibernating WebSockets, missed-event replay, and reconnect snapshots Pull request linking, review normalization, check status, merge completion, and closed-without-merge rollback Human-confirmed cancellation and archival, with matching server-side guards Anonymous read-only previews for public repositories and fail-closed access for private repositories Two-word task references such as amber-fox , so people and agents do not have to pass internal UUIDs Bounded untrusted-content handling throughout ticket, plan, progress, review, and GitHub data Architecture The React client renders the board and registers WebMCP tools through document.modelContext . It sends HTTP commands and receives revisioned WebSocket updates from a Cloudflare Worker. The Worker handles GitHub authentication, repository authorization, API routing, static assets, installation-token GitHub calls, webhook verification, and scheduled pull request reconciliation. D1 stores the global directory, GitHub identities, hashed sessions, installations, and permission cache. One SQLite-backed RepositoryBoard Durable Object per owner/repo owns tasks, plan revisions, assignments, pull request snapshots, processed actions, webhook deliveries, and the board event log. It serializes mutations before broadcasting the new revision. GitHub network calls finish in the Worker before normalized results enter the Durable Object. No serialized state path remains open across an external request. Testing Instructions Public judge flow Open https://webmcp-repo-board.zacwhite.workers.dev/boards/zac/test-repo-board in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Google Chrome 149+ with WebMCP enabled. Confirm that the public board has one synthetic example in each column: Todo, Ready, In progress, In PR, and Done. Ask the agent to call list_tasks , then inspect white-vine to see its approved plan and linked open pull request. Inspect teal-whale to see a completed task linked to merged pull request #4. To test mutations, sign in with GitHub and use a repository where the Repo Board GitHub App is installed and your account has triage , write , maintain , or admin permission. Create a Todo task, claim it for planning, save a plan, claim implementation, call start_work , and report progress. Link an open pull request from the same repository. Confirm that the task moves to In PR and exposes pull request, review, and check tools. After the pull request merges, confirm that the task moves to Done. Archive only if you want to hide it from the default board while retaining its history. Mutating tests require a repository where the tester can install or access the GitHub App. Public anonymous routes remain read-only by design. Local setup Requirements: Node 24 and pnpm 11. pnpm install --frozen-lockfile pnpm d1:migrate:local pnpm dev:worker Open http://localhost:8787 . Local development provides a labeled development session and public stand-in repositories, so the core workflow does not require production GitHub credentials. Automated verification Run: pnpm check pnpm deploy:dry Verified again on September 3, 2026: ESLint passed. Both TypeScript projects passed type checking. 58 client and shared tests passed. 42 Worker and Durable Object tests passed. The production Vite build passed. The Wrangler dry deployment assembled the Worker, assets, Durable Object, and D1 bindings successfully. The public homepage returned HTTP 200. The public zac/webmcp-repo-board board API returned HTTP 200 and identified the repository as public and materialized. The public zac/test-repo-board demo API returned HTTP 200 with one task in each workflow column. ChatGPT's in-app browser completed a signed-in lifecycle across planning, implementation, progress reporting, pull request linkage, status refresh, and merge completion. Pull request #3 remains open as the In PR example. GitHub's pull request webhook moved merged pull request #4 to Done. Local Worker tests print warnings w

title: Simple Post
pitch: Your AI writes. SimplePost publishes. Turn ideas into platform-specific posts and schedule them across social networks from your favorite AI assistant.
about_excerpt: Your AI writes. SimplePost publishes. Turn ideas into platform-specific posts and schedule them across social networks from your favorite AI assistant. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI assistants are already great places to develop ideas and write social posts. But getting those posts published often means copying text into another tool, adjusting it for each network, uploading media, and scheduling everything separately. SimplePost closes that gap. Instead of adding another AI writer to a social media scheduler, it brings publishing to the AI assistant you already use. The idea is simple: Your AI writes. SimplePost publishes. What it does SimplePost is an open-source social publishing platform for people, AI agents, and applications. It lets you preview, validate, publish, and schedule content across 11 social platforms, including X, LinkedIn, Instagram, Threads, and Bluesky. You can work through an AI assistant using MCP, use the web scheduler directly, or integrate publishing into your own workflows through the TypeScript SDK, HTTP API, and CLI. The goal is not to copy the same message everywhere. One idea can become several platform-specific posts, with different text, media, and thread structures. Where WebMCP fits WebMCP brings the person and their agent into the same visual workspace. SimplePost’s free social media preview tool exposes structured tools that let a browser agent read the current drafts, render platform-specific versions, edit individual previews, configure profile details, and bring a particular preview into view. For example, a user can ask: Turn this launch announcement into posts for X, LinkedIn, and Instagram, then show me the previews. The agent prepares the versions and renders them on the page. The user can edit them directly or ask for changes, such as shortening the X version or making the LinkedIn post more technical. Both work with the same underlying content. The preview experience requires no signup or connected social accounts. Its WebMCP tools do not publish anything. After the user approves the content, the agent can retrieve a structured handoff for a separate, authenticated SimplePost publishing workflow. WebMCP handles the shared browser workspace; the remote MCP server handles authenticated publishing and scheduling. How I built it SimplePost is built around a shared TypeScript SDK that handles platform-specific publishing. The web scheduler, HTTP API, CLI, and MCP server build on that foundation. The web applications use Next.js and React, with PostgreSQL and Prisma supporting the scheduler’s persistent data. OAuth connects AI clients to the user’s SimplePost account without exposing raw social platform credentials to the assistant. Social previews come from a separate open-source rendering library shared across the product. It supports platform-specific layouts, profile identities, text, images, videos, and threads. The WebMCP integration connects structured tools directly to the preview page’s React state. Tool inputs are validated before changes are applied, and manual edits are reflected in the state the agent can read. Challenges One challenge is keeping a consistent publishing interface across platforms with different authentication flows, media requirements, content limits, and error responses. A shared SDK centralizes those differences without pretending every network works the same way. Another is coordinating human and agent edits. The preview page needs to remain an ordinary, usable editor while also exposing meaningful operations to an agent. Both interaction paths update the same drafts, and changing a preview clears its previous approval. A third challenge is separating experimentation from external actions. Preparing a preview should not accidentally publish a post. The public WebMCP tools stay local to the preview experience, while publishing requires a separate authenticated action. What I learned Building SimplePost reinforced that generating content is only one part of an AI-assisted workflow. Reviewing it, adapting it to its destination, and controlling what happens next matter just as much. The WebMCP integration also highlighted the value of shared, visible state. An agent can do the repetitive work while the person sees the result, makes direct edits, and guides the next step. That is the experience SimplePost aims to create: keep the AI assistant you prefer, make the publishing work easier, and stay involved in what goes out under your name. title: Salesive Graphics
pitch: A browser SVG design editor that hands its full toolset (drawing, layout, gradients, icons, templating) to any AI agent over WebMCP, so the agent builds finished graphics on the live canvas you use.
about_excerpt: A browser SVG design editor that hands its full toolset (drawing, layout, gradients, icons, templating) to any AI agent over WebMCP, so the agent builds finished graphics on the live canvas you use. Like Comment Story Updates An AI agent builds graphics on the live Salesive Graphics canvas through WebMCP. Inspiration Any AI agent can talk about design, but when you ask one to actually make a graphic it usually hands back a raw SVG string or a one-shot image it can't revise. We wanted an agent to be able to sit down at a real design tool, the same canvas a person uses, and build a finished flyer, social post or promo one element at a time, with the human watching and free to take over whenever they want. WebMCP is what made that practical. Instead of building a separate agent API, we could just expose the editor's own tools to whatever agent the user brings. What it does Salesive Graphics is a browser based SVG design editor. You can draw, lay things out, add gradients and icons, drop in image slots, and turn a design into a reusable template with a generated JSON schema. The part that makes it different: the whole editor toolset is published to any connected AI agent through WebMCP (document.modelContext). Around 100 editor tools, the exact same ones the built in assistant uses, are exposed to outside agents. A curated core set of about 48 is registered directly so it stays inside agent runtime limits, and the rest stay reachable through two meta tools, list_editor_tools and call_editor_tool. Agents draw shapes and text, apply gradients, insert Lucide icons, run the layout and alignment helpers, build reusable component groups like buttons, badges and stat blocks, and map dynamic fields, all on the same live canvas the user is looking at. Coordination between agent and user is built in. set_agent_identity shows who is working, lock_canvas puts up a blocking overlay while the agent edits, ask_canvas_question opens a modal so the agent can ask the user to pick between options, and every tool call streams into a live Activity panel. Guests can use it without an account and let an agent build for them. Work is saved to localStorage. It's live at https://graphics.salesive.com How we built it React 19 and Vite 8, Tailwind v4, deployed on Cloudflare with static assets served through Wrangler. WebMCP comes from @mcp-b/global, lazy loaded after first paint as its own chunk. A useWebMCP hook registers each editor tool with an input schema and emits call, result and error events. One clientToolHandlers map is the single source of truth. Every tool is available both to the in app assistant over a socket and to external WebMCP agents, so any new editor capability is exposed automatically. The SVG engine renders live and serializes to a standalone SVG. A mapping step produces a schema.json describing text, image, color, icon, toggle and variant fields. The design guide we ship to agents through get_editor_guide is generated from the same skill file we use internally, so the guidance never drifts away from the actual tools. Challenges we ran into Tool count limits. Agent runtimes reject a page whose WebMCP config is too large, so we had to prioritize down to a core set and add meta tools to keep everything else reachable. Keeping the live renderer and the serialized SVG in agreement, especially around circles versus ellipses, text bounding boxes and gradient references. Designing the coordination UI so that an agent editing the canvas never feels like it is fighting the user for control. What we learned WebMCP works best when you expose the tools you already have instead of inventing an agent API. The hard part is the ergonomics, things like identity, locking, questions and an activity log, not the tool calls themselves. What's next More component helpers, richer templating, and multiple agents working on one canvas at the same time. title: Sizel
pitch: A WebMCP electronics shop where browser agents build compatible PCs and recommends tech.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP electronics shop where browser agents build compatible PCs and recommends tech. Like Comment Story Updates Homepage WebMCP Tools Product Catalog Product detail Inspiration What inspired Sizel was mostly my own experience while building my current PC. I barely knew what to look for or which specifications actually mattered. I had 30 tabs open just to research and compare the parts, yet i still felt lost when i found out that my graphic card doesn't fit in my desired case. It's not like the informations were hidden, but they were buried inside a long spec list, and for someone not very technical at that time it was a really hard task. Because the real challenge is understanding how each component affects the other. The experience made me wonder how many people encounter same problem, how many people buy wrong component because they lack the knowledge? I made Sizel expose WebMCP tools so that agents can connect details and explain compatibility. What it does? Sizel is a fictional Electronics e-shop. Internally, you may encounter another name - Rigsmith - that's no longer used internal project name. Shoppers can browse and filter products, inspect individual product pages, select multiple variations of the product, or assemble a PC from a floating build summary. Each build slot opens its own category catalog. The repo implements and registers 15 WebMCP tool descriptors. The tools do not automatically choose a winner or place a real order. For example the create_watchdog asks user before calling it. All products, brands, logos, reviews, prices, stock values and performance data are made up just for this demo. The important part for me is that the agent actually operates in the same tab in which you are. The shopper can watch what is happening, inspect the same products, and keep control over decisions like adding something to the cart or creating a watchdog. The agent helps with the difficult reasoning, but it does not silently take over. How I built it? I built Sizel using agentic development. The languages used are: Typescript, Vite and CSS. The project contains a self contained local catalog of 135 products, with color and storage variations. The JSON catalog is source for the front end, but there is a SQLite copy included for inspection. The application therefore does not depend on external api for its products. The UI and WebMCP tools share one central App.tsx . picks stores parts, while chosen tracks explicit selections. Centralized mutations and validation keep compatibility, totals, build summary, cart, and checkout aligned. Checkout field and progressions remains shopper-controlled. The tools are intentionally scoped as specific shopping capabilities. Searching and comparing listings, finding compatible components, and validating it. Challenges I ran into One of the biggest challenges was making the flow snappy. In the A/B runs from the video, the WebMCP flow took 2 minutes 35 seconds. Though this timing isn't an average across more runs, it usually stays around that 2:30 -3 minute mark. Initially, the process was a lot slower, the breakthrough came when i simplified the tools themselves, and let the agent use its own reasoning. Another challenge was deciding what the agent should not claim. The product reviews, stock and performance values are synthetic, so I had to make the tools say that clearly. League of Legends, for example, has no simulated benchmark in the catalog, and the tool reports that instead of inventing a number. Accomplishments that I'm proud of To be honest, I'm mostly proud of how the UI turned out. I wanted the store to feel like a real e-shop, so i took care with it. I am also proud that the agent does not just return a hidden answer. It can show products and categories in the storefront while it works, so the shopper can follow the process instead of only receiving a final block of text. What I learned I learned that agentic tools work best when they are as dumb as possible, because the agent's own reasoning is powerful enough, and when there is not that much of them. A large tool repertoire just makes agent slower, and occasionally makes his reasoning more complex because he has to figure out which of there 40 tools to use now, especially when they are all so similar. title: Skulora Outfitter
pitch: Outfit any mission across every store: a shared board where you and your agent plan together.
about_excerpt: Outfit any mission across every store: a shared board where you and your agent plan together. Like Comment Story Updates thumbnail board kit replan checkout architecture board codriving Inspiration Real shopping rarely happens one store at a time. "Outfit me for a 3-day desert backpacking trip, under $600, I already own a stove" is one job, but today it is eight product searches across as many stores, a spreadsheet to keep the budget honest, and a lot of tabs. Agents can help, yet the ones we have shop a single site per page and treat you as a spectator: you type, they act, and if you disagree with a pick you start over in chat. WebMCP's brief asks what people and agents can do together that was hard before. Our answer is a planning board both of them work on. The agent does the tedious part, searching every Shopify merchant and building a kit that fits the budget; the person does the part only they can do, locking the sleeping bag they trust, rejecting the shoes they hate, and the agent re-plans around those decisions instead of over them. Shopify merchants already expose public Storefront MCP endpoints, and Shopify's Global Catalog MCP searches across all of them, so the missing piece was not the data. It was a page that exposes the mission itself as tools an agent can use. What it does Skulora Outfitter is a shared board for shopping missions . Open https://outfitter.skulora.com in ChatGPT's desktop browser or in Chrome with WebMCP enabled and tell the agent what you need. Then: The agent plans the mission . create_mission parses the goal, budget, constraints and what you already own; plan_kit turns it into slots (pack, sleeping bag, pad, water, sun protection…) each with a reason and a share of the budget. It searches every store . search_products runs per slot, in parallel, over Shopify's Global Catalog MCP plus curated merchants' Storefront MCP, dedupes and re-ranks candidates for fit, and choose_candidate picks with a stated reason. The board shows a live budget meter across merchants. You co-drive on the board . lock a pick the agent must keep, reject one it must never retry, choose a candidate yourself, or change the budget. Every edit is queued and delivered to the agent as mission_delta inside its next tool result, so it re-plans around you without being told. It explains itself . explain_tradeoffs writes a grounded "why this, versus the alternatives" under every slot, using only candidates that are actually on the board. It hands off, it does not buy . prepare_checkout creates one real cart per merchant through Storefront MCP and the board shows one checkout link each. You complete the purchase; nothing is bought on your behalf. In the reference run the agent planned 8 slots in about 6 seconds, filled them from 6 merchants at $553 of a $600 budget, and produced real checkout links. In ChatGPT's desktop browser it discovered the tools, found the Stage B tools that appeared after the mission was created, ran every search in parallel and finished with 8 merchants at $554.51 of $600. The demo video is one unedited run each: ChatGPT fills the board at $373.17 across 7 merchants; a lock and a reject lead to a re-plan that keeps the locked pack and swaps the rejected tent, ending at $446.96 across 8 merchants with real checkout links. The four things the rules ask every description to answer, in their order: Fit: why this use case belongs on WebMCP. A mission is structured state with a small, well-defined set of operations. Exposing it as typed tools lets any agent complete the job faster and more reliably than guessing through a UI, and lets the page shape what an agent may do (plan, search, choose, explain, prepare) while the human keeps the decisions that matter. Better experience: what changes for the person. One sentence, "outfit me for a 3-day desert trip, $600, I own a stove", becomes a 9-slot kit searched across every merchant and chosen with reasons in 27 seconds, instead of eight store searches, a spreadsheet for the budget and a dozen tabs. The person never leaves the board and never re-explains: the agent sees each lock and rejection as first-class input, the budget is enforced across stores instead of per cart, and the finale is one checkout link per merchant with the reasoning next to it rather than a wall of chat. Together: what people and agents can now do as a team. Plan a multi-store purchase as a team, in one place, with the agent doing the breadth (every merchant, every slot) and the person doing the judgment (this one, not that one, this much), and each sees the other's moves immediately. Lock a pack and reject a tent, say "re-plan", and the agent keeps the pack, replaces only the tent and says why, because the edits reached it as data. How: the WebMCP implementation. The page registers nine typed tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) , disclosed in three stages as the mission advances ( toolchange tells the agent about each new stage), with readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint annotations and results sized for an agent's context. Every result carries mission_delta (the person's edits since that agent's last call) and next_suggested_tools , and every rule (locks, rejections, budget, an incomplete kit) is enforced on the server with errors that name the valid ids and the next tool, so agents that call out of order or in parallel recover on the next turn. The built-in agent drives the same tools through document.modelContext.executeTool , so Chrome's DevTools logs it like any external agent. Details below. How we built it Tool surface. One tool table ( src/lib/webmcp/tools.ts ) defines nine tools with JSON Schema inputs and compact outputs sized for agent context: Stage A get_mission , create_mission , set_budget ; Stage B plan_kit , search_products , choose_candidate , explain_tradeoffs ; Stage C prepare_checkout , get_checkout_status . Read-only tools carry readOnlyHint ; tools that return merchant content carry untrustedContentHint . Every result ends with mission_delta (the person's edits since that agent's last call) and next_suggested_tools . Registration. src/components/WebMCPTools.tsx calls document.modelContext.registerTool(...) for the tools of the current stage, one AbortController per tool. When the mission advances it registers only the tools new to that stage, leaving existing registrations (and any call in flight) untouched, and agents learn about the additions through toolchange . Chrome's DevTools WebMCP pane shows the list, the per-tool call counters and the invocation log. Progressive disclosure. Stage A is registered on load; Stage B appears once a mission exists; Stage C once every required slot has a pick. Within a mission a stage only ever advances, so a tool is never pulled out from under a call in flight. The agent only ever sees tools that make sense right now. Shared state. Missions live server-side (Next.js route handlers on Vercel, Upstash Redis). Because agents call tools in parallel, writes are compare-and-set with retry, and anything slow (planning, merchant search, LLM re-ranking) runs outside the mutation. The board polls and the human's edits are stamped with a cursor the agent's mission_delta is computed from. Merchants. Cross-merchant discovery uses Shopify's public Global Catalog MCP (with a self-hosted agent profile) and per-store Storefront MCP for details and carts; no store setup, no credentials. A planner and re-ranker run on a small OpenAI model with strict JSON schemas. Same tools, any browser. A built-in agent panel drives the same tool table through the OpenAI Responses API. Where the browser provides WebMCP it runs each call through document.modelContext.executeTool , so Chrome's DevTools logs the built-in agent's calls exactly like an external agent's; elsewhere it calls the tool's execute directly. It makes the page work in browsers without WebMCP and gives us a deterministic harness ( pnpm harness ), probe ( pnpm probe ) and co-driving check ( pnpm g3 ) whose outputs are the only source of the numbers we quote. Abuse limits. Agent steps, mission mutations and mission creation are rate-limited per IP (Upstash), with a kill switch for the judging window; pnpm probe --burst exercises the limit. Guardrails for careless agents. Every mutation is validated on the server and every error names the valid ids and the tool to call next; create_mission on a board with picks needs replace: true ; a re-plan keeps what the person locked or chose; carts are cleared the moment a pick changes and prepare_checkout refuses while a required slot is empty; merchant_domain is allowlisted before the server contacts any host; tool stages only ever advance within a mission. pnpm misuse drives all of it out of order through document.modelContext.executeTool in headless Chrome (36 checks). Challenges we ran into Agents call tools in parallel. ChatGPT fired every search_products at once and a read-modify-write race dropped candidates. Fix: compare-and-set writes in Redi

title: Acorn
pitch: Acorn is the academic planning workspace built for Stanford. You and your agent set goals, research courses, and track your progress together, for every quarter till graduation.
about_excerpt: Acorn is the academic planning workspace built for Stanford. You and your agent set goals, research courses, and track your progress together, for every quarter till graduation. Like Comment Story Updates The landing page. Julia's September: move-in, auditions, club meetings, and the start of classes. Todos are labeled by who added them, her or her agent. The week view. Her agent picked these sections around ballet rehearsals and her Friday work-study shift. The academics page: the autumn plan, her AP credit, and search over the full catalog. A course's real sections, each lecture paired with a discussion. Times can be corrected by her or her agent. Her clubs, with meeting times that show up on the calendar. The scratchpad: her quick notes and the goal her agent structured into milestones. The activity log. Each entry shows whether she or her agent made the change. Every time I switched between building something technical and researching what I need to do to prepare for freshman year at Stanford, while using the same frontier models at my disposal, I was hit in the face with a sharp divergence in performance. The same model that built an entire secure backend meant to withstand ten thousand users and connected it to a frontend without trouble (the CORS errors alone took me hours just 3 years ago), was reduced to a useless machine awkwardly misclicking around Stanford Axess trying to retrieve any piece of information at all. It searched from stale sources and did not know what to do with broken links. It misclicked and accidentally closed browsing sessions. It forgot everything about me in a matter of a few messages. I saw that consumer AI was nowhere near the frontier I knew in development, and the problem was context and browsing. Which is why, when I heard that WebMCP, a concept I had heard of but never seen working, was actually moving forward, I was thrilled. This hackathon came at the right time, and with it the idea to finally streamline the process I had been struggling with all summer: pointing frontier intelligence at possibly the most important planning task of my adult life. I named it Acorn, an homage to the infamous Stanford squirrels that were darting around during my visit. Acorn is as much a context layer as it is a website. When we build with agents, we use markdown files in the repo so the model can carry goals, constraints, and decisions from one session to the next. Acorn acts as that durable context window, a version of which the average person could meaningfully interact with. You can talk to your agent and have it write things down, or scratch a half-formed idea into the pad yourself and have your agent make sense of it later. Either way you are both working on the same workspace: your goals, your notes on frosh-friendly classes, and the professors who you think might give you a research opportunity -- all forming a plan built collaboratively. The page registers 22 tools with the browser using WebMCP, giving an agent human-level control over the workspace. Everything a student would otherwise keep in their head has a place: a calendar that shows your actual week, a plan for each quarter, the clubs you joined with their meetings, the credit you brought in from AP or IB, and a scratchpad for any other tidbits of information. The official Stanford catalog with 15,618 courses across 256 departments is included in the workspace. So when you ask your agent for a schedule, it makes use of the actual options: it remembers the hours you blocked off, plans around your club meetings, picks lecture times that fit your week, and puts the result on your calendar. The biggest question was how much to hardcode and how much to leave to the user's agent. An empty catalog is useless, but a catalog nobody can correct goes stale when anything changes. I ended up shipping verified reference data as the base and allowing edits on top of it. The student or the agent can amend (or add) any course, club, or activity. To test all of this, I spun up Fable agents that played the students, each of them using the agentic workflow of Codex to plan their quarters collaboratively. Those rounds, and then planning my own autumn in the app, caught a number of problems. For a while the catalog had every lecture at Stanford and not a single discussion section, because my importer failed to scrape them. The same goal once appeared twice on the scratchpad, one copy with a milestone checklist and one without, because onboarding and the agent each saved it their own way. Saves took 32 seconds at one point, because every save was carrying ten full copies of the workspace as undo history, so I capped the history and saves dropped to three seconds. And once the app said a change was saved when it never reached the server, so saves now confirm against the server with an idempotency key. Through this, I learned that the divergence I kept running into had nothing to do with model capability. Once the browsing was replaced with webMCP tools and the context was durable, the same model that built my backend planned my quarter just as well. Next, I want to ship a barebones version of the workspace, giving a user's agent more autonomy over it, allowing it to research any university and build its catalog, programs, and clubs from official sources, so Acorn can extend beyond Stanford to any college, and past college to any long-running task where a person and their agent need one shared memory. The squirrels I named this after bury acorns all over campus and find them again months later, and that is what I want from planning with an agent: whatever the two of you put down, you come back and it is still there.  Inspiration 
 The main inspiration making this project is nowadays job market situation. To be more precise, AI dramatically influenced how employers look to the job market. And many jobs became less demanding leading people to loose their jobs. And of course they are pushed to change their job, what they do and learn completely another sphere. But the process of changing the job, learning new things becoming more and more confusing as there are more technologies, instruments are being used day-by-day. That's why people try to use AI to get help in what to learn. But standard generative AI chat bots that provides the pathway, information in plain text format can not be as visual as people can need and thats why they keep being in confuse. But this project - my WebMCP solves this problem.
 
 What it does 
 The name itself is Career Switch MCP, however there is a big future behind it. Its only related to career only for now, in the future, I am planning to make it broader - giving AI agents hands to visualize what they are trying to explain - anything. So,... the application provides an interactive, visual skill tree canvas powered by the WebMCP protocol. Instead of reading plain text guides, users can interact with dynamic skill nodes. Browser-based AI agents directly invoke registered WebMCP tools (`build_skill_tree` and `highlight_skill_gaps`) to render customized roadmaps and instantly highlight missing skills or prerequisites in red.
 
 How we built it 

 Frontend Framework: * Next.js and React for rendering the core web application.
 Canvas Visualization: * React Flow to display interactive nodes, edges, and animated connections. 

 
 AI Integration:** Native WebMCP API ( document.modelContext ) to expose web-level tools directly to AI agents. 
 Styling & UI:** Tailwind CSS for modern design and clean devtools inspector layouts. 
 Deployment:** Hosted live on Vercel.
## Challenges we ran into
Implementing smooth integration with the newly introduced WebMCP browser protocols. 
 Dynamically mapping unstructured AI context calls into organized graph node structures in React Flow without causing state conflicts. 
 Synchronizing visual highlight states (skill gaps) seamlessly between WebMCP tool execution logs and the UI.
## Accomplishments that we're proud of
Successfully building a fully working prototype that bridges browser-native AI agents with visual UI canvases. 
 Creating an intuitive user experience that transforms confusing text into an actionable visual roadmap. 
 Registering functional tools inside document.modelContext that AI agents can invoke in real time.
## What we learned
Deepened my understanding of browser-native AI protocols and WebMCP tool registration. 
 Learned how to effectively optimize React Flow graphs for real-time state updates triggered by agent actions. 
 Mastered structuring project documentation and submission workflows under strict hackathon deadlines.
## What's next for Career switch WebMCP
While currently focused on career pathing, the long-term vision is to make this platform completely generalizable. I am planning to expand the WebMCP integration to allow AI agents to visually render anything - from complex software architecture diagrams and decision trees to educational mind maps.

title: Duet
pitch: Plan the room with your agent. You pin the judgment calls; your agent solves feuds, diets and table math through 25 WebMCP tools — live, on one shared floor plan.
about_excerpt: Plan the room with your agent. You pin the judgment calls; your agent solves feuds, diets and table math through 25 WebMCP tools — live, on one shared floor plan. Like Comment Story Updates Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Seating a room is a two-brain problem. One brain holds context no form can capture: who is divorced, which sponsor is feuding with whom, which aunt needs to sit near the exit. The other has to satisfy a combinatorial pile of constraints: table capacities, conflicts, introductions, dietary needs, accessibility, company-mixing rules, and table balance. Humans are great at the first and bad at the second. Agents are the opposite. Before WebMCP, neither interface worked well. A drag-and-drop floor plan is a terrible surface for an agent to operate through pixels, while moving the task into chat throws away the human's spatial judgment. Duet lets both work on the same live state, in the same tab: the human drags, pins, and visually evaluates the room while the agent uses structured tools such as seat_guest , add_constraint , set_group_rule , and a real constraint solver. How it creates a better user experience Duet gives human-agent collaboration an explicit contract, enforced in code. Pins are law. Any guest placed manually is pinned 📌. The solver plans around those decisions, and agent tools are refused if they attempt to move or remove a pinned guest. Agents propose; humans decide. The preferred agent tool, propose_arrangement , does not mutate the room. It displays the reasoning and complete move list first. Only the human can Accept or Dismiss it. The tool surface follows human attention. Selecting a table dynamically exposes table-scoped tools such as seat_at_selected_table and clear_selected_table . Deselecting it removes them. The agent's available capabilities therefore reflect what the human is currently focused on. Everything is visible and reversible. Agent actions appear as a violet cursor on the board, every action enters a shared activity feed labeled ✳ agent or ● you, and undo/redo works across both human and agent actions. What becomes possible — together — that wasn't before Load a 120-guest fundraising gala. The human manually places two important guests, pinning them in place. The agent records "press away from the board", applies "maximum two people from the same company per table", and proposes a complete arrangement for the remaining 118 guests. The solver honors every constraint without touching the human's pins. The human reviews the proposal visually and accepts it in one click. Create a conflict deliberately and Duet pans to the affected table, identifies who conflicts and why, and lets the agent call explain_seating to justify individual placements. Then ask: "Give me the caterer's brief." The agent calls export_plan and returns dietary counts by table. That loop — human judgment steering an agent and a constraint solver through conversation, directly on a shared visual surface — is what WebMCP makes possible. The same engine includes five scenarios: wedding, fundraising gala, corporate networking dinner, office seating, and classroom seating. How we implemented WebMCP Duet exposes 21 base tools through document.modelContext.registerTool , covering: guest and table CRUD pair constraints with notes group spread and cluster rules solver execution arrangement proposals pins dietary reports Markdown export template loading undo explain_seating get_activity_log , allowing a returning agent to understand what the human changed while it was away It also exposes 4 dynamic selection-scoped tools registered and removed with AbortController as the user's selection changes. The WebMCP tool surface itself therefore mirrors the human's current focus. Tool results return structured JSON, including the conflicts an action would create, so agents can reason about consequences before modifying state. Guardrails are enforced at the tool layer: pinned guests cannot be moved by agents, and propose_arrangement is explicitly presented as the preferred workflow so agents default to human review rather than silent mutation. The constraint solver is dependency-free and combines greedy assignment, local search, targeted repair, and three-way relocation. A 120-guest room solves in roughly 75 ms while respecting pins, pair constraints, group rules, accessibility requirements, and table balance. Duet is built with React, Vite, and TypeScript and has no backend. The entire collaborative state lives in the browser tab — exactly where WebMCP operates. title: SheetCanvas
pitch: A spreadsheet canvas ChatGPT can drive directly; no clicking, just tell it what to build
about_excerpt: A spreadsheet canvas ChatGPT can drive directly; no clicking, just tell it what to build Like 2 Comment Story Updates GIF SheetCanvas WebMCP Demo SheetCanvas.com Inspiration The real problem is that humans and agents don't have a place to actually work together on data. Ask ChatGPT to analyze something and it hands you a chart or a table inline; but that artifact is disposable. It lives in the scroll of one conversation, not anywhere sticky. Close the chat, come back tomorrow with a follow-up, and you're re-asking the same questions from scratch instead of building on what was already figured out. Existing BI tools don't fix this either, they were built for a person driving a mouse, and none of them have caught up to a workflow where an agent is a first-class collaborator rather than a text generator bolted on the side. Also most people isn’t good at data analysis, the tools has the data analysis knowledge built in, to write the best query, chose the suitable chart to tell the correct story. I built SheetCanvas to be that place: a canvas where a human and an agent cooperate on data analysis in real time, locally, the state persists, it's inspectable, and it's shared, instead of the agent's output vanishing back into a chat transcript the moment the conversation ends. I was building toward WebMCP specifically, before it existed. This tool is designed for an agent to drive the canvas directly, the same way a person does — and before document.modelContext was a real, shipped API, I got there with a workaround: a hand-rolled remote MCP server over a WebSocket, so an MCP-capable client like Claude Desktop could already act on the canvas. WebMCP isn't a feature I bolted on for this challenge; it's the primitive I was always building toward, and this challenge was the first chance to stop working around its absence. How I built it The reason this was cheap to build rather than a rewrite: SheetCanvas already had exactly one tool registry — 26 tools, defined once with zod schemas, covering everything from createSheet and setCells to chart creation and live connector queries — feeding a single executor. Three doors already used it: a person clicking around the UI, an in-app Copilot, and the WebSocket-based remote MCP server that had been standing in for WebMCP until it existed. WebMCP became a fourth door over that same registry — not a parallel build, but the door the other three had been waiting for. Concretely: document.modelContext.registerTool wraps every existing tool, converting its zod schema to JSON Schema with the identical call the backend already used, so the two doors can't quietly drift apart. A state-aware gating layer decides which of the 26 tools are registered at any moment — no point advertising queryConnection before a connection exists — keyed on durable facts (does a sheet exist? a note? a connector?) rather than conversation shape, since a tool that vanishes between the agent listing tools and calling one is an unrecoverable error, not a retry. A registration lifecycle manager reconciles the tool set on every relevant state change: diffed, coalesced, debounced, with one AbortController per registered tool (unregistering in WebMCP is only aborting a controller — there's no unregisterTool ). All four doors — clicks, Copilot, remote MCP, and now WebMCP — now route through one shared dispatch point, tagged by origin. That's what let me add a single activity trail that watches every tool call regardless of which door it came through, and a rewind control: "undo back to here," warning inline if it would also discard edits you made yourself in the meantime. Safety was the design question I spent the most time on, because there is no confirm() for an agent to hit — Chrome's own docs still reference a requestUserInteraction() primitive that was removed from the spec before it ever shipped. So instead of a dialog, safety became three structural properties: every tool is correctly annotated ( readOnlyHint , untrustedContentHint on anything returning warehouse- or CSV-authored text back to the model), every mutation is undoable, and every mutation is visible in the trail as it happens — plus ChatGPT's own confirmation on top. title: RabbitHole
pitch: Dense documents are hard to read, even in your own field. Rabbithole lets you zoom in on the parts you don't understand and the explaining is done by your personal assistant aware about your context.
about_excerpt: Dense documents are hard to read, even in your own field. Rabbithole lets you zoom in on the parts you don't understand and the explaining is done by your personal assistant aware about your context. Like Comment Story Updates history of pages you read your profile, you can edit for more fine tuned experience home page history of concepts you drilled in another example of drilling down further on a crispr related doc example of reading a text, drilling down Inspiration I read a lot - articles, papers, code, engineering spec, wiki pages and so much more. And I love going down rabbit holes, which there are many of when I'm reading dense documents or text in domains I'm not proficient in. So very often, I start at something, have a dozen open tabs a few hours later plus a long thread with an AI, and have lost track of whatever I was reading in the first place. I wanted to fix this workflow.You know how fun it is to read and figure something out with a smarter friend who also knows your gaps? Everything gets so much easier. Well, that's the experience I wanted to create. I'm also trying to imagine a future where web feels more collaborative, where you and your agent do things together, like partners. As agents become more personal, I don't just want them to be doing things for me on some remote cloud machine. I want them to be ambiently present with me, across every surface. Where RabbitHole fits If we divide reading into two axes - x axis - the granularity you read the text in - from "hand it over for a summary" to "every word" y axis - the amount of personalized help you have while reading(could be human but let's focus on AI here) RabbitHole sits on top right. It's immensely useful for cases where you want to actually read, understand or skim over a piece, than only working with a derivative of the original text(summaries or questions asked on top). There's a image of this linked in Readme that gets the point across better than words. Why WebMCP fits The key thing is that the assistant should not be inside the reading app. It should be your assistant, whichever one that is, and the app should be a place it can work. WebMCP is exactly the interface for that: any agent with a browser can find the page's tools and call them. What it does True to its name, it lets you go as deep as you want into anything, starting from something you want to read and understand. There is a nice sliding pane UI(Andy Matuschak's style). You start with pasting the text or link for what you want to read and asking your agent to help you with reading alongside. Your personal agent(codex, claude, openclaw, hermes, littlebird, anything that supports WebMCP) highlights the terms and parts that are non trivial "for you". A biologist probably doesn't know "apophenia"; a psychologist probably doesn't know "Cas9". So whatever terms are likely unfamiliar to you gets highlighted. But you're not limited to them, you can also pick anything else or even multiple sentences, and drill into that. Everything you drill into opens a pane on the right. From there you can keep elaborating on that thing, or go deeper into something else and open more panes. Every explanation, elaboration, and answer takes into account both the context it sits in and you — your goals, your familiarity with the concepts, other things you've been doing that might connect. You can set an explicit goal for why you're reading. Maybe you're reading papers on homeschooling to decide the best course for your child, or researching vocal technique to sing better. Knowing the goal, on top of everything else about your life, lets the agent explain things even better. It stores the concepts you drilled into so they're easy to revisit. Once you have it in your agent's memory, you can also just ask it - "open this thing in RabbitHole". How I built it Mostly vibing with my coding agent, what feels right, the direction I want, features I find joy and delight in on top of utility, thinking hard about balancing minimalism with power. The design inspiration is https://notes.andymatuschak.org . I've used this type of view for my personal notes in Obsidian as well and always liked it as a good UX to drill down without losing track. Challenges I ran into Duplex communication(app being able to invoke the agent on demand). I don't like the UX of chatting with agent to reactively make WebMCP tool calls. I wanted to focus on the actual reading for the most part, so I had to figure out ways to make it duplex. I tried an idea of having a long async call, sort of like long polling. But it didn't work as cleanly on its own due to client timeout. So I added polling asking the agent to sleep and check if there are no things to process in the queue, which works well. Accomplishments that I'm proud of The UI, the duplex trick, and honestly just building something I'm going to use often. I'll probably spend even more time on making it good lol(yeah there is an xkcd for it https://xkcd.com/1205/ 🥲). What I learned The web can be so much more collaborative than it is. I like WebMCP - it's directionally right, though still missing some important things. The usual demos of "filling in web forms" don't even scratch the surface of what's possible. What's next for RabbitHole Support for more types of inputs - PDFs for e.g. More software eng specific coverage - PRs for example. URL based state of the whole path which others can open and see the explanation in terms they would understand best. Login and server side storage to carry what you're reading and concepts you're interested in across sessions and AI agents. More proactivity - capture your attention and pass it to the agent. If you're lingering on a paragraph, the agent can proactively offer you help. Suggested actions — "add this to our repo" while reading an engineering blog, or "add this to your slides" if it relates to a presentation you're working on. title: xAgent.ID
pitch: A website and an AI agent onboard that site together: the agent assembles a verified install plan, the owner approves it in the page, and the commands never leave the owner's hands.
about_excerpt: A website and an AI agent onboard that site together: the agent assembles a verified install plan, the owner approves it in the page, and the commands never leave the owner's hands. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Live xagent.id. Every card on screen is the deployed page: real companies, real public evidence, nothing claimed on their behalf. The target published no public proof, so it stays pending. Missing evidence is never converted into a pass. After the click: four commands, bound to a digest of the exact plan on screen, handed to the owner. The page executes none. Machine speed, human authority. Live at xagent.id/agent, with a command and an expected result for every claim in VERIFY.md. One task, three conditions. Without WebMCP: 134,552 bytes over 9 requests. With it: 6,460 over 2. Wall clock: inconclusive. Asked for the install bundle before approval, the page refuses: human_approval_required. The bundle does not exist yet. Chrome's own WebMCP panel, in DevTools, listing this page's eight tools registered with document.modelContext.registerTool. Approval is a real browser-trusted click on a visible control. No tool parameter and no page script can assert it instead. Inspiration Onboarding a website to an identity service is a negotiation, not a page of text. It needs the current release, the exact target host, the modules the site is granting, the files that will be written, a rollback path, and a human decision in the middle. We watched both halves of that fail. An agent reading our rendered HTML could only guess at the contract, so it stalled or invented commands. A human owner opened the docs, copied four commands into a terminal, and hoped the version, the host and the grants lined up. Neither party had what it needed, and the one step that genuinely required a person, deciding, was the step that copy-paste quietly skipped. WebMCP suggested the fix. Not "let the agent click the buttons", but: let the page state its contract as tools, and keep the human decision a decision. What it does xagent.id registers eight top-level tools with document.modelContext.registerTool, so a WebMCP-capable agent can onboard a website together with its owner. inspect_onboarding reports the tool surface, the authority limits and the current step. Read-only. preview_agent_id previews the public Agent ID card for a target website. get_install_plan loads the target-bound install manifest, without commands. choose_verification_method selects public-file domain proof. request_owner_approval asks the human for a visible decision, and waits. prepare_install_bundle returns the approved commands for the human to run. verify_installation reads independent public evidence for the target. get_onboarding_status reports the current onboarding state. Read-only. Only those two carry readOnlyHint, because only those two change nothing. The shape of the journey is the point. The agent does the assembly: release identity, module grants, declared write paths, and a digest of the exact plan. The page shows the owner which files will change and which permissions are being granted. The owner approves on a visible control. Only then does prepare_install_bundle return commands, and it returns them to the owner. The page executes none of them. The agent executes none of them. Ask for the bundle before approval and you get human_approval_required. Not a warning. A refusal. Why WebMCP is the right fit here: the trust boundary already exists, and this keeps it intact. The tools live in the page the owner already trusts, so there is no connector to install, no API key to paste, and no third party standing between an owner and their own website. The agent gets the real contract, bound to one canonical HTTPS origin, instead of its own reading of the rendered page. What people and agents can now do together that neither could do alone: the agent assembles a plan a human would find tedious and error-prone, the exact release, the exact host, the module grants, the files that will be written, and a digest binding all of it. The owner supplies the one thing an agent must never supply, which is the decision. Before this, the owner did the assembly by hand and the decision collapsed into copy-paste. An agent alone still cannot finish, and that is the design, not a limitation. How we built it The tools are one vanilla JavaScript module shipped by the page itself, at /assets/webmcp-onboarding.js. No build step, no framework, and nothing for the owner to install. Approval is the part we spent the most care on. It requires a browser-generated trusted activation on the enabled, visible wizard control, and completion of the permissions-to-install transition on screen. There is no public approval mutator and no writable exported state, so no tool parameter and no page script can assert approval on the owner's behalf. Editing the target, changing the manifest, or a failed refresh all revoke it. For evidence we built two harnesses. The first walks the same task three ways, human, agent without WebMCP, and agent with WebMCP, and aborts the entire run if any request returns anything other than 200. The second drives a real Chrome over the DevTools Protocol with the WebMCP testing flag enabled, discovering tools through document.modelContext.getTools and giving approval with real mouse events at the control's own coordinates. The submission video is that second harness running on a clean cloud VM against the deployed site, with Chrome's own WebMCP panel open in DevTools counting the calls as they happen. Every frame is a recording, and the uncut source recordings are published alongside the film. Challenges we ran into A microtask that arrived too early. Approval worked in our tests and never worked in Chrome. The browser runs a microtask checkpoint between event listeners, so our approval landed while the page was still mid-transition and was discarded. The fix revalidates every precondition on a real timer instead of trusting a single moment. Our tests had passed because they dispatched listeners in an order no browser actually uses; the regression test now reproduces the real ordering. Feature detection that lied. executeTool kept failing with "Failed to parse input arguments" until we found that arguments must be passed as a JSON string rather than an object. A release pipeline that had never once succeeded. Deploying the fix meant first repairing six separate faults in it, ending with a skaffold key that is spelled cloudrun and not cloudRun. Until that was done the correct code existed only on our own machines, which is not the same thing as shipped. Measuring honestly when the numbers did not cooperate. Our wall-clock ranges overlapped between conditions, so we could not claim a speed win. Saying so turned out to be harder than not measuring at all. Accomplishments that we're proud of The refusal works, in a real browser, on the live site. Eight tools discovered, prepare_install_bundle refused with human_approval_required before approval, four commands returned after a real click, and none of them executed by the page. That run is recorded and published. The measured result is specific. To reach the same target-bound install plan, an agent following our own documented public trail takes in 134,552 bytes over 9 requests. Through WebMCP it is 6,460 bytes over 2. That is 20.83 times less material and 4.5 times fewer round trips, and both figures came out identical on every run. What we did not measure is stated as plainly as what we did. Wall clock is reported as inconclusive, because the ranges overlap. Human duration is reported as not measured, because no participant was timed. A test in the repository fails if either one is ever quietly converted into a number. Every claim in our public README has a command and an expected result in VERIFY.md. A reviewer never has to take our word for anything. What we learned The interesting question is not what an agent can do. It is what it must not do. The value of this integration is concentrated almost entirely in the one call that refuses. Everything else is convenience; that one is the product. Works in tests and works in a browser are different claims, and the gap between them was a single microtask. We now treat any test that models browser event ordering as suspect until it has been reproduced against a real browser. Honest measurement is a design constraint, not a reporting step. Once we decided that nothing unmeasured could appear as a number, we had to build the harness so that not measured was a value it could carry all the way to the screen. That changed how we built, not just how we wrote it up. A page can hand an agent a contract instead of prose, and it costs one module. The hard part was never the tool surface. What's next for xAgent.ID — WebMCP onboarding Measure the human path properly. Our comparison paths are scripted, not observed users.  1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 I spend a lot of time playing card games online, but learning them can be frustrating. Tutorials are not always available, translations can be unclear, and most lessons force players through a fixed sequence of prescribed actions. They also make it difficult to revisit a specific situation or experiment with alternative moves. 

 I wanted a more interactive way to learn existing card games, recreate scenarios, and design new games with an agent that can explain the state, suggest actions, and participate in the simulation. 

 What it does 

 How I built it 

 Playing Cards Simulator exposes WebMCP tools that let an AI agent create a custom card game from an XState-compatible finite-state machine definition or launch an existing game such as Blackjack, War, Go Fish, Crazy Eights, Euchre, Gin Rummy, Bullshit, or Texas Hold'em. 

 The agent can inspect the current game state, explain what is happening, highlight available controls, coach the player through the next action, wait for the player's input, and act as a bot or dealer. This makes tutorials adaptive instead of forcing every player through the same fixed sequence. 

 The app is built with Next.js, TypeScript, React, XState, and WebMCP. XState provides a predictable model for phases, turns, actions, rewards, and transitions, while WebMCP exposes tools for creating sessions, reading state, guiding players, and performing simulated actions. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 The hardest part was designing a general game model that could support both predefined and agent-generated card games. The tools also needed to stay synchronized with the browser session while handling navigation, stale connections, turn order, hidden information, and invalid actions safely. The latency was unbarely and the UX of the user nudging the ai via the agent chat every turn was awkward. 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 I built one simulator that supports both a catalog of familiar games and custom games defined by an agent. The same interface can teach rules, recreate a specific situation, guide a player interactively, and run bots or dealers without relying on a rigid tutorial script. I thought of the tool which waits for user input making the process fully immersive. 

 What I learned 

 Finite-state machines are a strong foundation for agent-controlled games because they make valid actions and transitions explicit. I also learned that effective agent guidance requires more than reading state: the agent needs tools to explain, highlight, pause for input, and act within clearly defined boundaries. 

 What's next for Playing Cards Simulator 

 Next, I want to expand the game catalog, improve custom game validation, add richer animations, and make tutorials more responsive to each player's choices. I also plan to improve session persistence and make it easier to share custom games and specific learning scenarios. I would love to repurpose this for RTS or create a DND game where the agent is the game master.

title: CargoMesh
pitch: Autonomous Agentic Freight Orchestration for Cross-Border B2B Logistics
about_excerpt: Autonomous Agentic Freight Orchestration for Cross-Border B2B Logistics Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Moving heavy freight across Latin America is complex and fragmented. Shippers juggle multiple carrier portals, emails, spreadsheets, and phone calls just to verify route coverage, check truck capacity, get rate quotes, and confirm bookings. Traditional automation relies on fragile web scraping or custom APIs that smaller carriers cannot maintain. We asked: what if carrier websites could directly publish typed, structured capabilities to an authorized browser agent through the open WebMCP standard? CargoMesh makes this possible. What it does CargoMesh is an agent-native B2B freight orchestration platform: Canonical Intake : Shippers define or load freight requests (e.g., FR-1042 Callao, Peru → Santiago, Chile). Dynamic Discovery : Discovers 0..N compatible carriers from an open registry without hardcoded lists. Native WebMCP Execution : The browser agent visits carrier portals (Andes, Inca, Pacific) and consumes 5 structured tools via document.modelContext : check_service_coverage , check_capacity , quote_freight , book_freight , and get_provider_booking_status . Result Bridge : Validates and persists commercial responses without client-side data tampering. Deterministic BALANCED Engine : Scores offers mathematically (25% cost, 25% reliability, 20% transit, 10% availability, 10% route experience, 10% org history). Recovery : If a carrier rejects a booking, CargoMesh offers authorized alternatives (e.g., Andes rejection → Inca confirmed). How we built it Frontend & Provider Portals : Next.js 15, React 19, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet for explicitly planned route corridors, and EN/ES support. WebMCP Runtime : Browser-side document.modelContext.registerTool with strict JSON schemas, abort handling, and tool cleanup on provider navigation. Backend & Security : Supabase PostgreSQL, Supabase Auth, RLS, and optimistic concurrency through draft_version . Result Bridge & Auditing : Server-side validation of tool envelopes, origin/classification, request correlation, and commercial responses. The Judge Drawer exposes auditable inputs, outputs, timestamps, and origin evidence. Challenges we ran into Separating browser execution from database truth : WebMCP tools execute in browser memory; we built the Result Bridge to validate signatures before persisting commercial offers. Dynamic 0..N provider identity : Preserving exact matchingServiceId across dynamic navigation without breaking idempotency. Clean context management : Ensuring active WebMCP tools are completely removed from document.modelContext when navigating away from a provider. Technical honesty : Avoiding artificial GPS simulation; planned corridors are explicitly labeled as planned references. Accomplishments that we're proud of Native WebMCP tool surfaces through document.modelContext . A deterministic, explainable BALANCED ranking for the canonical FR-1042 fixture: Andes 89, Inca 84, Pacific 72. Repository and client-bundle checks with no detected secret exposure, plus RLS-protected organization-scoped access. A demonstrated recovery flow: Andes rejection, explicit human selection of Inca, then confirmed replacement booking. What we learned We proved that WebMCP fundamentally shifts how B2B platforms interact: websites can expose clean, agentic tool surfaces without breaking the visual human interface, eliminating the need for brittle web scraping. What's next for CargoMesh Onboarding additional real-world carriers across the Pan-American corridor. Integrating independently hosted provider origins with external WebMCP adapters. Multi-modal freight orchestration (maritime and air freight handoffs). title: Live Canvas
pitch: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface.
about_excerpt: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration For as much as marketers have optimized for conversion, they haven't been able to cut through the number one reason that people leave open carts. they're not ready to buy. It had just happened to me while shopping for a microphone: I started at one site, then realized I needed more information to determine which was going to be the best fit. What if the shopping interface could have met me where I was at--researching the options, ranking the matches, explaining its rationale, and then designing a search result layout to fit its conclusions? That's just one glimpse of how web-interfaces of the future will adapt to their users' needs through a Live Canvas. What it does Each demo walks you through a conventional user interface, and then cordons off a bounded portion of it as WebMCP to redesign (the Live Canvas) The Storefront demo lets the agent curate the search results with a toolbox of approved card presets and badges. This constrained design is a good fit for the untrusted nature of the public internet, keeping users safe from XSS attacks. The Dashbord demo scales the idea up by giving you an entirely blank page. It imagine how the future of CRM / ERP dashboards might function. Prompt the agent to onboard you, collaborate on a vision with the agent as you would with your analytics team, and the end result is an entirely personal dashboard of controls, visualizations and reports. The Distribution demo scales the idea outwards by asking whether you distribute a Live Canvas as part of conventional component libraries. It demonstrates what a future Datatable component could be, with the ability to generate bespoke reports and save them to your browser - all without backend engineering or ai-vendor lock-in. How we built it The architecture north star is "agent composition, application execution". The application exposes its UI primitives through WebMCP. The agent supplies a composition, and then the live canvas renders that composition using application-owned components. This solution prevents data from leaking out of the organization's security boundary, and also prevents token bloat. Challenges we ran into and accomplishments that we're proud of There are two large challenges that required creativity: The largest challenge was discoverability. WebMCP is not bidirectional: an agent can invoke tools, but there's no mechanism for the website to initiate a conversation. The past 30 years of the web have trained users for the affordance of buttons and forms. I built a new set of visible prompts and verbs to communicate to surface the new modality which was an interesting accomplishment, but does highlight an apparent shortcoming in the standard. The second challenge is the built-in approval flow of agentic browsers. ChatGPT would auto-deny requests to access the user's simulated library to make recommendations, e.g. In the short term, this is solved with instructional text to ask for permission in advance. However, what WebMCP needs is a built in consent layer where tools are tied to required consent artifacts. What we learned WebMCP shows great potential to break interfaces out of the "ai chatbot jail". What's next for Live Canvas The most likely next step is to select an existing open-source component library and use it to build the first end-to-end WebMCP UI framework. That would turn the Live Canvas from just a demo pattern into a production-hardened implementation. AgentReady turns any public website into something AI agents can actually use, with cited answers, capability discovery, and safe, permissioned actions.
