 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 The web was built for people, but more and more of it will be used by software agents. Today, an agent visiting a website often has to guess where the useful information is, fetch pages one at a time, and deal with JavaScript-rendered content or inconsistent navigation. 

 That creates a basic problem: websites may be readable to humans but still difficult for agents to understand and use reliably. 

 I wanted to build the missing layer between websites and agents. Instead of asking every agent to build its own crawler, search system, and integration for every website, AgentReady gives sites a standard way to expose their content and capabilities. 

 What it does 

 AgentReady turns any public website into an agent-ready interface. 

 A user can submit a URL and AgentReady crawls the site, extracts the useful content, generates llms.txt , and creates a hosted MCP and /ask interface. Agents can then: 

 
 Discover indexed sites 
 Ask questions and receive cited answers 
 Inspect a site's capabilities and freshness 
 Create grounded, read-only action plans 
 Submit new sites for indexing 
 Refresh existing sites 
 Provide feedback on answer quality 
 

 If an agent asks about a site that has not been indexed yet, AgentReady indexes it automatically and continues with the requested workflow. This removes an unnecessary setup step. 

 The project also includes a safe sandbox for previewing agent actions. Any real side effect requires explicit confirmation and a connected action endpoint. 

 How I built it 

 AgentReady is built as a hosted web application with a Next.js frontend and API layer. Supabase stores sites, pages, chunks, manifests, action plans, receipts, and telemetry. 

 The indexing pipeline supports normal HTML sites, documentation sites, JavaScript-rendered applications, and sites that already publish llms.txt . Content is cleaned, split into chunks, embedded, and stored for retrieval. 

 The answer layer uses retrieval over the indexed content and returns the source pages used for each answer. The MCP server is available over HTTP, with a local npm bridge and CLI for terminal workflows. 

 I also built capability manifests so an agent can understand what a website exposes before planning an interaction. Plans contain the intended steps, evidence, risks, confirmation requirements, and a durable receipt. 

 Codex (GPT-5.6) was used throughout development as an engineering partner. It helped explore the product direction, design the architecture, implement the indexing and MCP workflows, debug production issues, write migrations and documentation, review the user experience, and validate changes before deployment. The final product decisions, testing, and deployment were reviewed and directed by me. 

 The application is deployed on Vercel and is available at agentready.it.com. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 The hardest part was making the system work across very different websites. Some sites have clean server-rendered documentation, while others are JavaScript-heavy or expose very little useful text in their initial HTML. 

 Freshness was another challenge. An answer can be correct when a site is indexed and stale a week later, so I added explicit refresh workflows and freshness metadata. 

 I also had to be careful with the word action. It is easy to make a demo that appears to execute something, but real agent actions need confirmation, validation, idempotency, audit trails, and a way to prove what happened. I designed the action layer around plans, receipts, and signed connectors rather than unrestricted execution. 

 Finally, I had to avoid treating every request as proof of agent traffic. I added better event tracking so I can distinguish indexing, querying, planning, refreshing, and feedback. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 I built and deployed a working product rather than just a prototype screen. 

 AgentReady now has: 

 
 A live indexing and retrieval pipeline 
 A global MCP server with seven tools 
 HTTP and local MCP connection options 
 A CLI for grading, asking, indexing, and refreshing sites 
 Automatic indexing when a workflow needs a site 
 Cited answers grounded in multiple pages 
 Capability manifests for websites 
 Read-only plans with durable receipts 
 WebMCP support for browser-based agents 
 A safe action sandbox with confirmation and connector controls 
 Public documentation, plugins, and a live directory 
 

 AgentReady also indexes itself, so the product can be discovered and queried through its own infrastructure. 

 What I learned 

 Making a website available to agents is not just a matter of adding an API endpoint. Agents need discovery, structure, freshness information, clear schemas, and reliable evidence. 

 I also learned that trust matters as much as capability. Cited answers, explicit plans, confirmation steps, and receipts make the system easier to inspect and safer to use. 

 The MCP server became an important part of the product because it gives agents a simple distribution point. Instead of integrating with every website separately, an agent can connect once and work across many sites. 

 What's next for AgentReady 

 The next step is to make the action layer more useful while keeping it safe. We are starting with first-party sandbox actions, then expanding to customer-owned connectors that agents can call only after explicit approval. 

 We also want to add background indexing, better freshness signals, richer capability schemas, and analytics that show how agents actually discover and use websites. 

 The larger goal is to help create a web where websites are not only readable by people, but also understandable and usable by agents.

title: disaster-safety-web-mcp
pitch: A WebMCP tool server for flood emergencies. Official JP/US/EU hazard feeds, first-principles flood modeling, and flood-aware evacuation routing — mapped, provenance-tagged, and agent-callable.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP tool server for flood emergencies. Official JP/US/EU hazard feeds, first-principles flood modeling, and flood-aware evacuation routing — mapped, provenance-tagged, and agent-callable. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Traditionally, AI agents have struggled during disasters to provide guidance that simultaneously ensures safety and accommodates individual needs. By leveraging WebMCP, an AI agent can dynamically access accurate, real-time disaster information and mapping data while understanding a person’s specific circumstances. Whether someone needs directions to a designated shelter, nearby high ground, or a destination compatible with mobility and transportation constraints, Untitled makes personalized evacuation guidance possible. We were inspired by the opportunity to move beyond one-size-fits-all evacuation orders and deliver practical, potentially life-saving support for each individual. ## What it does Untitled is an AI-powered disaster safety assistant that turns live geographic and emergency data into personalized evacuation guidance. Through WebMCP, the assistant can: Resolve natural-language place names while detecting ambiguous locations. Display flood forecasts and inundation zones on an interactive map. Find official evacuation shelters and classify them as clear, at risk, or unknown. Retrieve active alerts from authoritative agencies. Calculate walking or driving evacuation routes that avoid known flood hazards. Present map information as accessible text for screen readers and environments without WebGL. Rather than simply naming the nearest shelter, Untitled considers whether that shelter and the route leading to it are actually safe. ## How we built it We built Untitled as a TypeScript application running on Bun, with a MapLibre GL JS frontend and a Hono-based backend. The browser registers disaster-response capabilities directly through WebMCP, allowing an AI agent to discover and invoke tools such as geocoding, flood forecasting, shelter search, official-alert retrieval, map control, and evacuation routing. The backend integrates data from sources including the Japan Meteorological Agency, Japan’s Geospatial Information Authority, the US National Weather Service, MeteoAlarm, OpenStreetMap, Open-Meteo, and Copernicus services. Flood- aware routes are calculated using road-network data and dynamic hazard exclusions. We also developed hydrological modeling components for rainfall runoff, terrain-based inundation, river capacity, and flood-risk estimation. Every result carries provenance so the system can distinguish live observations, planning scenarios, cached information, and test fixtures. ## Challenges we ran into The greatest challenge was preventing the system from appearing more certain than its data justified. Disaster information can be delayed, incomplete, ambiguous, or temporarily unavailable, so we designed the application to report uncertainty explicitly instead of silently substituting a potentially misleading answer. Combining datasets was also difficult because each provider uses different geographic resolutions, update schedules, risk scales, and coverage boundaries. Flood forecasting introduced additional complications: some climate datasets are rate-limited, while Copernicus retrievals can take hours and must be managed as resumable jobs rather than ordinary requests. Mapping presented another subtle challenge. Data being present in application state does not necessarily mean it is visible on the rendered map. We therefore test the features that MapLibre actually draws after camera movement has completed. Finally, accessibility required us to create a synchronized text representation of every visual map feature so the experience would remain useful to people using screen readers or devices without WebGL. ## Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that Untitled provides an end-to-end workflow—from a natural-language request to hazard analysis, shelter evaluation, and a flood-aware evacuation route—through tools an AI agent can discover directly in the browser. We are especially proud of the system’s safety boundaries. Official alerts are preserved as attributed source material, ambiguous locations are not silently guessed, unavailable forecasts are not presented as “no danger,” and developer-only controls are completely excluded from the normal user experience. We also built a browser verification suite with 44 checks against the real application. It validates tool registration and invocation, error handling, accessibility, production-mode isolation, and what the map actually renders—not merely what the application intended to display. For Japan’s experimental flood-risk forecast, we achieved 98.5% exact level agreement in evaluated reference areas while documenting the more difficult flood-extent limitations honestly. That distinction reflects a principle that guided the entire project: in disaster response, trustworthy uncertainty is more valuable than impressive but misleading confidence. ## What we learned We learned that connecting an AI agent to live data is only the beginning. Useful disaster guidance requires provenance, freshness checks, spatial reasoning, uncertainty handling, and clear separation between observed hazards and planning scenarios. We also learned that “nearest” rarely means “safest.” A shelter may be close but located inside a hazard zone, and a destination may be safe while the route to it crosses floodwater. Most importantly, we learned that safety systems must test observable outcomes. A successful API response does not prove that a person can see the hazard, understand the warning, or follow the proposed route. Reliability has to be evaluated across the entire experience. ## What’s next for Untitled Next, we want to expand coverage to additional countries and disaster types, including wildfires, earthquakes, landslides, tsunamis, and extreme heat. We also plan to improve personalization for mobility needs, language preferences, family and pet evacuation, vehicle availability, medical requirements, and shelter accessibility. Offline and low-bandwidth support will make the assistant more resilient when communications infrastructure is damaged. What it does This Algorithm Visualizer runs Python algorithms, traces variables, and dynamically visualizes arrays, heaps, graphs, trees, DP tables, maps, sets, and scalars. WebMCP tools let an AI agent inspect the workspace, run code, read frames, control playback, configure visuals, and propose code/input changes for human review. It is a human-agent collaborative app powered by WebMCP. How we built it Built with React, Vite, Monaco Editor, Pyodide, Web Workers, and WebMCP. The app runs Python in an isolated worker, traces execution state, compiles variables into visual scenes, and exposes browser-native agent tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Accomplishments that we're proud of The agent can operate the app through real structured tools instead of screen guessing. Code/input edits are review-gated with red/green diffs, while visual/playback changes can happen dynamically. What we learned WebMCP works best when tools are small, structured, and grounded in the visible UI state. Good agent collaboration needs boundaries as much as capability. What's next for Agentic Algorithm Visualizer Add more automatic structure inference, richer heap/tree/graph layouts, hosted cloud AI providers, and shareable visualization sessions. title: Prompt My Game
pitch: Play a browser game, describe changes to your AI agent, remix and play.
about_excerpt: Play a browser game, describe changes to your AI agent, remix and play. Like Comment Story Updates Real demo: the assistant changes the character to Bobo, then I play the result. Built with KAPLAY; based on KAPLAYGROUND. Ivanna Butterfly Garden: a separately published result at ivanna-butterfly-garden.netlify.app, not a local saved-game sample. Inspiration Making a game is easier to understand when there is already something to play. I wanted a creator to start with a working browser game, describe one change to an AI assistant, and play the new version without first setting up a local development environment. What it does PromptMyGame is my WebMCP-enabled version of KAPLAYGROUND, an existing open-source browser game editor. The live interface still uses the KAPLAYGROUND name. A creator plays the current game, asks for a change in ordinary language, and keeps the editor open while a compatible assistant works. The AI agent can understand the open project, edit it, run it, and return useful checks. The creator remains the creative director and the play tester. The editor also works without an AI assistant. People can play, edit code manually, save projects in their browser, and export portable copies. The open-source foundation KAPLAY is the open-source two-dimensional JavaScript game engine underneath the project. It provides the building blocks for drawing, movement, collision, input, and sound. KAPLAYGROUND is the existing web-based editor for creating, editing, playing, and sharing KAPLAY projects. This entry builds on that editor; I did not create its original engine or editor foundation. KAPLAY grew from Kaboom.js , a JavaScript game engine originally developed by Replit. KAPLAY and KAPLAYGROUND are now maintained by the KAPLAY Team and community contributors. Built-in Crew assets are released under CC0. What I added for the challenge During the challenge period I connected KAPLAYGROUND to WebMCP and added the workflow around it. The editor can identify the exact game an assistant is working on, reject an edit made against an older version, apply related file changes together, and separate different kinds of evidence when it runs a game. What I learned The hard part was defining what a successful result means when a creator, an AI assistant, an editor, and a running game all share the same project.  Inspiration 

 Small and growing suppliers often miss procurement opportunities because finding relevant tenders, understanding requirements, comparing options, and preparing documents can be time-consuming and fragmented. 

 BidLens was inspired by the need to make public procurement more approachable for Zimbabwean suppliers. We wanted to explore what happens when a procurement dashboard is designed for both people and AI agents from the beginning. 

 What it does 

 BidLens helps suppliers discover and evaluate procurement opportunities through a unified intelligence workspace. 

 Users can: 

 
 Search and filter procurement opportunities 
 Review supplier fit scores and eligibility requirements 
 Identify risks and missing documents 
 Compare two or three opportunities 
 Prepare bid workspaces with checklists and notes 
 Track preparation status and bid readiness 
 Browse opportunities and records through paginated interfaces 
 

 BidLens also exposes WebMCP tools that allow an AI agent to work with the application: 

 
 find_opportunities 
 investigate_opportunity 
 compare_opportunities 
 prepare_bid_workspace 
 update_bid_workspace 
 

 Read-only tools can be used directly by an agent. Actions that change application state require explicit human confirmation. 

 How we built it 

 BidLens was built as a React and TypeScript single-page application using Vite, TanStack Router, and Tailwind CSS. The application uses realistic demonstration data modelled on Zimbabwean e-GP procurement structures. 

 The WebMCP integration is implemented through document.modelContext.registerTool() . Each tool has a clear description, structured JSON input schema, and an execution function connected to the application state. 

 The application is deployed on Cloudflare Pages, with SPA fallback routing configured so that nested pages remain accessible when loaded directly. 

 We tested the live application using ChatGPT's desktop in-app browser and Google Chrome with WebMCP testing enabled. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One challenge was translating a complex procurement workflow into a clear experience that would be useful to both experienced suppliers and new users. 

 We also had to connect agent tool execution to React application state while keeping the interface predictable. Browser implementations may provide tool input as either an object or a serialized JSON string, so the tool layer was designed to handle both formats. 

 Another important challenge was deciding which actions should be automatic and which should require human approval. We chose to keep discovery and analysis read-only, while requiring confirmation before creating or updating bid workspaces. 

 Finally, we converted the application into a reliable static deployment while preserving nested routes, responsive layouts, pagination, and WebMCP registration. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 Built a complete procurement intelligence experience rather than a standalone technical demo 
 Implemented five functional WebMCP tools 
 Connected WebMCP tools to live application state 
 Added human confirmation for state-changing actions 
 Deployed a working public application on Cloudflare Pages 
 Verified tool discovery and read-only tool execution in ChatGPT's desktop in-app browser 
 Added responsive layouts and pagination across the application's data-heavy views 
 Published the source code with an open-source license 
 Created a practical use case focused on suppliers and public procurement in Zimbabwe 
 

 What we learned 

 We learned that WebMCP works best when applications expose meaningful, task-oriented tools instead of forcing agents to reproduce every individual user-interface interaction. 

 Structured schemas make agent interactions more reliable, while clear tool descriptions help agents understand when each capability should be used. 

 We also learned that state-changing tools need strong human-in-the-loop safeguards. Agents can help users investigate and prepare decisions, but important procurement actions should remain transparent and explicitly approved. 

 Most importantly, WebMCP allows a website to become an active workspace where humans and agents can collaborate rather than treating AI as a separate chatbot layered on top of the product. 

 What's next for BidLens 

 The next stage is to connect BidLens to authorized live procurement feeds and persistent backend storage. 

 Future improvements include: 

 
 Supplier accounts and team collaboration 
 Real-time procurement notifications 
 Document extraction and compliance checking 
 More advanced tender and supplier matching 
 Audit logs for agent activity and human approvals 
 Persistent bid workspaces

title: Tour Booking WebMCP Adapter
pitch: Use LLM-powered WebMCP agents to discover and prepare tours directly with local operators—cutting out marketplace middlemen while keeping payment human-controlled.
about_excerpt: Use LLM-powered WebMCP agents to discover and prepare tours directly with local operators—cutting out marketplace middlemen while keeping payment human-controlled. Like Comment Story Updates Booking Interface Codex with WebMCP Inspiration Tour bookings are often controlled by large marketplaces that sit between travelers and local operators. These intermediaries can add commissions, weaken the direct customer relationship, and make small operators dependent on centralized platforms. Our inspiration was to use WebMCP to create a more direct model. A traveler can ask an LLM what they want in natural language, and the agent can interact directly with tools published by the tour operator's own website—without scraping the page or routing the customer through a marketplace. The agent automates repetitive steps such as discovering tours, comparing departures, checking current capacity, and preparing the visible cart. The operator retains ownership of its inventory, brand, and customer relationship, while the traveler remains in control of checkout, payment, and final confirmation. What it does Tours Booking WebMCP lets an AI agent work with the same inventory and cart that the traveler sees. It exposes four WebMCP tools: search_departures searches the page's current inventory snapshot. get_departure refreshes and re-checks the capacity, price, and transfer options for a specific departure. prepare_booking validates a complete selection against refreshed capacity and atomically replaces the visible cart. get_booking_summary reports the cart contents, total price, estimated authorization amount, editability, and recommended next action. An agent can help travelers discover suitable tours, verify that enough spaces remain, and prepare a cart for review. It cannot collect contact or billing details, handle cards, authorize payment, reserve inventory, or confirm a booking. Those actions remain human-controlled in the visible booking experience. The normal interface continues to work when WebMCP is unavailable, making the integration a progressive enhancement. How we built it We built a framework-independent TypeScript adapter around WebMCP's imperative document.modelContext.registerTool() API. The host booking page supplies normalized inventory and cart-state callbacks. The adapter owns the tool descriptions, strict JSON schemas, matching runtime validation, freshness rules, response formatting, cancellation, lifecycle cleanup, and safe cart-preparation protocol. For an exact departure check or cart preparation, the adapter asks the host to refresh inventory instead of presenting cached data as current. prepare_booking validates the complete replacement cart, checks the page state before and after the asynchronous refresh, and performs exactly one atomic commit. If validation or a state check fails, the existing cart remains unchanged. Inventory-derived results are marked as untrusted content. Read-only tools are annotated accordingly, while the cart-mutating tool is explicitly identified as non-read-only. The repository also includes a backend-free Vite demo with deterministic in-memory inventory, a fake document.modelContext test harness, documentation, and agent-evaluation scenarios. Challenges we ran into One challenge was designing around an experimental browser API whose availability and behavior may change. The application still needed to remain usable in browsers without WebMCP. Freshness was another major challenge. Availability can change between an agent's search and its attempt to prepare a cart, so saved inventory cannot be presented as current. We added explicit freshness metadata, forced refreshes for exact checks, and capacity validation immediately before committing cart state. Asynchronous refreshes also introduced race conditions. Checkout could begin, another browser tab could become active, or an invocation could be cancelled while capacity was being refreshed. We addressed these cases with before-and-after state checks, serialized preparation, abort-signal propagation, and an atomic commit boundary. Finally, we wanted useful agent capabilities without quietly turning a cart tool into a payment or reservation tool. Identity, billing, cards, payments, reservations, and confirmations therefore remain completely outside the tool contracts. Accomplishments that we're proud of Built a coherent four-tool WebMCP experience rather than a single demonstration call. Connected agent actions to the same visible cart controlled by the traveler. Implemented fresh-capacity validation and all-or-nothing cart preparation. Preserved a strict human boundary around personal data, payment, reservation, and confirmation. Added 21 deterministic tests covering schemas, freshness, time zones, capacity, atomicity, concurrency, cancellation, lifecycle cleanup, and safety boundaries. Defined nine agent-evaluation scenarios covering tool selection, argument accuracy, ambiguity, unavailable data, and unsafe payment requests. Kept search responses within a compact 1,536-byte target. Created an independently runnable demo requiring no credentials, customer data, private API, or payment provider. Passed the complete formatting, testing, TypeScript build, demo build, and package-verification pipeline. What we learned We learned that designing WebMCP tools is as much a product and security exercise as it is an API exercise. Tool names, descriptions, schemas, annotations, and results collectively shape how reliably an agent behaves. We also learned that freshness must be represented explicitly. "Available" is not meaningful unless the agent and traveler know whether the information came from a current refresh or a saved snapshot. Most importantly, we learned that useful agent assistance does not require handing over the entire user journey. Agents can reduce discovery and coordination work while preserving meaningful human control over sensitive and consequential actions. What's next for Tours Booking WebMCP Next, we plan to: Deploy the demo with the browser headers and origin-trial configuration required by the active WebMCP implementation. Connect the adapter to normalized production inventory through the existing host callbacks without exposing private booking endpoints. Run the evaluation suite across additional WebMCP-capable agents and browsers. Add more inventory scenarios, accessibility testing, and localized user-facing explanations. Continue refining consent and review UX while keeping payment and confirmation human-controlled. title: SlideForge
pitch: Ask an agent to build a slide, or edit it by hand — nothing regenerates. You're both on the same live deck.
about_excerpt: Ask an agent to build a slide, or edit it by hand — nothing regenerates. You're both on the same live deck. Like Comment Story Updates One tool call and the whole deck restyles instantly — no rebuild, no delay. Seconds later, another instant restyle to Emerald — every slide updates together, live. A real bar chart from live agent data, with every tool call logged in the Activity Panel. A simple bullet-point slide, written entirely by an agent — no templates, just a tool call. TL;DR One shared document. Click a region and type, or ask an agent to do it — both land in the exact same state a heartbeat later. No "apply AI changes" button, no regeneration, no separate modes. 19 real tools registered via document.modelContext.registerTool() — the actual WebMCP API, not a chatbot glued onto a canvas. We built an image-generation tool, tested it against real agents, watched it hallucinate a fake gstatic.com URL twice, and deleted it — replaced with real chart and diagram data instead, which models can actually produce. Live: webmcp-beryl.vercel.app · Code: github.com/Aswin-hash/slideforge Unscripted footage: apply_theme fires from a real agent call and every slide re-skins immediately — no rebuild, no delay. Inspiration Every "AI slide generator" we'd tried worked the same way: you prompt, it regenerates the whole deck, and whatever you had is gone. There's a human mode and an AI mode, and the two don't really talk to each other — editing by hand means you've opted out of the AI, and re-prompting means you've opted out of your edits. WebMCP looked like the way out. Instead of an agent screenshotting a page and guessing where to click, document.modelContext.registerTool() lets a page hand an agent a list of exact, callable actions — the same actions a human has, exposed directly. That's not "AI generates a slide deck." That's "a human and an agent share one editable document, through the same interface." We wanted to see if that idea actually held up once a real agent, not a scripted demo, was driving it. What it does SlideForge is a presentation editor with one shared state — a Zustand store — and exactly one way to change it. A slide is a named layout ( title-slide , two-column , media-split , …) made of typed, addressable regions: title , body , left_body , text, bullets, a real bar/pie chart, a flow diagram. A human clicks a region and types. An agent calls one of 19 tools — set_bullets , set_chart_data , apply_theme , reorder_slides — and the exact same store updates, the exact same way. Both are logged to a live Activity Panel, so nothing an agent does is invisible. There's also an Agent Console built into the app itself — pick any of the 19 tools, fill in its arguments, run it. It calls the identical code a real WebMCP host would call, which turned out to be essential, because most browsers don't support WebMCP yet (more on that below). The agent calls set_chart_data with real {label, value} numbers — that's an actual rendered chart, not a screenshot of one pasted into a slide. How we built it React 19 + TypeScript + Vite, Zustand for state (wrapped in persist , so a page refresh doesn't wipe the deck out from under a live agent conversation), Tailwind for styling. No backend, no API keys, no server — the whole thing is a static SPA. The part we're proudest of architecturally: every slide is rendered at a fixed 960×540 resolution and scaled into whatever container it's in via a ResizeObserver + CSS transform . The filmstrip thumbnails and the full canvas are the same component tree , just scaled differently — not two rendering paths that can drift out of sync. The WebMCP layer is intentionally thin: a ToolDef array, one runTool() function that wraps every call in try/catch and logs the result, and a single useRegisterTools() hook that registers all 19 at the app root. Every tool's execute() calls straight into a plain Zustand store action — the same action a click handler in the UI calls. That's the whole trick: there was never a second write path to keep in sync, because we never built one. Challenges we ran into This is where most of the real work happened — not in the initial build, but in what broke once real agents (Gemini, then Claude) started actually driving it. Stale ids that quietly broke everything. Every time the deck reset — a page refresh, a "Reset to sample deck" click — every slide and region got a brand new random id. An agent mid-conversation had no way to know that happened, so it kept confidently calling tools with ids that no longer existed. The fix was two-fold: persist the deck to localStorage so a refresh doesn't regenerate it, and default every tool's slideId to the currently active slide unless explicitly given (except the one destructive tool, remove_slide , which we deliberately left strict). Agents doing unnecessary reconnaissance. Early on, nearly every content edit was preceded by a get_slide_structure call just to learn a region's id — even for layouts the agent had just created itself. We let every content tool accept a region's name directly ( left_body , body , media ) instead of demanding an opaque id, and made a wrong guess fail with the slide's actual region names listed right in the error. That collapsed most two-call sequences into one. A tool description that was quietly sabotaging itself. set_region_type 's description told agents to "call this before filling a region whose type doesn't match" — which sounded reasonable, except every content tool already converts a region's type automatically. We watched an agent dutifully call set_region_type , get a success message, and then just... stop, having "completed" a step that did nothing useful. Fixing that one sentence fixed a whole class of dead-end conversations. We shipped an image tool and had to kill it. set_region_image took a URL, actually verified it loaded via a real fetch , and rejected dead links with a clear error. It worked exactly as designed — and it still failed, twice, because the model asked to "generate an image" doesn't have pixels to give you. It hallucinated a very plausible-looking gstatic.com/lamda/images/gemini_logo_...png URL — right domain, right path shape, completely fake. No amount of validation on our end fixes a model inventing a URL that was never real. We removed the tool entirely and replaced it with set_chart_data and set_diagram_steps : structured numbers and short labels are squarely inside what a text model can actually generate, and every test since has worked. Model tier mattered more than any tool design decision we made. The exact same tool set, the exact same prompts, went from stalling constantly on a "lite" model tier to completing 12+ chained tool calls without a single error on a larger one. No prompt engineering on our side closed that gap — it's a genuine capability difference in multi-step planning, and it taught us to design tools that are forgiving of a weaker model's mistakes (clear errors, sane defaults, informative failures) rather than assuming a strong one. What we learned Tool descriptions are the UX. We spent as much time rewriting a sentence in a JSON Schema description field as we did writing components — and it mattered just as much. A tool that quietly implies an unnecessary step, or doesn't say what it can't do, will get an agent to confidently waste a turn on nothing. You cannot design this by imagining how an agent should behave — you have to watch a real one behave, badly, and fix exactly what actually happened. Every hardening decision in this project — the name-based region targeting, the default-to-active-slide behavior, the image tool's removal, the rewritten set_region_type description — came from a specific, reproduced failure, not a hypothesis. And WebMCP itself is genuinely early. No mainstream consumer browser calls document.modelContext tools by default yet — we built the Agent Console specifically so the tool layer was testable without needing bleeding-edge browser flags. That's not a workaround we're embarrassed by; it's proof the tools work independent of which host eventually adopts the standard. What's next Import an existing PowerPoint's theme and fonts so a deck starts from your brand, not a blank slate. More layouts. And, when a model actually can hand a tool real image bytes instead of a hallucinated URL, set_region_image gets to come back. title: EventReady
pitch: Hiring vendors for an event is the part everyone knows how to do, and EventReady helps. The harder part is whether all of it holds together on the day, and that is what it keeps track of.
about_excerpt: Hiring vendors for an event is the part everyone knows how to do, and EventReady helps. The harder part is whether all of it holds together on the day, and that is what it keeps track of. Like Comment Story Updates Developer docs covering the nine WebMCP tools, the session they share with the UI, and the trust boundary that keeps vendor text as data. Source compares real service plans built from eight provider contracts, showing coverage, cost and coordination burden for each. A plan chosen through the WebMCP tools rather than the UI. The agent selected it and the interface you are watching updated with it. Describe an event and EventReady plans it, then tells you whether all the pieces actually work together on the day. The run of show after an agent assigned every open responsibility. Readiness reached Ready to run and the day has a real timeline. Inspiration I was inspired by my day job and my hobby, as they both played a part to this idea. I work for a major grocery retailer that does catering, and we'll be launch a AI concierge chat bot soon. Watching that come together, I ultimately thought I could do better. It helps you build a basket inside one catalog, and you make a purchase. Easy peasy right, but what if your event requires purchasing and coordination across multiple vendors? You've got food from one vendor, tables from the venue, a friend driving warming trays across town, and there's no single place that knows whether all of it adds up. The other half comes from concert photography. I shoot live music, which puts me in the parts of a venue an audience never sees, watching how a show actually gets run. Big events don't go well because every vendor is good. They go well because somebody's holding and coordinating across the seams. Who's where at what time, what happens when the truck's late, who owns the thing nobody put their name on. That work is coordination, and it's almost never written down anywhere. EventReady points those two observations at the same problem. Hiring people for your event is the part everyone already knows how to do. The part that goes wrong is everything between them. What it does You describe the event, and EventReady walks it through five phases. Shape the brief, source the services, coordinate the owners and the money, close the gaps, then run the day. The piece I care about most is the readiness layer. It reads what each provider has actually committed to, works out what that leaves uncovered, and tells you plainly what isn't going to work. Nobody's bringing the warming trays. The transport window doesn't fit the service time. Four responsibilities don't have an owner at all. Coordinate shows that as two columns, everything without an owner on the left and everything settled on the right, and a card crosses over the moment somebody takes it. Run turns the whole thing into a printable run of show with a real timeline. The agent side isn't a second product. Nine WebMCP tools sit on document.modelContext , and they mutate the same EventSession the visible interface renders. An agent can assess readiness, compare plans, change the service level, assign an owner, or pull the run of show, and you watch it happen in the UI. Every change writes a decision receipt with before and after cost, coverage, ownership and readiness, so you can see what a tool call actually did instead of trusting that it did something. How I built it Using a combination of Codex and Claude Code. Deployed onto Vercel. Challenges I ran into Mostly compounding defects working across two different agents and environments. I have multiple setups and the commits and merges kept colliding. So I had to hand a lot of the refinement and polish more to Claude Code as Codex was really churning. Codex was mainly where I tested the WebMCP protocol in the in app browser. Accomplishments I'm proud of I was able to get a viable working concept up and running pretty quickly. Even though it's not perfect, with some additional tuning it could be really helpful with tons of integration potential across a variety of cases and industries. What I learned Most of what an agent does on the web today is guesswork. It reads rendered text, infers structure that was never declared, and hopes the number it pulled off the page is the number the page actually meant. That's slow, it burns context on markup that carries no meaning, and it's wrong often enough that you can't trust it with anything that matters. WebMCP flips that. The page declares what it can do and what it knows as narrow typed contracts, so the agent reads a structure instead of reverse engineering one. Nine outcome shaped tools replaced what would otherwise be thousands of DOM nodes to crawl and guess at. The agent doesn't ask what's on the screen, it asks whether the event is ready, and gets back a typed answer with coverage, blockers, ownership and timing already resolved. The accuracy gain matters more than the speed. Because the tools mutate the same session the interface renders, the agent and the person are reading one number, not two that drifted. There's no second pipeline to keep in sync and no chance the agent reports a total the screen disagrees with. I built a source gradient demo to check this properly, comparing what's knowable from WebMCP tools against schema.org markup, a plain price table, a document transcript, and a provider that publishes nothing. The difference isn't subtle. Structured capability is the only one of those that lets you act with confidence rather than infer and hope. The part I didn't expect is that structure is also what makes safety possible. When provider data arrives in fixed declared fields, you can draw a hard line between data and instruction, because you know exactly which bytes are which. Free text gives you nothing to defend. My hostile vendor fixture is only defeatable because its blurb is a field with a known role, so a sentence aimed at the agent can be quarantined instead of obeyed. Standardizing the shape of the data is what made the trust boundary enforceable at all. What's next for EventReady Scale to make it functional end to end. Full catalogs and payment processing? Provenance on every row, so you can see which obligations the engine derived from a contract and which ones a person added. Real provider handoffs behind the copy-the-checklist step. And multi-device collaboration, which is honestly the whole point of coordination work and the one thing this build deliberately doesn't claim to do yet. title: NexusOps
pitch: NexusOps lets specialized agents investigate production incidents through real WebMCP tools, resolve disagreements with evidence, and keep humans in control of remediation.
about_excerpt:
NexusOps lets specialized agents investigate production incidents through real WebMCP tools, resolve disagreements with evidence, and keep humans in control of remediation.

 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 Incident response is often stuck between two extremes: humans doing everything manually, or automation acting without enough context and control. We built NexusOps to explore a safer middle ground where agents investigate operational incidents, compare evidence, and recommend actions while humans remain responsible for approval. 

 What it does 

 WebMCP makes this possible directly inside the website. NexusOps exposes operational tools that compatible agents can discover and call, while the human operator sees the same evidence, reasoning, activity trace, and safety boundaries. 

 How we built it 

 NexusOps is an agent-native operations control plane for investigating production incidents. It exposes 20 WebMCP tools covering observation, investigation, recommendations, human approval, remediation, and verification. 

 For the simulated incident INC-1042, specialized SRE, NOC, Developer, and SOC perspectives inspect different evidence sources. They form independent hypotheses, identify supporting and conflicting evidence, and allow an Incident Commander to arbitrate the disagreement.
The environment is intentionally simulated. Metrics, logs, services, deployments, and remediation state are deterministic demo data. No real production system is monitored or changed. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 I ran into challenge when I was not familiar with WebMCP at all before starting working on project. Also was lacking of AI credits to actually develop the app in 3-4 days. 

 Accomplishments that I am proud of 

 NexusOps exposes 20 genuine WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(), allowing compatible agents to discover and call operational capabilities directly from the website.
I built a complete incident workflow covering observation, investigation, multi-agent analysis, disagreement, Incident Commander arbitration, human approval, controlled remediation, and verification.
The SRE, NOC, Developer, and SOC perspectives use different evidence sources and produce deterministic, explainable conclusions from the same operational data.
I also added a schema-driven Tool Inspector, evidence and causal-chain views, risk and approval metadata, shared execution tracing, and an audit activity feed. 

 What I learnedx 

 First of all, understood concepts of webmcp and its usage.
I learned that WebMCP is most valuable when agents can use the same tools and page state as the human operator instead of interacting through a separate hidden integration.
I learned that agent assistance must be paired with clear safety boundaries, especially when tools can change operational state.
I also learned that specialized agent perspectives are more useful than a single generic assistant because different roles can focus on different evidence and reach different conclusions. 

 What's next for NexusOps 

 The next step is to connect the same WebMCP control-plane pattern to real observability and incident-management systems while preserving human approval for high-risk actions.
Future versions could support additional incident types, organization-specific tools, richer agent arbitration, and persistent audit history.
The current priority is validating the live WebMCP experience in Chrome and compatible agent environments, then using that feedback to improve reliability and real-world integrations.

title: Briefly
pitch: Briefly lets content teams research trends, bring in business context, and co-write briefs with an AI agent that sees and acts on the same app state.
about_excerpt:
Briefly lets content teams research trends, bring in business context, and co-write briefs with an AI agent that sees and acts on the same app state.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Selecting a trend and offering makes the relevant tools available for agents to compose and save a brief. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Turn a rising trend into a structured, on-brand content brief ready for review. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Give agents your audience, brand voice, offerings, and claim guardrails to guide every brief. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Explore trend signals, growth charts, and sample content to find your next angle. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Review the draft and approve it when it’s ready—AI assists, you decide. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Selecting a trend and offering makes the relevant tools available for agents to compose and save a brief. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Turn a rising trend into a structured, on-brand content brief ready for review. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Give agents your audience, brand voice, offerings, and claim guardrails to guide every brief. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Explore trend signals, growth charts, and sample content to find your next angle. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Review the draft and approve it when it’s ready—AI assists, you decide. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Selecting a trend and offering makes the relevant tools available for agents to compose and save a brief. 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 



 
 Inspiration 

 A trending keyword is easy to find. A useful content brief is harder. You need
the source material, the right audience, the product you actually want to sell,
and a clear list of what the business can and cannot claim. 

 We kept thinking about the annoying part of this workflow: why do we still copy
a trend from one dashboard, open the product notes somewhere else, explain all
of it again in a chat, then copy the answer back into a document? Every move
loses a little context. 

 So we built Briefly around one idea. What if the agent works in the same
workspace as the person, understands what they are looking at right now, and
writes the result back into the actual workflow? 

 What it does 

 Briefly puts trend discovery, business context, content briefs, a calendar, and
performance examples in one browser workspace. 

 The flow is simple. A person opens a trend, reads its source material, and
chooses a business offering. Once both are selected, the agent can read the
full context and write a draft into the brief library. The person can inspect
the draft, create their own version in the composer, change its workflow
status, or schedule it on the local calendar. 

 This is where WebMCP matters. Briefly does not give the agent one giant static
list of tools. Its tool surface changes with the interface. Open a trend and
the detail tools appear. Open the business-profile editor and the editing tools
appear. Select both a trend and an offering and get_brief_context ,
 generate_brief , and save_brief become available. Remove either selection
and those tools disappear again. 

 There are 37 tool definitions in the app, but they are not exposed all at once.
The point is not the number. The point is that the right tool appears when the
person and the agent have enough context to use it. 

 The current prototype uses seeded trend and performance data. It does not fetch
live social metrics, prove engagement growth, or publish anything to a social
platform. A "published" status in Briefly is local planning state, not a real
network post. Saved briefs can be inspected and moved through the workflow,
but their content cannot yet be edited in place from the library. 

 How we built it 

 The frontend is built with React 19, TypeScript, and Vite. We kept the runtime
small: React + React DOM are the only runtime packages. Browser-local stores
hold the briefs, business profile, watchlist, calendar, and tool traces. 

 WebMCP tools register through document.modelContext.registerTool . Their
lifecycle follows the same React route and selection state that controls the
interface. The human controls and agent tools call the same store functions, so
when the agent navigates or saves a draft, the person sees it happen on screen. 

 We also built a local console bridge that exposes the same schemas and executor
functions in browsers without native WebMCP support. It is useful for
development and inspection, but we do not treat bridge access as proof of a
native WebMCP flow. 

 Two optional Vercel endpoints use Gemini for trend analysis and draft
generation. The core agent flow does not depend on them. A connected agent can
read the context, write the brief itself, and save the draft through
 save_brief . 

 The interface uses CSS custom properties with warm off-white surfaces and
oxidized-iron accents. We added committed checks for tool contracts, surface
changes, important UI states, and the production build. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The hardest part was not registering a tool. It was deciding when that tool
should exist. 

 A static catalog looked complete, but in practice it gave the agent actions
that could not succeed yet. Briefly had to track the route, the open trend, the
selected offering, and whether an editor was open. That is what made the tool
surface feel connected to the product instead of attached on top of it. 

 Host compatibility was another real problem. Some WebMCP hosts support tool
registration but do not provide the event-listener methods the inspector first
expected. We changed the inspector so native registration stays intact while
its discovery view can fall back to the local registry. 

 We also had to be strict about what this prototype proves. Seeded metrics are
not customer results. Local workflow state is not social publishing. The
optional deployed model endpoints still need repair and a full retest, and
some captured cover images still need documented permission or replacement.
Hiding those limitations would make the demo sound stronger, but the product
less trustworthy. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are proud that the demo is not just a chat response beside a dashboard. The
agent can navigate the same workspace, read the selected context, and leave a
real draft inside the library for the person to review. 

 The app now has 37 state-dependent tool definitions across eight tested surface
states. It covers discovery, business context, brief creation, scheduling,
performance, and the trace log. Human controls and agent calls share the same
stores, so the two paths do not quietly create different versions of the app. 

 We are also proud of the less visible work. generate_brief returns an unsaved
draft. save_brief always creates a draft. Tool calls receive trace IDs, and
the agent can inspect the same trace log shown to the person. The tool-contract
suite currently passes 51 checks, including invalid inputs, refusal paths,
idempotent operations, and recovery actions. 

 What we learned 

 More tools do not automatically make a better agent experience. Sometimes the
best tool is the one that stays hidden until the context is ready. 

 We learned that human and agent parity also goes both ways. If the person can
add something to a watchlist, stop a video, correct a calendar entry, or inspect
a failed action, the agent needs a safe way to do that too. Creation alone is
not enough. The agent needs to read, undo, and recover. 

 We also learned to separate saving from deciding. save_brief creates a draft,
but another tool can still move its local status forward. That means Briefly is
not a human-only approval system yet. Being precise about that distinction is
important, especially in a demo where a local "published" label can easily be
mistaken for a real post. 

 What's next for Briefly 

 First, we want to replace the seeded trend data with a transparent source of
real data and test whether Briefly actually saves time for content teams. 

 Second, we want to add authentication, shared persistence, and proper review
permissions so a team can see who changed a brief and who approved it. 

 Third, we need to finish the unglamorous but necessary work: repair and retest
the deployed Gemini endpoints, resolve or replace the cover images with missing
permissions, and test the full workflow across more native WebMCP hosts. 

 The bigger goal is still the same. We want the agent to understand the work
that is already happening on screen, help at the right moment, and leave
something useful behind when the conversation ends.

 Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP 

 WebMCP DevTool Ultimate IDE is built for the moment agents and humans start sharing the same web pages. Every site that registers tools via document.modelContext.registerTool() becomes a programmable surface — but today there is no developer tooling to discover those tools, inspect their schemas, invoke them locally, or stress-test edge cases before shipping integrations. This project fills that gap: it is a browser-native IDE for the agentic web. 

 How it creates a better user experience 

 Developers open the extension popup on any tab and instantly see every WebMCP tool exposed on that page — names, descriptions, and input schemas — without reading source code or wiring up an LLM. One click generates a mock payload from the schema; another invokes the tool in-page and surfaces the result or error inline. A formatted "Copy LLM Prompt" export lets teams hand off exact tool contracts to ChatGPT, Gemini, or other agents in seconds. 

 What people and agents can do together that was difficult before 

 Before WebMCP, integrating an agent with a web app meant reverse-engineering hidden APIs or building bespoke MCP servers. With WebMCP, the page itself advertises its capabilities. Our extension makes that contract visible and testable: a human developer can validate tool behavior, catch schema mismatches, and export orchestration context — while an agent on the same page can call the identical tools. Humans debug and design; agents execute — on the same open-web surface.

title: Sweet Spot
pitch: SweetSpot helps people find the right area to live by combining their preferences, such as commute time, groceries, parks, schools, and healthcare and see it visually on the map
about_excerpt: SweetSpot helps people find the right area to live by combining their preferences, such as commute time, groceries, parks, schools, and healthcare and see it visually on the map Like Comment Story Updates application-page Inspiration We work for Apple Maps, so maps and geographic information systems are a big part of our daily work. For this hackathon, we wanted to explore the GIS domain from a different angle: helping people make complex location decisions with an AI agent. Choosing where to live often means balancing several needs at once. You may want a short commute, groceries within walking distance, a nearby park, and easy access to healthcare or nearby school for your child. Most map products can answer these questions separately, but finding the areas where all the requirements overlap takes a lot of manual work. That inspired us to build Sweet Spot. What it does Sweet Spot helps people find areas that match several travel and lifestyle needs. A user can ask: “Find an area within an 8-minute bike ride of San Francisco City Hall, a 5-minute walk of a supermarket, and a 4-minute walk of a park.” Using WebMCP, ChatGPT can work directly with the Sweet Spot map. It can search for real places, add travel limits, combine conditions, rank different areas, explain trade-offs, update the plan, undo changes, and create a shareable result. Some preferences are difficult to describe with words or forms. In those cases, the agent can pause and ask the user to draw an area directly on the map. The agent then continues its work using that boundary. Sweet Spot also records whether each action came from the user or the agent, keeping the process visible and reversible. How we built it We built Sweet Spot as a client-side web application using React, TypeScript, MapLibre, Web Workers, H3 spatial indexing, and WebMCP. The application uses real OpenStreetMap street and place data, along with official neighborhood data where available. Instead of drawing simple circles around a destination, Sweet Spot calculates reachable areas using the street network and different travel modes. The product exposes 18 WebMCP tools. These tools use the same application logic as the visible interface, so every agent action immediately appears on the shared map. The geographic calculations run on the user’s device. We use a Web Worker, spatial indexing, and reusable distance caches to keep the interface responsive. Challenges we ran into Our biggest challenge was running large geographic calculations inside the browser. Early versions were slow because they repeatedly searched the road network and recalculated the same distances. We improved this with H3-based lookups, bounded caches, and per-layer progress updates. Location search was also harder than expected. Users often enter partial names, different spellings, or small typos. We added normalized, word-aware, typo-tolerant search with an online fallback. We also learned that WebMCP tools need to support complete user goals, not merely copy individual button actions. We created an atomic planning tool for full requests while keeping smaller tools for later edits and conversation. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that Sweet Spot is a complete product experience rather than a WebMCP demonstration added to a map. It was good to see that ChatGPT could build a real geographic plan, update the visible interface, explain the results, and hand control to the user when human judgment is needed. The agent can pause in the middle of its task, ask the user to draw a personal boundary, wait for the response, and then continue calculating. What we learned The agent is good at turning a natural-language request into several structured operations and comparing many results. The user is better at expressing personal preferences, judging the map visually, and making the final decision. WebMCP connects those strengths. The user no longer has to copy an AI recommendation into another product and rebuild the search manually. The agent can use the product’s real tools while the user watches, guides, and corrects the process. What's next for Sweet Spot Next, we want to support more cities and add public transit, live traffic, elevation, housing costs, accessibility needs, and other real-world factors. We also want to improve collaborative planning so families, friends, or teams can contribute their own destinations and preferences to the same workspace. Our larger goal is to make Sweet Spot useful for more than choosing where to live. The same approach could help people select an office, plan public services, compare business locations, or explore where community resources are most needed. Also, we feel that these sort of tools should be available in Google and Apple Maps. It will be very helpful for users in real life. Clients can find trusted freelancers, while freelancers can discover suitable jobs and prepare proposals. How I built it Gigoo uses Ruby on Rails, PostgreSQL, Hotwire, Stimulus, Tailwind CSS, and WebMCP. The WebMCP tools use the user's existing authenticated session and Rails authorization rules. Challenges and learning The main challenge was deciding what agents should be allowed to do. Gigoo lets agents search, evaluate, shortlist, and create drafts, while important actions like submitting a proposal remain human-controlled. I learned that WebMCP works best when it exposes real product capabilities instead of adding a separate AI chat layer. title: Clip Magic- WebMCP on an Existing Contact Form
pitch: A live business website where a user’s AI agent prepares a contact form enquiry for human review and submission.
about_excerpt: A live business website where a user’s AI agent prepares a contact form enquiry for human review and submission. Like Comment Story Updates Using WebMCP on an existing website Clip Magic: making a real-world SMB website agent-ready Inspiration Most small businesses do not need another chatbot. They need fewer obstacles between a potential customer deciding, "I need help with this," and actually taking the next step. That was the attraction of WebMCP. The interesting part for me is that the user owns the AI agent . A business website does not have to create its own assistant, replace its existing workflow or force visitors to learn a new interface. Instead, it can expose a small number of safe, useful capabilities that a person's chosen agent can understand and use. Clip Magic is a real small-business website, so I deliberately chose a practical task for this challenge: preparing a website-review enquiry. I chose a pragmatic approach rather than a dramatic one. The problem is familiar: people often know what they need, but do not know which service label to choose or how much detail to type into a set of fields. For some users, especially those who find dense, field-by-field interfaces difficult, a conversational route can be useful. It is not a replacement for accessible form design, and it does not remove human choice. The ordinary form remains available; the agent simply helps a user reach the same workflow and leaves the final decision with them. Most people I know would rather explain what they need than fill in boxes on screen or on paper. The opportunity extends well beyond one website. Small and medium-sized enterprises represent around 90% of businesses worldwide , yet reliable data about the proportion of websites they operate is not generally available. What is clear is that there is already a large installed base of small-business websites: in 2025, 76.67% of EU small enterprises with 10–49 employees reported having a website ( Eurostat e-business data ), while 17% reported using AI, compared with 55% of large enterprises ( Eurostat AI statistics ). That suggests a practical path between the old web and the AI-first web. Most small businesses are not going to abandon their CMS, rebuild their website, or become AI companies overnight. They may, however, be able to add small, useful, standards-based capabilities to the websites and workflows they already rely on. The question behind the project was simple: Can a user's AI agent understand that Clip Magic may be able to help, gather the minimum missing information, and prepare the existing enquiry form without bypassing the human or creating a separate AI workflow? The aim was not to build the most elaborate WebMCP demo. It was to see whether WebMCP could remove friction from something businesses and customers already do every day. What it does The live Clip Magic website exposes one bounded WebMCP capability: request_website_review A user can describe what they want in natural language. Their agent can inspect the public website, determine whether the request is relevant, ask for missing information, open the existing Contact workflow and populate the visible form. The important part is what happens next: nothing is submitted automatically . The user can read the completed form, change anything they want, and decide whether to click Submit. The human and agent therefore use the same underlying workflow: Contact dialog → existing FormBuilder form → existing validation and spam controls → human review → human submission WebMCP does not bypass that process. It progressively enhances it. If WebMCP is unavailable, the standard human form still works exactly as before. How I built it Clip Magic is an existing ProcessWire website. Its Contact form is managed by the commercial ProcessWire FormBuilder module, which already handles validation, spam filtering, storage and email delivery. Rather than duplicate any of that logic, I kept FormBuilder authoritative and added a thin WebMCP layer around the existing form. The implementation has two parts. First, the rendered form carries declarative WebMCP metadata describing the capability and its parameters. This keeps the agent-facing schema close to the real form instead of maintaining a separate copy of the business rules. Second, I added a small imperative compatibility bridge. During testing, Chrome's WebMCP client could discover the declarative tool, but ChatGPT's in-app browser did not. The bridge derives its name, description, parameters and required fields from the rendered declarative form, so it provides compatibility without becoming a second independent schema. WebMCP tools are discovered at the document level, so the capability is available as soon as the page loads. The Contact form remains the existing destination for the agent's prepared data, and the existing FormBuilder workflow remains unchanged. The capability is not tied to the Contact dialog's open or closed state. The dialog can be opened and closed normally without changing WebMCP availability; when the agent uses the capability, it opens the existing Contact workflow and populates the visible form. The live implementation was tested in both ChatGPT's in-app browser and Chrome with WebMCP enabled. Challenges The biggest challenge was not creating the tool. It was making WebMCP coexist safely with a real website that already had years of working behaviour and production constraints. Working with an existing form The challenge was to add an agent-facing capability without rebuilding the Contact system or duplicating its business rules. The solution was to keep the WebMCP layer close to the existing visible form while leaving the shared dialog system and FormBuilder workflow intact. Different WebMCP client behaviour Declarative WebMCP worked in Chrome testing but was not discovered by ChatGPT's in-app browser during development. Even Google's public declarative demo showed the same limitation in that environment. Rather than abandon the declarative implementation, I kept it as the primary definition and added the small compatibility bridge. This let both clients exercise the same capability without duplicating the schema manually. Preserving human control It would have been easy to make the demo look more impressive by allowing the agent to auto-submit the form. I chose not to. Sending an enquiry is a consequential action. The useful boundary for this project is that the agent can do the repetitive preparation work, but the person sees the actual values in the real form and remains responsible for submission. Testing beyond the happy path Because this runs on a real production website, successful population was only the start. The workflow was tested for cancellation, required-field validation, stale tool reuse, rapid double-submission, unexpected parameters, honeypot handling, email-header injection, unsafe URL schemes, prompt-injection text, session/token behaviour and controlled network failure. The supplied website URL is treated as form data only. The site does not fetch it, and no CMS, customer, authenticated or administrative capability is exposed through WebMCP. What I learned The most useful lesson was that WebMCP does not have to mean rebuilding a website for agents. For an existing business site, the better approach may be to identify a useful customer outcome, find the authoritative workflow that already handles it, and expose the smallest capability needed to help the user's agent reach that workflow reliably. I also learned that progressive enhancement matters just as much for agents as it does for browsers . The human path should not become dependent on WebMCP. The WebMCP path should not gain privileges the human path does not have. Both should meet at the same validation, security and business rules. Finally, testing natural-language requests reinforced an important distinction: the website does not need to encode every sales or qualification decision as another tool. The agent can reason from public website content. The site only needs to expose the capability that benefits from a reliable machine-readable contract. What comes next This prototype uses a website-review enquiry, but the same pattern applies to many everyday service-business tasks: checking whether a business services a location; preparing a quote request; checking suitability for a service; finding relevant booking options; preparing an appointment or reservation. The commercial opportunity is not "install WebMCP." It is helping businesses identify where a customer's AI assistant can remove friction from an existing journey, then integrating that capability into the systems the business already trusts. For Clip Magic, this challenge was a small proof of that idea: customer intent → less hunting and fewer clicks → the same trusted business workflow Source Public challenge repository: https://github.com/clipmagic/webmcp-challenge Built With formbuilder html javascript php processwire

title: The Board
pitch: Agents now participate in consequential processes. Capability, action and provenance must be observable. WebMCP is a browser-enforced capability boundary. The Board is that architecture, demonstrated.
about_excerpt: Agents now participate in consequential processes. Capability, action and provenance must be observable. WebMCP is a browser-enforced capability boundary. The Board is that architecture, demonstrated. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I spent five weeks inside a dispute I could not see into. I sent an evidence file, and never learned whether anyone opened it or which rule the outcome rested on. Losing was survivable. The blindness was not. On the other hand, I built that entire evidence file with an AI agent. It read the record and drafted the case, and I could not show a single person what it had opened or why it concluded what it did. My own side of the argument was as unauditable as the decision I was arguing against. The agent was already in the room. Nobody could see it working, including me. In the 180 days to 2 September 2026, 367 platforms filed 3,804,771,378 statements of reasons to the EU's Digital Services Act transparency database. 43% of those decisions were fully automated, meaning no person looked at them. Every one is somebody sitting where I sat. Now we send agents into rooms like that one. The companies shipping them settled the question of whether agents act for us. They left the other one open: can you see what yours was allowed to touch, and what it opened. I built the room I wanted to be standing in. What it does Two people disagree. Each sends an AI agent to argue for them. Four agents sit in four separate origins, two advocates and two readers, and a fifth origin holds the record. Each agent holds a different set of tools, and the browser decides which. To contest a fact, an agent has to open the other side's exhibit and quote it. The page checks that quote against the document and writes a read receipt under that agent's name. Close filing, and the filing tools leave both hands mid-session. Prompting does not bring them back. confirm ends the case. I never gave it to an agent, in any phase. The agents assemble the record. A named person owns the decision. Two opposed parties can now put agents into one process and each check what the other's agent was able to do. I looked for a product that already does this: online dispute resolution, agent negotiation, the agent-to-agent protocol drafts. The nearest one runs each side's agent inside its own private tenancy, so no shared surface hands out the capability and neither side can read the other's calls. My search came back empty. That is not proof nothing exists. How we built it A disagreement is the sharpest version of the problem WebMCP solves. Two agents work the same record from opposite sides. Neither should reach the other's capabilities, and neither should reach the control that ends the case. A server integration cannot say "this capability belongs to this browser tab's origin and to no other, ever." exposedTo says it, and the browser checks it the moment a cross-origin frame asks. The record registers each WebMCP tool with exposedTo , naming the one origin allowed to call it. Chrome answers every frame's getTools({ fromOrigins }) request. My application never sees the question. Each phase owns an AbortController . Closing a phase aborts its signal, and every tool tied to that phase goes with it. An append-only ledger keeps every call that reaches a tool and what came back, refusals included. A judge can run it three ways: scripted panels with no model at all, a configured model, or their own Claude Code or Codex agent over an MCP-to-WebMCP bridge. The boundary is identical in all three. Challenges we ran into WebMCP tool names are unique per document, not per origin. My first registrations collided and left one advocate holding nothing. An empty column looks like a boundary doing its job, which is what makes that kind of bug dangerous. Namespacing every actor's tools fixed it. Payload limits have to be measured after serialisation. A paged response fit on paper, then broke once JSON escaping doubled every quote inside a claim and cut the result mid-string. The implementation measures the finished string now. Cross-origin frames and mid-session tool withdrawal both needed a real browser. My unit tests were more permissive than Chrome, which is how the name collision above reached production. Accomplishments that we're proud of The Board shows absence. Its manifest lists what each agent holds and what it never received, so a refusal lands in the record instead of disappearing into an error. An agent cannot dispute an exhibit it never opened, or cite a fact it never assessed. The page checks every quote against its source. Prompt injection can fool a reader. It cannot conjure a tool the browser never granted, reopen a closed phase, or reach confirmation. The project runs on five deployed origins under 897 automated tests, and in live runs both Claude Code and Codex honoured a mid-phase tool withdrawal without restarting. Chrome's agent-security guidance names nine agent-side defences. The one mechanism the browser answers for itself, exposedTo , sits somewhere else: the guidance Chrome wrote for site authors. The Board implements the agent-side protections, then puts that browser-held boundary underneath them. What we learned The dangerous bugs do not crash. They return a plausible answer built on part of the record, or an empty tool list caused by a name collision. I found both by driving the deployed product and by reviewing it adversarially. Neither showed up in a diff. Provenance has to be captured while the work happens. A model describing what it remembers doing is not an audit trail. A read receipt written as the call lands is. What's next for The Board Two prose fields still clip, so a party can end up reading a cut-off version of why they lost. That one is first. After it: cursor-based access to longer records, more than two readers, and stronger identity around the human confirmation. Every consequential process that takes an agent's input has to answer two questions. What could it reach, and what did it do. The browser can make both visible, and it is the only party in the room with no stake in the outcome.
