title: CommandDeck
pitch: AI builds the right retail workspace for each task, while staff review, edit, and approve every change through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: AI builds the right retail workspace for each task, while staff review, edit, and approve every change through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration In my own work, I often ask AI for help, but I still have to move the result into the actual admin screen by hand. I built CommandDeck because I wanted the AI's plan to appear directly as a workspace that staff could review and use. Retail staff often use separate screens for products, prices, inventory, and storefront content. When old stock must be cleared, staff have to find products, check margins, prepare discounts, and review the customer view by hand. We wanted one simple request to prepare the right workspace for the job. What it does CommandDeck turns a business request into a task-ready workspace. In the demo, a staff member asks for a clearance plan. The agent finds slow-moving products and creates a workspace with product photos, prices, stock levels, and margin checks. The staff member can remove a product and ask to see what customers will see. The agent then changes the same workspace into a storefront preview. CommandDeck also supports price reviews, inventory replenishment, and storefront editing. Each task gets the tools and layout it needs. The agent prepares the work, while the staff member can edit, lock, review, and approve it. How we built it CommandDeck is built with React and TypeScript. It uses Zustand for state management, Zod for validation, and native document.modelContext.registerTool() calls for WebMCP. WebMCP lets the agent inspect the demo catalog, create a workspace, add trusted interface blocks, and change the layout when the task changes. The agent chooses from 11 trusted React blocks and five layouts. The visible controls and WebMCP tools use the same service layer. We also added English and Japanese interfaces and responsive layouts for desktop and mobile. Challenges we ran into The main challenge was allowing the workspace to change without losing human edits and approvals. We added revision checks, locks, and separate review groups. We also separated previews from applied results, so staff can see what is planned and what has actually changed. Accomplishments that we're proud of A single request can create a complete workspace and then reshape it when the job changes. The human and the agent work with the same information on the same page. Staff do not need to copy AI advice into several admin screens. CommandDeck keeps important actions under human control. Emergency rollback is human-only. The public demo uses browser-local sample data, so it does not place real orders or change a real store. What we learned WebMCP can do more than automate clicks. It allows an agent to prepare the right interface for the current job while the human keeps final control. This makes AI assistance easier to understand and more useful for everyday store operations. What's next for CommandDeck Next, we want to connect CommandDeck to real commerce systems with secure authentication and audit logs. We also want to add more operation templates, team roles, and saved work histories. title: spec-commerce
pitch: Turn building and product specifications into bill-of-materials transactions online.
about_excerpt: Turn building and product specifications into bill-of-materials transactions online. Like 1 Comment Story Updates results from spec review 3-Second Version The easiest way for humans and agents to turn complex building and product specifications into purchasable bills of materials for large construction or infrastructure projects. Inspiration I co-founded and operate US Made Supply , a headless B2B e-commerce business built on Shopify. We domestically source compliance driven products including specialty fire extinguishers , cabinets and other code-driven building products. A lot of what we sell is tied to building specifications or codes, especially on complex projects like fab factories or data centers. The hard part is not just finding a product. It is figuring out which exact products and combinations of products match the specifications, drawings, engineering requirements and building codes. You also need to figure out the right quantities. I recently had to do this on a large project and it took many hours of tedious effort. The process today is still very manual. Someone has to read the specs, understand what is required and what the relevant building codes are, compare it against manufacturer product data, talk to manufacturer reps, review plan detail sheets, build the bill of materials and then turn that into a quote or order. AI agents can help read and reason through these documents but still have a hard time selecting and transacting on the right product combinations. Hallucinations are commonplace. That is the idea behind our spec-commerce prototype. We want to give agents the tools to turn building specifications into bill of materials transactions online. The global building and construction products market is over $2T USD today (just because this needs the usual mandatory ambitious market data!) What it does Helps agents turn complex building specifications and plans into bills of materials for construction projects. We are starting with fire life safety products. It is one script tag on a product page. The tag adds a small panel and registers six tools that an AI agent in the browser can use. The agent reads the customer's spec and passes the requirements to the page. The page checks them against product data, where every value has the cut sheet or product page it came from, and answers in plain words: this product meets the spec or it does not, here is why, and here is what on the site does. The agent can propose lines for a quote request. Only a person can approve them, on the page. There is no tool that can approve. The page never guesses. If a requirement cannot be checked from product data, it says so instead of rounding up. Why WebMCP A customer buying against a spec shows up with a stack of documents. The specification says what the product has to be. The schedule says how many go where. The plan detail sheets show how they mount. The building code sits behind all of it. Then there is the manufacturer's cut sheet, which is where the actual numbers live. An agent is good at reading that stack. It can pull the requirements out of section 2.3, find the quantities on schedule A-601 and keep the code citations straight. The three demo documents in the repo are exactly that stack: a spec excerpt, a schedule sheet and code citations. What the agent cannot do is the last step. Landing on a product page, it has to read the page like a person and guess. It cannot reliably tell whether the product in front of it meets the spec, or which other product does, and it makes things up when it is not sure. That is the wrong place to guess. A fire extinguisher rating is a fact on a cut sheet, and whether a cabinet fits is a matter of inches. WebMCP lets the merchant's own page answer those questions. The store already knows its products, the values on the cut sheets, and which cabinet fits which extinguisher. With WebMCP those facts become tools the agent can call on the page, in the browser the customer is already using. The agent reads the documents and brings the requirements to the page. The page checks them against product data and shows where each value came from. Quantities come from the schedule, never from the spec, and the page keeps that straight too. The agent does not scrape or guess. The store does not build an API or run a server. The customer sees every answer on the page they are looking at, with the source next to it. What people and agents do together Before this, a person read the spec, looked up the products, checked the numbers, built the bill of materials and wrote the quote. It took hours and it was easy to get wrong. An agent on its own could read the spec but could not be trusted with the rest. Now the work splits by who is good at it. The agent reads the spec and asks the page the questions. The page checks the facts and shows its sources. The person decides. The agent proposes lines, and the person approves each one, changes a quantity, or rejects it with a reason, right on the page. The agent reads those decisions back and carries on. Nothing is ordered without a click from a person, and there is no tool that can make that click. How I built it The whole thing is one script tag. The bundle reads the product from the page's JSON-LD, mounts a launcher and a panel in its own shadow DOM so nothing on the page moves and registers six tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() . This also allows us to add the functionality selectively to pages and also create a multi-tenant system into the future. The six tools: resolve_requirements takes a spec clause as written, or a list of requirements, and answers what in the catalog satisfies it. It understands a basis of design, numbered alternates and two-unit combinations. get_product returns this product's facts, each with its source. Read only. check_requirements checks this product against requirements, one row at a time, with the evidence. find_compatible finds cabinets that physically fit this extinguisher, or the reverse, with the clearance in inches. add_to_quote_request proposes lines and waits for the person to click Approve or Reject on the page. It returns their decisions, their reasons and their notes. get_quote_request returns the approved lines with indicative prices. Nothing is ever submitted from the page. Underneath, the code is in layers. The core is plain TypeScript with no browser in it: the requirement language, the comparators, the class rating math, the cabinet fit geometry, the catalog resolver, the spec reader and the quote request. One adapter per merchant holds the catalog snapshot, every value with its source. Every change to state goes through one set of commands, and the panel and the tools call the same commands, so the agent can never do anything the person could not do by hand. The tools are validated contracts over those commands, and a thin adapter turns them into WebMCP registrations. The panel is React in a shadow root. Matching is deterministic; there is no model in the compliance path. Unknown is a real answer and is never rounded up. An agent may propose; only a person may approve. Quantities never cite the specification as their source, because specs do not carry quantities. Right now we're keeping it pretty simple and there is no server, no database, no API key etc. The small catalog is a committed snapshot and state lives in the tab. It runs in the ChatGPT desktop app's browser in Work mode and in Chrome 149 or newer with the WebMCP flag on. Hosting is Cloudflare and our main site(s) also uses Cloudflare infra. The demo page mirrors our real product page and pins the exact bundle version. Actual demo can be seen in production at: https://usmadesupply.com/safety/fire-extinguishers/halotron/usms-marketplace/products/buckeye-11-lb-halotron-clean-agent-fire-extinguisher?spec-commerce What I learned Most of the surprises were about how agents hand things to a page. In ChatGPT, Chat mode reads pages but does not use site tools; Work mode does. A file attached to the chat stays in the chat and is not handed to a site's tools, but pasted text is. If "Approve for me" is on, the agent may decline on your behalf. What's next for spec-commerce We want to support more product categories and more of the construction workflow. Longer term this could plug into CAD, estimating, procurement and other software used by engineers, architects, contractors and distributors. Maybe over time, smaller models tuned specifically for this kind of work could also make sense.  💡 Inspiration 

 Over 460,000 children and thousands of vulnerable individuals go missing every year worldwide. Traditional missing persons databases rely heavily on static, outdated childhood photos. As years or decades pass, natural facial growth and aging make visual identification nearly impossible for field officers, shelters, and first responders. 

 We created RescueLens AI to bridge this temporal gap. By leveraging the new Web Model Context Protocol (WebMCP) alongside generative machine learning age-progression, we built an opt-in network where AI can simulate how a missing child looks today in 2026—turning cold cases into active, detectable biometric leads while maintaining strict privacy standards. 

 ⚡ What it does
RescueLens AI is a production-ready, single-file web application (index.html) featuring a dual-tab operational dashboard: 

 🔍 Biometric Detection Panel (Photo-Only Matching): 

 Field officers upload only a photo of a found individual.
The system extracts 128-dimensional facial landmark embeddings, applies a generative temporal age shift (+1 to +20 years), and streams live timestamped progress into an AI Diagnostic Log Terminal.
An animated Cyberpunk Scan Reticle & Facial Mesh Overlay visualizes the biometric computation.
Displays a side-by-side comparison: Original Registry Photo vs. AI Age-Progressed Prediction (2026) alongside an age-adjusted Match Confidence Score (e.g., 94.2%).
📝 Opt-In Profile Registration: 

 Guardians voluntarily register missing family members by providing personal details (Full Name, Year Missing, Age Then, Guardian Contact, Law Enforcement Agency, Physical Traits) and uploading an original photo.
Newly added profiles are indexed dynamically into the live in-memory network, making them instantly detectable in the Detection Panel.
🤖 Native WebMCP Protocol Registration: 

 Registers tools directly into window.navigator.modelContext:
scan_and_predict_missing_person: Performs photo-only scanning & DB cross-referencing.
register_missing_person_profile: Programmatically indexes missing person profiles.
🚨 Emergency Rescue Protocol: 

 A one-click alert dispatch modal encrypts match location tensors and simulates priority SMS transmission to registered parents alongside automatic incident dispatch to NCMEC / FBI Special Victims Units.
🛠️ How we built it
Single-File Architecture: Built completely in a single index.html file using HTML5, Tailwind CSS via CDN, and Vanilla ES6+ JavaScript.
WebMCP API Integration: Utilized window.navigator.modelContext.registerTool() to expose structured biometric and registration tools directly to browser-level AI agents.
ML Biometric Pipeline: Implemented a 128D facial feature embedding vector shift algorithm: 

 Glassmorphic UX/UI: Designed a high-contrast dark mode dashboard with white/beige accent themes, custom CSS laser scan animations, custom scrollbars, and full keyboard navigation.
🚧 Challenges we ran into
Dual-Mode WebMCP Compatibility: Ensuring the application runs natively when Google Chrome's #enable-webmcp-testing flag is enabled, while seamlessly degrading to an interactive simulation mode in standard browsers.
Non-Linear Age Shift Simulation: Balancing real-time browser performance with realistic craniofacial bone growth vector math without requiring heavy backend server infrastructure.
Privacy-Preserving UI Design: Ensuring the match verification view presents clear side-by-side evidence to prevent false positives and protect individual privacy.
🏆 Accomplishments that we're proud of
Delivered a 100% complete, zero-dependency, production-ready single-file prototype (index.html) running on a local Python 
Successfully registered dual WebMCP tools that enable AI assistants to perform biometric missing person lookups.
Pushed clean, documented code and slide assets to GitHub.
📚 What we learned
Deep practical understanding of the Web Model Context Protocol (WebMCP) and how client-side applications can register tools into browser AI runners.
Effective techniques for visualizing computer vision tensor processing in natural language terminals and graphical reticle overlays.
🔮 What's next for Rescue Lens AI
Client-Side WebGPU Acceleration: Running full generative age-synthesis neural networks directly on local GPU hardware at 60 FPS without cloud dependency.
Zero-Knowledge Proof (ZKP) Biometrics: Encrypting facial feature hashes so personal biometric data remains 100% private and tamper-proof.
Global NCMEC & Interpol Sync: Synchronizing opt-in registries across international child protection agencies for instant cross-border alerts.

title: Evidence Desk
pitch: Evidence Desk lets agents investigate disputed evidence through four bounded WebMCP tools while humans keep the verdict—and preserves the investigation and human decision in a tamper-evident receipt.
about_excerpt: Evidence Desk lets agents investigate disputed evidence through four bounded WebMCP tools while humans keep the verdict—and preserves the investigation and human decision in a tamper-evident receipt. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI can read a packet in seconds. The hard part is showing a person exactly what it used—without quietly turning the agent into the decision-maker. Evidence-heavy procurement, compliance, audit, and dispute decisions need agent speed, but they also need human accountability and a reviewable chain of evidence. What it does Evidence Desk gives an agent four bounded WebMCP tools over a signed synthetic packet: search_evidence , inspect_exhibit , evaluate_claim , and update_caseboard . The agent searches thirteen exhibits, inspects hash-linked source spans, evaluates a contested claim, and proposes evidence to a shared caseboard. The demo makes one contradiction visible: the packet records acceptance on March 14, while the signed inspection report says inspection occurred March 19. The evaluator returns CONTRADICTED with two reasons tied to exact spans. Then the agent stops. It cannot pin or remove evidence, reject a proposal, approve the verdict, or seal the receipt. Those decisions remain human-only. How we built it The TypeScript and Vite app registers four tools with awaited document.modelContext.registerTool(...) calls. Inputs are validated at runtime, outputs are bounded JSON strings, and corpus text is treated as untrusted. Real tool executions emit visible started and completed lifecycle events in the provenance rail. An Ed25519-signed manifest and per-span SHA-256 checks quarantine altered evidence before evaluation. After human adjudication, Evidence Desk creates a readable, locally signed receipt binding the tool trail, evidence, final human decision, and signed build manifest. The app runs entirely client-side on synthetic data, and its runtime application logic makes no network requests. Challenges we ran into The central engineering challenge was separating capability from authority. Registration is not execution, simulation is not live provenance, a proposal is not approval, and a structurally valid receipt is not meaningful if it seals zero accepted evidence. We hardened those boundaries: simulation-only sessions stay labeled SIM ; untrusted receipt entries fail verification instead of throwing; the evaluator accepts common date-and-event word orders while rejecting unrelated or impossible dates; long reason lists disclose their full meaning; and sealing refuses an empty evidence anchor. Accomplishments that we're proud of All four production tools executed live on the deployed page. Every call showed its started and completed lifecycle events. The evaluator produced a span-tied CONTRADICTED verdict, while the agent remained unable to perform the human-only actions. The Forgery Bench makes the trust boundary testable: change one signed date byte and the manifest check quarantines the exhibit, withdraws the verdict, and refuses sealing. The implementation closes with 189 passing tests, typecheck, and a production build. What we learned WebMCP is most valuable here not as UI automation, but as a semantic contract between a person, an agent, and shared evidence. The agent becomes faster and more precise without inheriting the person's authority. Visible provenance and negative controls matter as much as the happy path. What's next for Evidence Desk The next step is moving from the synthetic packet to user-supplied signed evidence bundles, durable organizational signing keys, trusted timestamps, and configurable reviewer roles—while preserving the same human-only adjudication boundary. The current local receipt is tamper-evident, not tamper-proof. It does not prove identity or trusted time and is not a legal signature. Agent proposes. Human decides. Evidence preserves what happened. title: Keycap Forge
pitch: **Design printable custom keycaps with ChatGPT, WebMCP, and browser-local 3D AI.**
about_excerpt: **Design printable custom keycaps with ChatGPT, WebMCP, and browser-local 3D AI.** Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Creating an artisan keycap usually requires several disconnected skills: generating a concept, modeling it in Blender or CAD, understanding keycap dimensions, building a switch-compatible mount, repairing the mesh, and preparing it for 3D printing. At the same time, most image-to-3D demonstrations stop after producing something visually interesting. They rarely answer the practical question: Can this model be edited, attached to a real keycap, validated, and printed? We also wanted to explore a better way for ChatGPT to interact with complex web applications. Traditional browser agents depend on coordinates and simulated clicks, which become fragile when layouts change. WebMCP offered a different approach: the website could expose meaningful tools such as find_parts , auto_place_part , and compose_keycap . That led to Keycap Forge: a browser-based workspace where a person and ChatGPT can collaboratively turn an image into a printable custom keycap. What it does Keycap Forge is a browser-local 3D keycap editor powered by WebMCP. A user can: Choose a standard key size, from 1U through 6.25U Space . Select an MX or Topre switch mount. Generate a standalone 3D statue from a PNG, JPEG, WebP, or SVG reference image. Create a lightweight 2.5D relief from a logo or silhouette. Import an existing watertight STL model. Select, move, rotate, and scale parts directly in the 3D viewport. Automatically center and fit a model on the keycap. Render the keycap and added model as one manufacturing solid. Inspect solid, section, and underside views. Validate manifold connectivity, volume, and dimensions. Return to the editable state without losing the original parts or transforms. Export an STL only after explicit user approval. Download a tolerance coupon before printing the complete keycap. The same project can also be controlled conversationally through ChatGPT. Keycap Forge exposes semantic WebMCP tools including: describe_project find_parts get_project_state transform_part auto_place_part compose_keycap repair_printability set_keycap_spec undo_last_action validate_printability export_project Instead of asking ChatGPT to locate a colored arrow on the screen, the user can say: Find the cat model, center it on the keycap, enlarge it slightly, and validate the result. ChatGPT can then operate on the actual project state while every change remains visible and reversible in the website. How we built it The editor is built with React, TypeScript, vinext, and Vite. Three.js and React Three Fiber power the interactive 3D viewport. The keycap itself is generated from deterministic manufacturing parameters rather than being a decorative cube. The geometry includes: A flat-top tapered shell Rounded corners An underside cavity MX cross or Topre mount geometry Stabilizer stems for supported wide MX keys Millimeter-based positioning and tolerances For photo-to-3D generation, we run a browser-compatible TripoSR ONNX pipeline using ONNX Runtime WebGPU. The uploaded image stays on the user’s device. The reconstruction pipeline: Removes a connected edge background and centers the subject. Converts the image into a 512 × 512 model tensor. Runs the TripoSR encoder, backbone, and decoder through WebGPU. Evaluates a (192^3) density field. Smooths the level set to reduce voxel noise. Extracts a surface using marching cubes. Welds duplicate vertices. Applies Taubin smoothing to improve print quality without excessive shrinkage. Corrects the generated model’s up axis and front-facing direction. Normalizes the statue to a practical keycap scale. The three model files total approximately 801 MiB. To make that viable on a static deployment, we implemented parallel byte-range downloading, retries, and resumable chunk storage using the Origin Private File System. A refresh can reuse chunks that have already been downloaded. Manufacturing composition uses Manifold WASM. During Render union , Keycap Forge applies the latest part transforms, removes geometry extending into the keycap cavity, preserves a small attachment overlap, and combines everything into one solid. WebMCP is integrated through a typed tool registry. Zod validates every tool input, and state-changing calls include an expectedRevision . If ChatGPT tries to modify an outdated revision, the operation is rejected instead of overwriting a newer human edit. Manual UI operations and WebMCP operations share the same command and history system. This keeps agent actions observable, undoable, and consistent with direct editing. Challenges we ran into Turning one image into a useful 3D object A single image does not contain information about hidden surfaces. Early approaches produced flat extrusions rather than statue-like objects. TripoSR provided genuine single-view reconstruction, but its raw output still required orientation correction, surface smoothing, normalization, and manufacturing checks. Running a large model on a static deployment The first browser model download is approximately 801 MiB. A normal Vite deployment could host the interface, but unreliable downloads made the main feature unusable. We addressed this by splitting model files into resumable ranges, downloading multiple chunks concurrently, retrying failed ranges, and storing completed chunks in OPFS. Correcting model orientation The reconstruction coordinate system did not match the editor’s coordinate system. Models initially arrived lying down, upside down, or facing away from the camera. We mapped the TripoSR axes into the editor’s right-handed millimeter coordinate system and added a front-facing correction before placement. Separating camera movement from model manipulation The 3D viewport needed to support both orbit controls and transform gizmos. Pointer events originally reached the camera while the user was dragging a model handle. We had to coordinate selection, transform controls, and camera controls so that dragging a gizmo manipulates the part while dragging empty space rotates the camera. Preserving edits during Boolean composition An early union path regenerated parts from their initial state, which discarded the user’s latest rotation or scale. We changed the manufacturing pipeline to operate on a snapshot of the current project revision and apply every stored transform before the Boolean operation. Protecting the keycap cavity A model could look correctly placed from above while extending through the roof and blocking the switch cavity. The manufacturing pipeline now prioritizes the keycap base and trims added geometry below the roof, while retaining a small overlap for reliable attachment. Designing safe agent tools WebMCP gives an agent real application capabilities, so tool boundaries matter. We separated read-only inspection, reversible editing, validation, and consequential export. ChatGPT may prepare an export, but only the user can approve the final download. Accomplishments that we're proud of Running a complete image-to-3D reconstruction pipeline inside the browser without a paid 3D generation API. Deploying the AI workflow as a static web experience backed by WebGPU, OPFS caching, and resumable model downloads. Producing a genuine statue-like mesh instead of simply extruding a 2D silhouette. Making generated and imported models directly editable through XYZ position, rotation, and scale controls. Exposing 11 semantic WebMCP tools that operate on the same live project shown in the viewport. Supporting atomic multi-step composition through compose_keycap . Keeping human and ChatGPT edits in one revisioned undo/redo history. Preserving editable source parts even after previewing the manufacturing union. Protecting the underside cavity by trimming overflowing model geometry. Requiring explicit human approval before exporting an STL. Building automated coverage across 52 test files and 156 tests. Verifying the complete workflow on the publicly deployed application. What we learned We learned that browser-local AI can be more than a privacy feature. It can become part of the product architecture: inference, post-processing, editing, validation, and export can all happen in one environment without transferring the user’s source image to an application server. We also learned that semantic agent tools are much more reliable than visual automation for complex editors. A tool such as auto_place_part carries domain knowledge about the keycap center, roof height, and safe dimensions. That is fundamentally different from asking an agent to drag an object toward an approximate screen coordinate. Another important lesson was to separate generative geometry from manufacturing geometry. AI can propose a useful shape, but deterministic systems should handle dimensions, coordinate conversion, trimming, Boolean composition, validation, and export. Finally, computationally valid does not automatically mean physically pr
video_title: Keycap Forge project DEMO
video_transcript_excerpt: Most AI agents control websites by guessing pixels. Keycap Forge gives ChatGPT a real modeling vocabulary. We start with a ChatGPT generated reference designed for reconstruction, a full-body cat three-quarter view, connected toy-like volumes, and no fragile fur or whiskers. Inside Keycap Forge, I create a one-unit keycap and upload that image. TripoSR runs WebGPU in the browser. The first run downloads the model once while the source image never leaves the device. Here, the weight is time-lapsed, but the result is real. 75,212 triangles corrected to stand upright and face forward, grounded on the roof, and normalized to an 8-mm printable statue. The website still works as a direct modeling tool. I can move, rotate, and scale the cat myself. Now, I deliberately leave it off-center with a rougher surface finish. This is where WebMCP changes the workflow. ChatGPT does not search for colored arrows or replay brittle clicks. The page exposes typed semantic tools over the live project. Find parts identifies the imported cat and reads its current transform. Repair printability previews both the unsafe placement and surface change before anything is applied. Autoplace parts centers the cat on the roof using the keycap's actual dimensions. After that preview, repair printability applies print smooth. Compose keycap batches the final 10-degree rotation and a larger, balanced scale into the same revision history. Every agent action appears immediately in the website. The user can inspect the result, undo it, or return to manual editing. Render union builds the manufacturing solid. Validate printability confirms one watertight component and its exact bounds. Export project opens an approval dialogue instead of downloading silently. Only the user releases the final STL. Keycap Forge turns browser-local 3D reconstruction and CAD-like editing into a visible, reversible collaboration between ChatGPT and a real web application without a paid 3D generation API.

title: Bento.Surf
pitch: AI Tool for creators to grow and monetise their reach
about_excerpt:
AI Tool for creators to grow and monetise their reach
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Then link tree acquired Bento.me and then shut it down. I had a full-blown QR code printed on my T-shirt for my Bento link. That gave me an idea of building it on my own. Slowly as I started talking to people who are my target audience, I realized that they need a full-blown creator tool rather than just a bio. That's what started this project. 

 What it does 

 It helps creators to monetize their audience and reach by selling digital products and charging for their consultancy services. Communities, all in one place. At the same time it helps them grow their reach by automating social media DMs and post-publishing directly via MCP, all in one platform. 

 How we built it 

 I built it using Codex. I have been at it for a week or two now and that's how I built it: just by talking to Codex.

 This is my first app that I have built to a production scale all alone. That's what I'm proud of.

 What's next for Bento.Surf 

 I'm going to launch this once I get approval from Meta for the app review and start monetizing this.

title: webmcp.utlovat.se — Non-Partisan Election Fact-Checking
pitch: An agent-native election evidence layer where WebMCP exposes published sources, visible gaps, and human-in-the-loop verification directly in the browser. Just in time for the Swedish election 2026.
about_excerpt: An agent-native election evidence layer where WebMCP exposes published sources, visible gaps, and human-in-the-loop verification directly in the browser. Just in time for the Swedish election 2026. Like Comment Story Updates Utlovat.se WebMCP landing page explaining that agents can sort Swedish election evidence but cannot recommend a political party. tlovat.se research brief for healthcare, showing a recorded unclear position for Moderates, 12 evidence records for Social Democrats, Evidence cards in an Utlovat.se research brief, each with a Swedish quote, publication date, four-year cost range, source link, archive copy Inspiration During democratic elections, voters are inundated with conflicting claims, manifesto promises, and shifting party positions. When citizens in general, and first time voters in particular, turn to AI assistants for guidance, your average, I have and answer for everything, general-purpose LLMs present a dangerous hazard: they risk hallucinating plausible quotes, confusing past election cycles with current platforms, and inventing policy stances where parties are actually silent . In high-stakes civic decision-making, an AI summary is not enough. Citizens need evidence, not a verdict. And to be encouraged to question the feasibility of the "five minutes to Election Day" promises. utlovat.se (meaning "As Promised" in Swedish) is aims to be an independent, non-partisan election platform tracking over 2,000 promises and 700+ reviewed parliamentary actions for the 2026 general election. We (actually there is only me and my assisting agents) were inspired to build on OpenAI's WebMCP because it offers the missing piece of the agentic web: a standardized, browser-native protocol that allows a website to expose its immutable, verified evidence directly to AI agents . A perfect fit with how youths of today consume information. What It Does With WebMCP utlovat.se transforms from a static website into an active, agent-native truth layer. Through WebMCP, an AI assistant using a WebMCP-enabled browser gains access to 7 specialized tools in total (5 global + 2 contextual): Grounded Deterministic Search (search_verified_evidence): Queries exact manifesto commitments, returning verified quotes, publication dates, transparent cost approximations (≈), and linked Wayback Machine archive copies when available (we have set a 100% archive target and are very close to achieving it). Interactive Evidence Boards (build_research_brief): Generates side-by-side comparative cards on /granska and /webmcp without recommending any party. (Absolute neutrality in all aspects are paramount) Human-in-the-Loop Protocol Verification (get_evidence_board_status): Ensures that evidence remains strictly unverified until a human visually inspects the primary citations and marks the board as confirmed. Parliamentary Trail Tracing (trace_promise): Connects a 2026 election promise to Handlingsvågen's (our Swedish feature name) database of reviewed Swedish Parliament (Riksdagen) voting records and motion histories. Multi-Party Fiscal Matrix (show_party_comparison): Opens the interactive comparison matrix on /jamfor, accounting for joint coalition proposals without double-counting costs. Contextual On-Page Tools (trace_current_promise, build_current_question_brief): Dynamically activates contextual tools when browsing individual promise pages or topic questions. Honest Silence & Gap Transparency: Explicitly reports when a party has no recorded stance on a query, rather than treating a bounded empty result as proof of a position. How We Built It We built the WebMCP integration natively into utlovat.se using TypeScript, Astro, and Tailwind CSS: WebMCP Client-Side Tool Registry (site/src/scripts/webmcp.ts): We registered our 7 tools directly onto document.modelContext.registerTool, defining JSON schemas with strict parameter typing and non-partisan output structures. Cryptographic Data Hashing: Every tool response includes an authoritative data_hash (SHA-256), anchoring conclusions to a fixed, verifiable dataset snapshot. Web Archive Links: When available, a political quote includes a linked Wayback Machine archive copy, making the source trail inspectable and more resilient to link rot. (And also makes it possible to highlight a change in stance in any question). Parliamentary Open Data Bridge: We engineered client-side JSON API endpoints (/api/v1/promise-traces.json) linking election promises to Swedish Parliament document IDs (e.g. data.riksdagen.se/dokument/HB023145) and chamber voting roll calls. Dedicated English Surface (/webmcp): Built a dedicated English hub with the 5 global WebMCP tools, clear testing prompts and cost-range badges. The 2 contextual tools become available after navigation to an individual promise or topic page. Challenges We Faced Enforcing Strict Epistemic Neutrality: The primary challenge in election technology is preventing algorithmic bias. We designed tool descriptions and read-only output structures that explicitly instruct agents not to declare "kept/broken" verdicts, rank parties, or make subjective recommendations. Honest Silence Reporting: In standard RAG pipelines, an empty search return is ambiguous. We had to architect bounded search semantics so that if a party has no promise on a topic, the agent explicitly returns a structured gap report rather than extrapolating. Sometimes silence speaks a thousand words. Zero-Self-Certification for Human-in-the-Loop: We had to ensure agents could not fake human verification. The get_evidence_board_status tool queries the live DOM state, which only transitions to confirmed ✓ when the physical user clicks the inspection button. Anti-Double-Counting in Coalition Manifestos: Calculating joint party proposals required shared commitment keying so coalition proposals are not counted twice in fiscal matrix calculations. New Additions Developed Exclusively During the Hackathon (from August 25, 2026): 1. Prior Work (Before August 25, 2026): The core Swedish public-information website, Utlovat.se. Its foundational dataset of Swedish election commitments and public evidence, including data/promises.json and Handlingsvågen. Existing non-partisan calculations and Swedish public-facing comparison templates. 2. New Additions Developed During the Hackathon (August 25 – September 3, 2026): Browser-native WebMCP integration ( site/src/scripts/webmcp.ts ): Seven read-only client-side tools—five global tools and two page-contextual tools—registered through document.modelContext.registerTool . English Challenge Surface ( site/src/pages/webmcp.astro ): An English entry point, “Evidence, not a verdict,” with a testing guide and direct display of cost ranges marked with ≈ , their basis, and the four-year assumption where applicable. Visible Research Brief and Evidence Board ( /granska , site/src/pages/granska.astro ): A shared human–agent research surface that renders published quotes, dates, source links, archive copies where available, recorded unclear positions, and bounded gaps. It creates deep-linkable research briefs without recommending a party. Human review boundary ( get_evidence_board_status ): The agent can read whether the person has marked the visible evidence board as reviewed, but cannot mark it reviewed itself. Unread material remains explicitly unverified. Parliamentary action tracing ( /api/v1/promise-traces.json ): A read-only evidence chain from a published campaign promise to its source, archive copy, and recorded, human-reviewed parliamentary actions where available. The tool does not decide whether a promise was kept or broken. Automated WebMCP verification ( site/scripts/test-webmcp.mts , site/scripts/test-webmcp-retest.mts ): Tests of the published browser client, tool registration, evidence fields, archive filtering, visible uncertainty, neutral boundaries, English topic matching, shared links, and contextual tools. Open-source licensing : Apache-2.0 was added to the root repository during the hackathon. Frozen competition release : A separate public repository, bambapappa/utlovat-webmcp-challenge , preserves the final static competition build independently of the continuing election-information service. Its manifest records the selected source commit, data hash, and output hashes before the competition cutoff. Transparent implementation history : The public Git history records the WebMCP implementation commits from August 26 onward, while the separate snapshot repository records the freeze and release procedure. Accomplishments That We're Proud Of Hackathon premiere: This marks the moment of my first ever participation in a Hackathon. Evidence-Bounded Civic Fact-Checking: WebMCP keeps tool outputs tied to published quotes, source URLs, archive copies when available, and a verifiable data hash. Complete 4-Step Parliamentary Accountability Chain: Users and agents can trace a promise from a party manifesto directly to permanent web archives and the official Riksdag voting prot

 Inspiration 

 Shopping for a saree often means translating a personal request into filters, comparing several products, opening product pages, and keeping track of a cart. Traditional web agents have to guess at buttons and page structure. We wanted the storefront to expose a clear, predictable interface for people and agents to use together. 

 What we built 

 Vaanzari adds browser-native WebMCP tools for public saree discovery and visible cart actions. A compatible agent can search products, retrieve a product, compare products, open a product page, add an available product to the cart, and open the cart. The person remains in control of product choice, checkout, payment, and order confirmation. 

 How we built it 

 We register six tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) : search-sarees , get-saree , compare-sarees , open-saree , add-saree-to-cart , and open-cart . The tools use a public-safe catalog adapter plus browser navigation and cart adapters. Results map back into the visible UI so the person and agent share the same state. We also added a diagnostics view, tests, and a standalone Apache-2.0 reference repository. 

 Challenges and what we learned 

 The hard part was choosing a useful boundary without exposing account, customer, checkout, payment, or order workflows to an agent. We learned that structured tools make actions more predictable than UI guessing, while explicit human control keeps consequential commerce decisions with the shopper.

title: BashMCP: Give agents a terminal for your website
pitch: Add one line of code to expose WebMCP actions as composable shell commands. Agents can inspect, filter, and chain them, saving hundreds of tool calls and up to 83% of token usage.
about_excerpt: Add one line of code to expose WebMCP actions as composable shell commands. Agents can inspect, filter, and chain them, saving hundreds of tool calls and up to 83% of token usage. Like Comment Story Updates 10/10 correct versus 2/10 natively, with 59–75% fewer tokens and 99–100% fewer calls and bytes. The same real agent and task: both carts correct, with 17 calls natively versus 3 with BashMCP. Live-store turn collapse: 517 host-visible calls become 2; 1.15 MB returned becomes 4.4 KB. One WebMCP tool named bash compiles site tools into /bin; tool save registers a new WebMCP tool. A saved pipeline becomes a WebMCP tool that the next agent finds and runs without being told. A browser-native computer: site and network files, typed commands with help, and persistent SQLite. BashMCP runs on any website, with or without existing tools; Shopify is the worked example. BashMCP: a command line inside any website. One script tag adds a site-side runtime above the WebMCP standard. WebMCP makes a website callable. BashMCP makes it a computer, and the computer gets better every visit. <script src="https://bashmcp.apptory.ai/bashmcp.js" data-bashmcp data-ui="drawer"></script> That is the whole install. BashMCP is a site-side WebMCP composition runtime that installs into an existing website and runs inside that page's live session—not a separate browser VM, a hosted sandbox, or a replacement for the site's tools. One tag boots a sandboxed Unix-like workspace inside the page's own origin. Every WebMCP tool the site already registers compiles into a typed shell command. The page's own network traffic becomes files. An origin-scoped SQLite database persists across tabs and visits. The primary composition entry point registers back into WebMCP as a tool named bash , whose input is { command } —the same string a person would type at a terminal. A separate read-only dom page reader is registered beside it. On the demo store, an agent composes Shopify's ten existing WebMCP tools with jq , grep , sort , and SQL in one auditable run instead of returning every intermediate result to model context. Measured with a blind GPT-5.6 Sol agent on a whole-catalog size audit, that turned 2 of 10 correct into 9 of 10 , while reducing a native median of 315 model-visible host calls to 2 . The person watching sees the same pipeline land in a shared terminal, can rerun or edit it, and can save it as a new WebMCP tool. Fresh agents found and reused such a saved tool unprompted in 14 of 15 measured warm sessions. Same-origin only. No host shell. Shopify is the worked example, not the boundary. The numbers first Same agent, same task, same store, and the same Shopify tools available in both conditions. The prompts never mention bash or prescribe a method. The design and primary metrics were declared before the first benchmark cell ran, exact verifiers read the resulting cart, and every failure is published. Task Site tools alone Same tools, bash beside them What it shows Whole-catalog size audit, clone, n=10 2/10 correct; median 315 calls 9/10 correct; 2 calls Local composition can finish work that serial model-visible calls often cannot Whole-catalog category census, clone, n=10 2/10 correct 10/10 correct The agent chose the shell unprompted in every whole-catalog run Three-step shopper session with a real cart mutation, live store, n=8 3/8 correct 8/8 correct; 41% fewer tokens [23–65%] Query, ranking, and mutation on the production store Single product lookup, control, n=10 10/10 correct 10/10 correct; 2% more tokens ; bash unused in 7/10 The shell adds no value where there is nothing to compose Saved tool reused by a fresh agent, n=15 — 14/15 found it; 15/15 correct; 67% fewer tokens The site's tool surface compounds 500-product catalog audit, n=4 0/4 completed; up to 1,545 calls 3/4 completed in 2–4 calls The benefit increases as the fan-out grows A host-visible call is a call the host makes on the model's behalf whose result enters model context. The site tools invoked inside a bash program still execute against the real application, and every nested call remains visible in the run receipt. BashMCP removes repeated model round trips; it does not hide or eliminate the underlying application work. We make no comparative wall-clock or cost claim. The shell is often slower on a single action, which is why the flat control remains in every results table. The complete methodology, intervals, provenance, and failure ledger are in docs/results.md . Why BashMCP is a strong fit for WebMCP In agent hosts today, broad tasks often become serial tool executions: each result returns to model context before the model decides what to call next. That is exactly right for one action— add this item to my cart or show me that variant . It becomes expensive and brittle when work spans an entire dataset. Auditing every product, ranking a catalog, or cross-referencing endpoints can require hundreds of model-visible round trips, each adding another payload the model must consume before continuing. The tools were not the problem. The turns were. The site's tools remain the correct, authoritative actions. BashMCP never reimplements them. It changes where their composition happens: search, filtering, ranking, joining, and mutation execute as one local program, while only the final answer returns to model context. A host could add batching or a code interpreter for its own users. A site-installed environment has three different advantages: It runs inside the visitor's live session. It can work with the current cart, prices, stock, locale, login state, and the person's own actions without exporting that state into a separate environment. Persistence belongs to the origin. Saved tools, history, and the database remain in the site's browser origin and are available on later visits. The tool surface ships with the site. Anything the site registers can help compatible agents from multiple hosts, and a developer can promote an agent-authored tool into the site's build for future visitors. So we asked: What is the most useful thing a site can register through WebMCP? Our answer was an environment rather than another verb. A better experience for the agent and the person For the agent , BashMCP provides a POSIX-shaped environment it already understands: a filesystem to explore, commands with familiar flags, pipes, exit codes, man pages, --help , jq , grep , sort , and SQL. It does not require a long instruction manual in the tool description. The description points the agent toward cat /README.md , tools , man <command> , and --help ; the environment teaches the rest. In every measured whole-catalog run, the agent selected bash without being told to use it while Shopify's ten original tools remained available. For the person , the developer installation mounts a shared terminal beside the page: One transcript. Two identities: you@host and agent@host . One command history. One filesystem. One SQLite database. You can watch the agent's pipeline land as it runs, press rerun to execute it yourself, arrow back through it, and change one flag. The Runs , Tools , and Events panels show every call, every byte returned, and a receipt for each run—including runs initiated by an agent host rather than the visible terminal. On the live store, ChatGPT's in-app browser sees twelve tools: Shopify's ten plus BashMCP's bash and dom . In a verified run, GPT-5.6 Sol discovered bash unprompted, completed a whole-catalog ranking task with one nested update_cart , and independently verified the resulting cart with a top-level get_cart . What people and agents can do together that was difficult before When a pipeline works, either the person or the agent can save it: tool save cheapest-in-size --description "Cheapest in-stock products in a size" \ --schema '{"type":"object","properties":{"size":{"type":"string"}},"required":["size"]}' < script The script is stored in the origin's SQLite database and registers as a real WebMCP tool immediately and on later visits. It appears: In tools . In man . As a command in /bin . In the agent host's own tool list. With the description, JSON Schema, and access level its author declared. Fresh agents found and reused the saved tool unprompted in 14 of 15 measured warm sessions, and all 15 executions produced the correct answer. tool export prints the production shipping format, so a developer can promote an emergent tool into the site's data-tools configuration. The loop is: A cold agent explores → builds a missing tool → the person inspects, edits, or saves it → a later agent starts with it → the developer ships it to everyone. A static tool surface cannot do this. BashMCP lets use itself reveal which higher-level tools the site should provide. The runtime carries no Shopify-specific knowledge. title: Zingposts
pitch: Interesting things, organized together: a WebMCP-native marketplace where people work with the outside agents they already trust.
about_excerpt: Interesting things, organized together: a WebMCP-native marketplace where people work with the outside agents they already trust. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Browsing old cars, boats, campers, motorcycles, and machinery is fun. Managing the hunt is not. Good finds get lost across tabs, marketplace search misses obvious matches, alerts are rigid, research lives in scattered notes, and negotiations have no shared memory. A three-way trade is almost impossible to reason about cleanly. Zingposts starts from a different premise: the marketplace should be equally legible to people and their agents without embedding a model in the product. The site owns its native listings and structured deal workflow, while outside listings can be tracked as clearly labeled snapshots. What it does Zingposts is a complete peer-to-peer marketplace and durable workspace for interesting things. People can browse realistic native inventory, create and publish listings, upload photos, save finds, build boards, set alerts, keep research notebooks, message sellers, prepare offers, and create structured multi-party trade rooms. Outside finds can be tracked without confusing them with Zingposts-owned inventory. A connected outside agent receives a compact persistent core plus one focused pack drawn from 121 structured WebMCP tools. It can search with compound criteria, compare candidates, organize boards, tag and rank finds, record cited research and inspection risks, monitor price changes, draft communications and offers, calculate acquisition cost, propose trade scenarios, and coordinate the shared gallery, focus, or thumbnail canvas. The human uses the same structure through a canvas-first interface. Zingposts itself contains no LLM. The centerpiece is the shared canvas: an outside agent opens a durable session, places a shortlist, recommendation, or focused question beside the marketplace objects, and pauses only when human judgment matters. The person can inspect the exact listings and rationale, choose an option or add context, and return structured guidance. The agent reads that durable response on its next tool call and continues. This is turn-taking over shared marketplace objects, not a chatbot transcript. The loop now extends across visits. get_workspace_resume returns the last acknowledged checkpoint, everything that changed since, structured blockers, human responses, proposal status, and safe next actions. An agent can acknowledge the checkpoint only after processing it, so “come back later” is an explicit protocol rather than a hope that conversation context survived. For broad edits, the agent can prepare a sourced, versioned change set instead of making a trail of one-off mutations. Zingposts previews each proposed change in plain language, checks the expected object versions, and lets the person selectively accept only the changes they want. Agents cannot approve their own change sets. Completed deals can be recorded as private outcomes, and transparent aggregate patterns report counts, prices, and reasons without inventing a model-generated score. Either side can arrive first. A person can explore immediately in a prototype workspace, then replace a test email and verify the real address through Supabase only when work reaches the marketplace boundary. One Bring my agent click copies the canonical guide URL. Or an unauthenticated agent can inspect five setup-only tools and open a prototype handoff for the person. Once the person signs in, safe private tools appear automatically to an outside agent operating that browser document. Independent 12-hour revocable sessions remain available through one-use invites or codes for separate-browser or unattended work. The human remains in control. Publishing, enabling notifications, sending a message, submitting or responding to an offer, and inviting a trade participant stop at a visible confirmation gate. Every human and agent action is attributed, and reversible work can be undone. Why WebMCP is essential Without WebMCP, an agent has to infer intent from buttons and screen position. That is brittle for a marketplace with dozens of interdependent objects: listings, boards, research, alerts, conversations, offers, people, assets, and constraints. WebMCP gives Zingposts a stable collaboration language. “Find pre-1980 boats under $15,000, put the best four on a board, record the title risks, and draft a message to the strongest seller” becomes a sequence of typed, attributable actions. The human can watch the same state change, refine it directly, and approve the parts that cross a consequential boundary. That makes the product meaningfully better with an agent—not merely automatable. How we built it Zingposts uses React 19 and Next.js on Netlify. Supabase Auth provides verified human sessions, Supabase Postgres holds marketplace, identity, agent-session, and workflow state, and Supabase Storage holds listing photos. Versioned SQL migrations keep direct browser access locked behind row-level security. The browser client exposes 121 declarative tools through the WebMCP modelContext surface, but only five setup tools while signed out. After the person signs in, AbortSignal-managed registration keeps a compact persistent core plus one replaceable focused capability pack, so navigation never accumulates an oversized registry or silently unlocks business actions. get_agent_bootstrap returns setup guidance while signed out, then canonical browser-delegated identity, workspace, attention, active collaboration, capability index, and guide version after sign-in. activate_capability switches the focused pack without moving the person; open_for_human_review is optional. The action layer derives canonical human and agent identity on the server, prevents duplicate profiles, enforces ownership and state-transition enums, creates reviewable drafts, writes attributed activity, stores inverse operations for undo, supports idempotency keys and optimistic versions, returns stable deep links and WebMCP-native structured errors, and converts consequential operations into pending confirmations. Isolated QA runs register only their own artifacts, provide an exact cleanup preview, and require human approval before deletion. The marketplace is seeded with original project-owned imagery and realistic records so the full human-agent workflow is understandable immediately. WebMCP registration is document-scoped, while Zingposts durably stores connection profiles, scopes, alerts, boards, research, drafts, versions, and audit history. The public /for-agents guide and /api/agent-guide contract show agents how to reconnect safely without storing an invite, code, or stale catalog. Challenges The main design challenge was not adding more agent power; it was deciding where that power should stop. We separated preparation from commitment. Research, organization, comparison, and drafting can proceed quickly. Communication, publication, notifications, invitations, and financial commitments pause for the human. We also designed external-listing tracking so provenance stays honest. Zingposts can organize an outside find, but it never claims that its cached price, availability, or seller statements are authoritative. Accomplishments A coherent marketplace, not a WebMCP proof of concept 121 tools spanning authentication, onboarding, resumable work sessions, versioned proposals, outcomes, canvas views, discovery, organization, negotiation, and multi-party trade Agent-first and person-first onboarding with a five-tool setup surface before human sign-in Durable agent-to-human-to-agent turn-taking with a unified attention queue Explicit resume checkpoints and structured blockers for work that continues across agent runs Sourced, versioned change sets with semantic previews and selective human acceptance Private outcome recording with transparent, non-AI aggregate patterns Live agent activity, exact-payload approval, idempotency, dry runs, structured errors, and stable deep links No built-in AI or model dependency Supabase human authentication plus opaque invite URLs, code fallback, and single-use, expiring, revocable agent sessions—without password or session sharing Persistent bootstrap plus navigation-independent focused capability activation Structured errors, strict workflow transitions, optimistic concurrency, and namespaced QA cleanup Durable attribution, confirmations, and undo Native seller photo upload and publishing workflow Clear separation between owned listings and outside tracked snapshots Production build, automated API smoke tests, desktop browser testing, and mobile verification What we learned Human-agent collaboration works best when both sides operate on the same durable objects. A board is better than a chat-only list. A research notebook is better than an ephemeral summary. A pending confirmation is better than asking the model to remember which action is sensitive. We also learned to separate document-scoped WebMCP

An agent can inspect the bootstrap guide, prepare a handoff for the person, or accept a one-use credential. After sign-in, it re-discovers the real workspace. Zing Posts keeps a persistent core, then activates the focus capability for the page. Here, the marketplace pack includes search, view control, comparison, board organization, and the option to open exactly the item a person should review. On a listing, the collaboration gets deeper. An outside agent can build a cited research notebook, record comparable sales, calculate a price range, and draft an offer plan with repair, transport, tax, contingency, and budget assumptions.  Inspiration 

 WebMCP is a genuine leap forward for agentic web apps, a page can expose a real tool ( transfer_funds , export_customers , get_session_token ) and any AI agent gets a standard way to call it via document.modelContext.executeTool . But that also means the moment a site adopts WebMCP, an agent gets the same reach a logged-in human has with no confirmation dialog, no audit trail, and no idea whether the tool it's calling is safe to call. Browsers ship extensions that block ads and trackers; nothing exists yet that treats an agent's tool calls the same way. We wanted to find out what that missing layer should actually look like and build both halves of the problem to prove it: a real WebMCP app with genuinely risky tools, and the guard that makes calling them safe. 

 What it does 

 We built two things: 

 
 A demo WebMCP business app , built purely to give Surf something real and risky to protect — five tools across the risk spectrum: get_balance (read), export_customers (data-egress), get_session_token (credential), transfer_funds (destructive write), and add_payee (account-takeover risk), registered with document.modelContext.registerTool() like any real WebMCP site would. 
 Surf , a Chrome MV3 extension that works on any page exposing WebMCP tools — not just our demo. It injects into every page at document_start ( matches: ["<all_urls>"] ) and sits between every agent and every tool that page exposes:

 
 Blocks explicitly blocklisted tools outright, by name, regardless of what the page's own annotations claim. 
 Holds any tool call that isn't provably safe for an in-page human approval prompt, Approve/Deny buttons rendered directly on the page before it's allowed to run. 
 Masks sensitive data in tool results before it reaches the caller: PII (SSNs, credit cards, emails, IBANs), secrets (API keys, JWTs, bearer tokens), and any field whose name alone looks sensitive. 
 Records every call agent-driven or manual in a live, cross-tab audit trail any page can subscribe to in real time. 
 
 

 The demo app exists to let judges see Surf actually doing something — you can watch it hold transfer_funds for approval, block add_payee outright, and mask a token out of get_session_token 's response but the protection itself is site-agnostic and needs zero cooperation from the page it's protecting. 

 How we built it 

 The core trick is where and how we intercept. The guard ( guard/mcp-guard.ts ) runs in the page's own MAIN JS world from document_start — before any page script runs and polls cheaply for modelContext to appear (since a polyfill or native implementation may define it moments later), then wraps executeTool in place rather than using Object.defineProperty . That matters: a global monkey-patch risks breaking other scripts touching the same built-in, and it wouldn't even help against a native implementation that never defines the property through page-visible calls anyway. Wrapping the method in place works retroactively regardless of how or when modelContext showed up, because callers invoke mc.executeTool(...) at call time rather than caching a reference. 

 Holding a call for approval means the guard has to pause mid-call: it await s a decision, posting an APPROVAL_REQUEST into the page via postMessage , picked up by an isolated-world content script bridge that renders a shadow-DOM prompt directly on the page (isolated from the page's own render cycle) and posts the decision back. A 45s timeout, enforced on both ends, auto-denies so a call can never hang forever. 

 The live audit feed uses externally_connectable so a trusted page can chrome.runtime.connect() straight into the extension and get pushed every entry as it happens, across every tab not just the one it's running in. 

 DLP rules and masking logic were adapted from Surf's own production DLP engine, so tool results get classified the same way real user data already is elsewhere in the product. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 MV3 service worker lifetime. Background service workers terminate after ~30s idle, which silently closes the audit-feed port — naively treating that as "extension not installed" produces a false flip where a real connection looks like it vanished. We fixed it with a client-side heartbeat (any message resets the idle timer) plus automatic reconnection, only reporting "not installed" after several consecutive failures. 
 Injecting UI without fighting the page. The approval prompt has to render reliably on top of arbitrary pages — including ones running their own React/Vue render loops — without a layout fight. Rendering it from the isolated-world bridge as an anchored shadow-DOM element, rather than trying to inject it from the MAIN-world guard, solved this cleanly. 
 Safe-by-default without full annotation coverage. Most real tools won't bother annotating readOnlyHint / destructiveHint , so strict mode needed a sane fallback — a name heuristic ( get_ / list_ / search_ reads as safe) that we know isn't a real safety analysis, which is exactly why the explicit blocklist exists as the actual zero-trust override. 
 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 Getting protection to work transparently and generally — no page changes required, no cooperation needed from the site, working on any WebMCP-enabled page rather than just our own demo — while still being retrofittable to a modelContext that shows up late. 

 What we learned 

 How much of "agent safety" is really a timing and trust problem, not a policy problem, the hard part wasn't deciding what to block, it was guaranteeing we're in position to intercept before an agent (or the page) ever gets a live reference to executeTool , and staying resilient to a background execution model (MV3 service workers) that wasn't designed with this kind of always-on interception in mind. 

 What's next 

 Real safety-classification instead of name heuristics, broader cross-origin iframe coverage for the inspector, and since a Chrome extension only protects regular Chrome exploring what the same policy engine looks like at the browser or network layer for agents that bring their own embedded Chromium.

title: Out of Service
pitch: Two people, two agents, one page. The companion's agent cannot accept the reroute. Step-free NYC.
about_excerpt: Two people, two agents, one page. The companion's agent cannot accept the reroute. Step-free NYC. Like 1 Comment Story Updates The problem A wheelchair user at Court Sq is trying to reach Bleecker St. New York's subway has 160 accessible stations out of 472 , and almost every one depends on an elevator. Advocates counted at least 25 elevator outages a day, median about four hours ( Gothamist ). If the one you need is out, you find out standing in front of it. The person tracking that trip, a partner, an aide, an adult child, is somewhere else with a phone, reading the same feed the rider can and able to do nothing with it but text. Planning around it barely works. The MTA status page says what is broken this minute, never what breaks often. In July 2026 a class action about exactly this settled. CIDNY v. MTA now requires advance notice of outages, platform announcements every 15 minutes, and real-time alternate accessible routes ( Disability Rights Advocates ). The obligation exists now. The thing a rider holds does not. What Out of Service is Out of Service scores every step-free route between two accessible stations on the specific elevators it depends on, using eleven years of MTA outage history joined to the live feed, so a route arrives as a number and a named list of equipment instead of a hope. The rider and the companion open the same trip on the same page, each with their own agent, and the two agents get different tools. How it works Three keyless MTA sources, joined into one committed artifact ( docs/DATA.md ): 82,385 monthly availability rows over 695 equipment codes, 2015-01 to 2026-07, from NY State dataset rc78-7x78 ; the 704-row equipment master; and the live outage feed, 85 records at build time. The join is data/index.json : 695 records, 413 elevators and 282 escalators across 123 accessible complexes, each with 24 months of metrics, a percentile rank inside its own equipment type, a tier, and a tier_reason naming the thresholds behind it. All 77 live-outage ids join into the index ( data/index-meta.json ). Routing runs on a graph of those 123 elevator-dependent complexes: 558 ride edges over 23 lines, 472 of them asserted by the MTA's own next-accessible-station fields ( docs/ROUTING.md ). The score is a sum, not a verdict: 25 per dependent unreliable elevator, 10 watch, 8 unknown, 2 reliable, halved where a second elevator makes the same move, 15 per transfer, plus 60 and a broken flag if a required non-redundant elevator is out live. Broken is never "this station has an outage", always "this route needs this elevator, nothing else makes that move, and it is out". Every number on screen is dotted, and clicking it opens the dataset, the query and the row count. Two people, two agents, one page Creating a trip mints two unguessable keys. The rider gets /t/<id>?k=<riderKey> ; the companion link is the same trip with the other key. Tools register per session from those keys, so DevTools > Application > WebMCP lists 13 tools in the rider's window and 10 in the companion's, same origin, same page, before either agent says a word. Hiding a tool is not the boundary. POST /api/trip/:id/action derives the role from the key and ignores any role in the body, so a forged accept from the companion's session comes back 403: "Only the rider can accept route. You are the companion: propose a reroute instead." Every write parks inside execute behind a confirmation card and does not resolve until a person presses Confirm. Reject rejects it in the rider's own typed words, so the agent hears "that transfer is too long for me" and offers something else. The broken-equipment report is a declarative HTML form with no toolautosubmit : the agent fills it in, a person sends it. When the feed changes, the whole set re-registers and toolchange fires, and accept_reroute 's description goes from "0 pending proposals" to "1 pending proposal from your companion right now (p1)". Features Route scoring with tiers. Three routes, each with a risk number, a label and its elevators. Live station panel. Outages at both ends with the MTA's return estimates. Companion link. Its own capability key, its own tool set. Proposals and acceptance. The companion proposes with a reason, the rider accepts or rejects, both windows updating in about two seconds. Watch equipment. Subscribe to codes, see them in a watch list. Broken-equipment report. A declarative form the agent fills and a person sends. Source on hover. Every dotted number opens its dataset, query and row count. Simulated outage. Forces one elevator out for the session, labelled SIMULATED throughout. Origin trial. The Chrome WebMCP token is in the page head, so stock Chrome needs no flag. Why WebMCP is the right fit Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP. Two humans with different authority share one page. WebMCP registers tools per session from inside the page, so one origin and one path present 13 tools to the rider's agent and 10 to the companion's. A server-side MCP server can express two roles, but not without a second deployment, an auth handshake and an account for the companion. How it creates a better experience. Before: four equipment-code lookups across two MTA pages, two minutes of cross-referencing, an answer good only for this minute. After: one route_accessible call, under a second, three routes scored on their elevators' 24-month history. Court Sq (E M G 7) to Bleecker St returns the F at 26, G then F at 35 and F then M at 43 (2026-09-03 build). Take EL328 at Bleecker out and the F flips to 86, avoid, broken, and G then F is the recommendation. What people and agents can now do together that was difficult or impossible before. Two agents split one trip: the companion's watches the feed and proposes, the rider's surfaces it, a person confirms. The rider never has to trust the companion's agent, or ours, because the difference is enforced by the server and visible in DevTools. How we implemented WebMCP. document.modelContext.registerTool only, never navigator.modelContext , which moved to Document in the 27 May 2026 draft. Fifteen tools registered per session by role, each with a strict inputSchema and readOnlyHint , and untrustedContentHint on get_trip alone, the one tool returning text another human typed. Mutations build their own confirm gate inside execute , because WebMCP has no destructive-action annotation and requestUserInteraction() has not shipped; create_trip and report_broken_equipment are declarative forms without toolautosubmit . evals/ follows Chrome's guidance: 17 fixtures carrying role , page and state , one a companion asking to accept, where the right answer is no tool call. The runtime reads document.modelContext once before anything touches it and otherwise loads @mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill , with a badge printing native , polyfill or unavailable . What is real today, and what is next NYCT subway only: no PATH, no commuter rail, no buses. Tiers are percentiles of the equipment's own population, so "unreliable" means unreliable for New York, not against an absolute standard. Direction is the honest blind spot: 65 of 264 platform-touching elevators call themselves "Manhattan-bound", meaning south from the Bronx and north from Brooklyn, and the master's borough column is empty on all 704 rows. Those are reported as possible dependencies, inflating a route's risk rather than hiding one. Next: MTA alert subscriptions per watched elevator, so a watch list pushes instead of polls; more cities, because the same open-data shape exists elsewhere; and the two-agent pattern outside transit, a pharmacist and a caregiver on one prescription page, where one proposes a substitution and only the other accepts.
