title: Marinela AI Concierge
pitch: WebMCP lets compatible browser agents match clients to current salon services and prices, check live availability, and open a prefilled review while booking confirmation remains human.
about_excerpt: WebMCP lets compatible browser agents match clients to current salon services and prices, check live availability, and open a prefilled review while booking confirmation remains human. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Marinela Hair Design is an operating hair salon in Solin, Croatia. Its production website already had protected booking, public pricing, dashboard-managed services, and calendar connections. For the challenge, we added a WebMCP layer that lets a compatible browser agent turn a natural-language request into structured, current salon data—without handling personal information or final booking confirmation. What it does Marinela AI Concierge exposes five focused WebMCP tools directly from the public salon website: get_salon_information returns public salon details, staff, and opening hours. find_bookable_services searches the active service catalog. search_price_list searches current public price-list rows. check_appointment_availability checks live availability for a service, stylist, and up to seven dates. prepare_booking_for_confirmation rechecks one selected time and opens the salon's first-party booking page with the service, stylist, date, and time preselected. The first four tools are read-only. The fifth performs only visible page navigation: it cannot reserve, create, or confirm an appointment. The client must review the summary, enter personal details, acknowledge the privacy notice, complete Cloudflare Turnstile, and click the final confirmation button. No WebMCP tool can cancel or reschedule bookings, look up customers, or access salon administration. The system also keeps two different price concepts honest: the matched bookable Balayage color service remains price on request , while the separate public price list provides current €100–€200 Balayage variants as context rather than a guaranteed quote. How we built it The production application uses TypeScript, React, Next.js, Vite/Vinext, and Cloudflare infrastructure. Native imperative WebMCP tools are registered through document.modelContext.registerTool . Each tool has a constrained JSON input schema with additionalProperties: false , followed by runtime shape and value validation. Tools are registered only on approved public routes and are removed during navigation or component unmount. Same-origin, rate-limited, no-store routes expose a sanitized salon catalog and availability results. Availability is checked against salon hours, existing booking claims, and the selected stylist's connected Google Calendar. A verification failure is returned as an error and is never represented as a fully booked day. The booking handoff rechecks the selected slot, passes only non-personal selections to the first-party booking page, and never calls the booking-creation endpoint. If the client later submits the visible form, the existing server validates the slot again. The public repository contains sanitized production source, setup and security documentation, an MIT license for code, a separate brand-asset notice, and a GitHub Actions workflow. The latest public workflow is green and the release suite passes all 35 tests. Challenge scope The salon website, visual identity, staff dashboard, Google Calendar integration, public price list, and conventional protected booking flow existed before the challenge. During the submission period, the project was meaningfully extended with five WebMCP tools, the live Concierge catalog, agent-prepared booking review, a dedicated /concierge experience, explicit privacy boundaries, fail-closed safety controls, documentation, and regression tests. Challenges The main challenge was making agent capabilities useful without exposing private customer or administrative data. We also had to preserve honest distinctions between a bookable service and an informational price row, a currently unavailable time and a verification failure, and a prepared review and an actual booking. Accomplishments Shipped five focused WebMCP tools on a live production salon website. Connected service discovery, public price context, and live availability in one agent-ready flow. Kept appointment creation and every personal-information field outside the WebMCP tool surface. Added strict schemas, runtime validation, same-origin checks, rate limits, and fail-closed behavior. Published reproducible public source with automated quality gates and 35 passing tests. What we learned Effective WebMCP design is not only about exposing functions. Tool scope, failure semantics, data provenance, and the boundary between assistance and consequential action are equally important. A visible human-confirmation step can be a product advantage: the agent reduces discovery work while the client retains control over identity, consent, and the final transaction. What's next Next steps include testing with additional WebMCP-capable clients, refining tool descriptions from real salon scenarios, and adapting the same human-confirmed pattern to other appointment-based small businesses without expanding write authority. title: Spot
pitch: Your workout, spotted by an agent that can't drop the bar.
about_excerpt: Your workout, spotted by an agent that can't drop the bar. Like Comment Story Updates Spot is a workout tracker where a person and an AI agent work on the same live session, in the same browser tab. Most AI fitness apps just talk at you. They write you a plan and leave. Spot lets an agent actually execute that plan, and work on the session with you. Tell you when to progress, and when to ease off. The app you use at the gym, and the tools the agent uses, hit the same data. All your lifting history, preferences, and personal context can factor into your lifts. Spot makes the plan, you log the sets. Live at https://spot.mootoo.co — no login. Source under AGPL-3.0 at https://github.com/moolikethecow/webmcp-workout . Why this use case fits WebMCP A workout is a living document that changes every ninety seconds while you're in the middle of it. A chat model can't hold that state: it remembers what you said, not what you did. The tracker holds the truth but can't reason with you. WebMCP puts the agent inside the page that owns the truth. Tools register on document.modelContext from the page you're actually looking at, run in your own browser session, and read and write the exact session the logger renders. No API keys, no sync, no drift. How it creates a better user experience You train. You tap sets done. Then you say "my shoulder's bugging me and I've got 30 minutes, keep what I've done, work around the shoulder, hit whatever's freshest" — and the remaining exercises change while the sets you finished stay exactly as you logged them. The replacements weren't hallucinated: the app filtered a 1,318-movement catalog by your stated constraint and your equipment, and the agent picked from that pool. Ask why the next incline press session says 80 lb and the answer cites your last six sessions and the double-progression rule that produced it. Ask it to log a set and it won't invent the numbers — it asks what you actually lifted. What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before Restructure a workout mid-session without losing what's been done. Every write carries the session revision; a stale edit is rejected with current state and the agent re-reads. State a training constraint once and have it enforced everywhere — search, drafts and live edits all pass through one eligibility function over a precomputed biomechanical demand profile for every exercise in the catalog. Choose today's work from per-muscle readiness derived from your own history, not generic advice. Get progression answers that are auditable: explicit policy in, next target out, rule quoted. Say "I'm in a hotel gym, dumbbells and a smith machine only" and have the catalog narrow to the room you're standing in. A gym never recorded before is created from the description. Let an agent stage a claim about your body without being able to assert it. The training-constraint tool is a form: the agent fills it, the call stays pending, and it completes when you press Add. The human is better at feeling how a set went and calling an audible. The agent is better at querying six weeks of history, reconciling constraints with readiness, and doing the arithmetic. The page is where they meet. How WebMCP is implemented Both halves of the API are used, and the split between them is the design. Sixteen page-scoped tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool by a React hook on mount and unregistered through an AbortController on navigation: get_training_context , get_active_workout , edit_active_workout , log_active_sets , search_exercises , get_muscle_readiness , get_training_constraints , set_training_constraint , draft_workout , edit_workout_draft , start_workout , get_exercise_progress , get_workout_history , get_training_plan , list_gyms , switch_gym . Each execute performs a same-origin fetch to the app's own API routes, which call the same library functions the UI uses, then invalidates the page's data so the logger refetches. Mutations pass expected_revision and return the new revision. Read tools carry readOnlyHint . Descriptions carry the invariants: completed sets preserved, warm-ups are not working volume, substitutions come from the eligible pool only, constraints are hard limits, no diagnosis. get_training_context returns the collaboration rules so an agent has a one-call orientation. The tool list is page-scoped because a tool list is a prompt: edit_active_workout and log_active_sets aren't offered where there's no live session. One declarative tool, registered by markup. report_training_constraint is a <form> on the dashboard carrying toolname and tooldescription . There's no registerTool call for it — Chrome reads the controls and derives the schema: required becomes JSON Schema required , a <select> becomes an enum carrying its option labels. The reason to use a form is what it does to timing. Chrome fills the fields and then waits. The call doesn't resolve until the form is actually submitted, so an agent can put shoulder_joint / limiting / left shoulder on screen but a person commits it. SubmitEvent exposes agentInvoked and respondWith() , so one handler serves both callers. ChatGPT's built-in browser implements a subset of WebMCP with no declarative API, so a <form toolname> isn't a site tool there. Rather than lose that beat in the client judges are told to use, the page treats the form as the definition and the declarative API as one way to publish it : where the browser hasn't published the form, the same report_training_constraint is registered in code, and its execute fills the same form and waits for the person's press. Chrome's indefinite wait is the one thing registerTool can't reproduce, so after twenty seconds the call resolves with awaiting_confirmation and the values stay on screen for the press. One name, one form, one submit handler, three callers. That gives the app an honest line: what the agent may do alone is registered in code; what needs a hand on the button is a form. Reading, searching, drafting and re-prescribing work not yet done are the first kind. Asserting a limit on your own body is the second. And because it's a real form, a browser with no WebMCP gets an ordinary constraint editor. Every visitor gets an isolated Postgres schema seeded with a fictional athlete's six weeks of training, so judges can mutate freely and reset from Settings. Inspiration I already had a workout tracker I'd built for myself. What I didn't have was any way for an agent to actually use it. When I injured my shoulder, there was no way to change my workouts on the fly, or update my progressions. Every AI fitness tool I tried would happily write me a program and then have no idea what I did in the gym, and couldn't adapt. I wanted to close the loop. Building the app with WebMCP now means that Spot can plan my workouts, monitor my lifts inside the workout with me, look at my results, adjust my plans, and frankly, just handle my workouts. How I built it Next.js 15 and React 19 over Postgres, with every query written as SQL through Drizzle rather than an ORM abstraction. Each visitor gets their own Postgres schema, provisioned on first request and pinned per connection, so the app stays single-tenant code and all the isolation lives in one file. The training engine is deterministic (constraint eligibility, readiness and progression are pure functions over logged sets) and covered by around 1,400 tests, which is what made it safe to let an agent write to a live session at all. What I learned A tool description is a prompt, and so is the tool list. Page-scoping which tools exist changed agent behaviour more than any wording change I made. The bigger lesson: a tool's success message can lie. Three of mine reported work they had not done. Search claimed to apply an equipment filter it never ran, eligibility counts were taken over a sample but presented as the whole catalog, and a constraint that excluded nothing said it had excluded things. All three passed their tests. They surfaced only by driving the deployed app and reading what the tool actually said, rather than checking that it returned ok. Challenges ChatGPT's WebMCP is a subset with no getTools and no declarative forms, so the form tool would not exist at all in the client judges are told to use. The page now detects that and registers a code-defined stand-in that fills the same form and still waits for a human to press the button. Chrome cancels a pending declarative call if the form is reset, which meant an agent-invoked submit had to leave the values on screen rather than clearing them. Where it comes from Spot is the open agent surface of a larger health ecosystem app I built. The logger and the deterministic training engine were extracted from it; the WebMCP layer, per-visitor workspaces and the demo athlete were built for this challenge. docs/PRIOR_WORK.md in the repo draws the exact line, with commit timestamps. Spot only sees the gym. The system it came from sees the

title: CallScope
pitch: A WebRTC rescue room where developers and AI agents safely diagnose, repair, and verify live browser calls through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A WebRTC rescue room where developers and AI agents safely diagnose, repair, and verify live browser calls through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration When a browser call fails, developers often jump between application state, WebRTC statistics, developer tools, logs, and manual controls. This is slow, difficult to explain, and risky: an AI assistant may either lack access to the live runtime or receive too much authority to change it. What CallScope does CallScope is a browser-based WebRTC Rescue Room where a developer and an AI agent investigate and repair a live call together. The workflow is: Observe → Diagnose → Explain → Propose repair → Human approval → Apply → Verify The developer starts a deterministic browser call and introduces a real fault by disabling the audio track. Through focused WebMCP tools, the agent inspects the actual runtime state, explains the evidence, stages a recovery plan, waits for explicit human approval, applies only the approved repair, verifies the before-and-after result, and generates a sanitized incident report. Why WebMCP is essential CallScope is not ordinary browser automation. The agent does not guess from screenshots or scrape UI text. WebMCP gives it structured, purpose-built access to the live technical state of the call. This makes a previously difficult workflow practical: the developer and agent can inspect the same call, share evidence, agree on a bounded repair, and verify the result together—without giving the agent uncontrolled authority. How it works CallScope is built with Vue 3, Vite, JavaScript, and Pinia. It creates a deterministic browser-only WebRTC loopback, so the demo does not depend on a backend, PBX, SIP service, or external caller. The WebMCP layer exposes narrow tools with structured schemas for inspection, diagnosis, recovery staging, approved repair, verification, and incident reporting. Read-only inspection is separated from state-changing recovery, and recovery remains blocked until the developer approves the staged plan. Key features Deterministic browser-only WebRTC loopback lab Reproducible disabled-audio failure Structured WebMCP inspection and diagnosis tools Visible evidence and diagnosis timeline Staged recovery plan with explicit human approval Bounded repair through WebMCP Before-and-after recovery verification Sanitized incident report Lifecycle cleanup, error handling, and privacy-aware outputs How we used AI and Codex The AI agent acts as the diagnostic collaborator: it selects WebMCP tools, interprets structured WebRTC evidence, explains the likely cause, proposes a bounded recovery plan, and verifies whether the repair worked. Codex helped translate the specification into an implementation sequence, challenge design assumptions, implement and review the application, harden approval and lifecycle behavior, design deterministic tests, improve privacy boundaries and error handling, and prepare the documentation and demo. Try it Open the live app in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Google Chrome with WebMCP enabled. Start the demo lab, disable the audio track, and ask the agent: What is wrong with my call? Follow the visible diagnosis, approve the staged recovery, and let the agent apply and verify the fix. No account or credentials are required. Limitations CallScope demonstrates deterministic browser-side WebRTC diagnosis and recovery. It is not a backend monitoring platform or an infrastructure observability service. The focused demo centers on a reproducible disabled-audio failure so the human-agent workflow remains fast, reliable, and understandable. title: Life Manager
pitch: An open-source, 24/7 AI money printer that finds paid opportunities, performs bounded work, and asks only for the human 1%.
about_excerpt:
An open-source, 24/7 AI money printer that finds paid opportunities, performs bounded work, and asks only for the human 1%.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Title 

 Life Manager 

 One-line Summary 

 An open-source, 24/7 AI money printer that finds paid opportunities, performs bounded work, and asks only for the human 1%. 

 Problem 

 People share many isolated ways to use Claude, Codex, and other AI systems to make money through bounties, gigs, apps, content, and online work. What is missing is a public, reproducible end-to-end agent system that continuously discovers opportunities, evaluates them, performs bounded work, pauses only at a genuine human boundary, resumes after an answer, submits or delivers once, and follows the result to an official receipt. 

 Solution 

 Life Manager turns paid opportunities into persistent, isolated workrooms. Its provider-neutral architecture can expand across the public Web, X, GitHub, mail, Lancers, Mercor, and other marketplace URLs; the currently verified scout path is the public Web. Citation-backed public URLs enter a durable Railway Postgres queue, where the dedicated money-printer-worker qualifies them. 

 The person does not supervise ordinary agent turns. When identity, authority, private payment information, judgment, or a real-world action is genuinely required, the workroom contract defines one prepared Needs You task. The intended flow is a versioned answer in the same Dashboard followed by continuation from that workroom; live creation/answer/resume E2E is pending. 

 The currently verified Lancers evidence is an application receipt for project 5593484 / proposal 27863414 , not revenue. Paid & verified remains zero until an independently verified payment receipt exists. 

 Why This Matters 

 AI earning advice is easy to publish but difficult to reproduce. Life Manager makes the process inspectable and open source: opportunity source, requirements, agent work, human handoff, external effect, cost, and provider receipt are visible in one system. Applications, offers, opportunity value, and model claims are not counted as revenue; only official payment evidence is. 

 Official WebMCP Questions 

 Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP 

 Money Printer is a strong WebMCP fit because earning work spans many turns while still containing moments when a person and an agent must share exact context: approving a consequential public delivery, providing identity-bound or payout information, making a genuine judgment, or performing a physical action. WebMCP turns the live Dashboard into a shared control surface for that work. 

 The page exposes typed tools for the current board and workrooms: inspect_money_printer , add_opportunity , inspect_workroom , inspect_next_human_task , and the state-dependent record_human_answer . These tools complement the 24/7 Railway worker; they do not replace the backend runtime. The same durable state is rendered for the person and read or updated by the site tools. 

 How it creates a better user experience 

 Without WebMCP, an agent must infer Life Manager's interface from pixels and DOM controls, while the person has to translate state between a dashboard, chat, and external opportunity sites. With WebMCP, the intended flow is a typed read of the board, a visible workroom inspection, and a versioned human answer only when a genuine boundary is open. The person can inspect the same state and evidence instead of supervising every ordinary turn. 

 The deployed judge tenant is isolated and blocks external application, delivery, payment, and money effects. Its current Lancers receipt is read-only, and an application is never presented as payment. Live ChatGPT/Chrome discovery and live creation/answer/resume E2E are pending rather than being implied by the UI contract. 

 What people and agents can do together that was difficult before 

 Life Manager divides real earning work according to what each side does best. The agent handles discovery, qualification, research, planning, creation, execution, recovery, submission, and receipt reconciliation when the relevant capability and authority are available. The person contributes identity, authority, judgment, payment information, or physical action when one of those is genuinely required. 

 Both sides work from the same durable workroom state. In the verified current slice, a cited Web scout cycle completed on retry, state survived a worker restart, and the system preserves a read-only Lancers application receipt with replay duplicate count zero. The broader external-submit and human-resume path remains evidence to collect. 

 How WebMCP was implemented 

 The top-level /money-printer page registers focused tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() . The currently registered set is: 

 
 inspect_money_printer — read metrics, board columns, and safe recent activity 
 add_opportunity — add one public HTTPS opportunity to the durable queue with an idempotency fence 
 inspect_workroom — read the selected opportunity, job, and receipt timeline 
 inspect_next_human_task — read the oldest exact open human task 
 record_human_answer — record a versioned answer and resume the same job when a task is open 
 

 Each tool uses the same server-validated state as the visible UI. Revision checks, tenant boundaries, idempotency, and effect fences protect internal writes; the zero-login judge tenant has no external-effect authority. No separate receipt-writing tool is registered; receipt evidence is read through the workroom projection. 

 How We Used AI 

 
 Model-led opportunity qualification using reward, deadline, eligibility, required work, cost, and risk 
 A provider-neutral capability worker that selects browser, web, GitHub, code, file, and media actions from environmental feedback 
 Durable state and worker restart recovery for continuation across turns; live creation/answer/resume E2E and three-cycle proof remain pending 
 Minimal-human task generation at genuine identity, authority, private-fact, judgment, or real-world boundaries 
 Failure recovery and receipt reconciliation without blindly repeating uncertain external effects 
 

 How We Used Codex 

 Codex was used to research WebMCP and the official challenge contract, inspect and extend the existing Life Manager codebase, design the WebMCP tool surface, implement the Dashboard and runtime integration, and prepare the public repository and submission materials. Client discovery was verified end to end in Google Chrome 152 with WebMCP enabled (--enable-features=WebMCPTesting,DevToolsWebMCPSupport): document.modelContext.getTools() returned the page's five registered tools, and executeTool ran the page's real handlers against the real backend. Discovery inside ChatGPT's in-app browser has not been verified by us, so we do not claim it. 

 Key Features 

 
 Citation-grounded public-Web scouting and a durable opportunity queue (verified current path) 
 Provider-neutral expansion path for X, GitHub, mail, Lancers, Mercor, and other public marketplace URLs (architecture, not current live-discovery proof) 
 Bounded agent workrooms and one durable board for opportunities, agents, artifacts, human tasks, effects, and receipts 
 Needs You questions issued one at a time at genuine human boundaries; live creation/answer/resume E2E is pending 
 Effect fences, idempotency, uncertain-effect quarantine, and official readback 
 Verified-money ledger that distinguishes activity, applications, and opportunity value from received money 
 Five top-level WebMCP tools backed by the same domain state as the human UI 
 

 Architecture 

 
 Netlify: responsive Life Manager Dashboard at /money-printer and top-level WebMCP registration 
 Railway money-printer-worker : running cloud scout/worker process with durable queue and restart-stable state 
 Durable state: opportunities, workrooms, agent events, human tasks, effects, and receipts 
 Existing agent runner: provider-neutral model execution with browser, web, GitHub, code, file, and media tools 
 Provider adapters: read-only Lancers application receipt readback; Mercor and additional marketplace adapters are expansion paths, not current live-discovery proof 
 

 Testing Instructions 

 This is the safe judge path for the live guest tenant; no login, payment, API key, or private Life Manager account is required. 

 
 Open https://aniccaai.com/money-printer in ChatGPT's desktop in-app browser. 
 Confirm the banner says Judge guest — external effects disabled . 
 Ask: List the Site tools exposed by this page. Call inspect_money_printer, summarize the board and money truth, then inspect one qualified workroom. Do not perform an external appli

title: Trialbook
pitch: Run science experiments with your agent, and keep the lab notebook together.
about_excerpt: Run science experiments with your agent, and keep the lab notebook together. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Interactive simulations are how a lot of students first meet physics; PhET alone reports hundreds of millions of simulation runs a year. But a simulation is a solitary tool. The part of real science a slider cannot do, running the same experiment thirty times while changing one thing and then fitting a law to the numbers, is exactly what an agent is good at. And teachers now face a second problem: how do students use AI in a lab without the AI doing the lab? WebMCP answered both at once. A lab is a small set of well-typed actions with a human watching: set parameters, run, sweep, repeat, optimise, plot, fit, write. That is precisely the shape a WebMCP tool wants. An agent that scrapes the screen cannot drag a slider eight times, read eight numbers off a canvas and fit a curve to them. With tools it calls sweep_parameter once, gets eight measurements back as JSON in about four seconds, calls fit_model , and gets period_s = 2.021·length^0.5 with R² = 1.000. Tools also give the page a way to say no: a screen-scraping agent cannot be refused, but a tool can, and Trialbook uses that to keep the student in charge. What it does Trialbook is a physics and biology lab in the browser with four experiments: projectile motion, a pendulum, predator–prey populations, and an RC circuit. You move sliders and watch the simulation. Your agent, working through fourteen WebMCP tools on the same page, runs trials and sweeps, fits laws, finds optima, quantifies uncertainty, and writes in the shared lab notebook under its own name. What people and agents can now do together that was difficult or impossible before: Discover a law in one conversation. "Sweep the length from 0.25 to 4 m in 8 steps, fit a power law to the period, and record what it means" comes back as a chart with the dashed fitted curve, the equation, and a notebook entry: exponent 0.50, R² 1.000, the period grows with the square root of the length. Least squares on the page, not the model's arithmetic. Find an optimum properly. optimize_parameter runs a golden-section search. Under heavy drag it found the best launch angle, 39.08°, to a 0.08° bracket in 19 trials. By hand that is an afternoon of slider-dragging. Put an uncertainty on a number. With simulated measurement error on, "repeat the current trial ten times" comes back as 41.61 ± 0.08 m (mean ± standard error), with error bars on the chart. Use AI in a lab without the AI doing the lab. Assignment mode turns the agent into a lab partner: it cannot run a sweep until the student has written a hypothesis, and every agent conclusion arrives as a proposal the student accepts, edits or rejects. The exported report has a "who did what" table with those counts. Keep one notebook with two authors. Hypotheses, observations and conclusions from both sides, each stamped with the experiment and the parameters in force at the time. How it creates a better experience. Before, a student who wanted to know whether the pendulum period depends on release angle dragged one slider twelve times and copied numbers into a spreadsheet. Now they ask, watch the sweep run on the stage with a progress bar and a cancel button, see the chart appear with its fitted curve, and read the conclusion in the notebook with the settings it came from. About a minute in ChatGPT's built-in browser, end to end. The person never loses the wheel: move a slider mid-conversation and the agent's next get_lab_state reads "you: set gravity to 1.59 m/s²"; ask "what did I change?" and it names the change, predicts the effect and runs a trial to check (range 41.5 m on Earth became 82.5 m at lunar gravity). Agent changes glow purple on the sliders and arrive as toasts; yours are blue. Anything the agent wrote can be edited or deleted. Live: https://minewefu.github.io/trialbook/ · Source: https://github.com/minewefu/trialbook (MIT) How we built it React, TypeScript and Vite, deployed to GitHub Pages; no backend. The physics engines are plain functions: a closed-form projectile with a semi-implicit Euler integrator when drag is on, fourth-order Runge–Kutta for the nonlinear pendulum and for Lotka–Volterra, and the exact first-order solution for the RC circuit. How WebMCP is implemented: Every tool is registered with document.modelContext.registerTool through one 150-line wrapper. It feature-detects the API, keeps a local registry that powers an in-page Tools panel (anyone can run any tool without an agent, through the same code path), clamps outputs, and turns thrown errors into { ok: false, error, hint } the model can act on. Fourteen tools: eight lab-wide ( get_lab_state , open_experiment , get_results , plot_results , fit_model , notebook_add_entry , notebook_read , export_report ) and six per experiment ( set_parameters , run_trial , sweep_parameter , run_repeats , optimize_parameter , reset_experiment ). The experiment group is registered when an experiment opens and replaced when another opens, so the schema always describes the current sliders; the handlers act on whichever experiment is open, so a cached schema still behaves. readOnlyHint on every reading tool; untrustedContentHint on notebook_read , the one tool that returns text people typed. The execution AbortSignal is wired into sweeps, repeats and optimisations: cancelling from the agent or the on-page button stops the loop and returns the partial results with cancelled: true . Validation is strict and specific: angle = 120 is outside the allowed range 0 to 90 deg ; Unknown parameter "mass". Valid parameters: speed, angle, … . In assignment mode the refusal says exactly what to ask the person for. Outputs stay under about 1.4K characters: results are paged, sweep summaries shrink to fit, and the lab state drops detail in tiers rather than truncating mid-JSON. 66 unit tests cover the physics (projectile within 0.5% of the closed form, pendulum within 0.5% of the exact elliptic-integral period, the Lotka–Volterra invariant conserved, RC time constant equal to R·C), the fits, the tools' output sizes, cancellation and assignment mode. The tools reference is generated from the tool definitions by a test that fails if it drifts. Verified end to end in ChatGPT's built-in browser (GPT-5.6 Sol, Windows desktop app) and in Chrome 151 with the WebMCP flags. Challenges we ran into The output budget. Chrome's guidance asks for tool outputs around 1.5K characters, and a seven-parameter experiment with seven measurements blows through that fast. The fix was structural: paged results, sweep summaries that shrink row by row until they fit, and a lab-state snapshot that drops detail in tiers, so the agent always gets valid JSON rather than a truncated one. Conclusions that stayed in chat. In the first live test the agent answered "the exponent is 0.50" in the conversation and never wrote it into the notebook, which made assignment mode pointless. Every batch result now ends by asking for the conclusion to be recorded, and in assignment mode a chat-only conclusion does not count. Tool groups that change under the agent. Switching experiments swaps six tools. If the client caches the old schema, the calls still have to work, so handlers act on whichever experiment is open and validate against it, and the schema is only a description. Layout. The first version spent its pixels vertically. Two rounds of screenshots later, parameters sit under the stage in fixed-width rows, tools are a chip cloud, and the readouts follow the cursor without jumping. Accomplishments that we're proud of The whole loop works from a plain conversation in ChatGPT's browser: sweep, fit, propose, accept, report, with numbers that match the physics to the last digit. The agent asked for a hypothesis before it would sweep, and its conclusion showed up as a proposal with Accept, Edit and Reject buttons, exactly as designed. And the physics is honest: every engine is tested against an exact solution. What we learned Tools are a better place for policy than prompts. Putting "write a hypothesis first" into a tool's refusal message, rather than hoping the model remembers, made the behaviour reliable. Small, well-described tools with strict errors let the model self-correct in one turn. And a specific "what changed since you last looked" feed is worth more than any amount of state dumping, because it tells the agent what the person cares about right now. What's next for Trialbook Real data import, so a student can compare their own pendulum timings against the model. More experiments, chosen for the laws they let you discover. A teacher view of the attribution report across a class. And, as WebMCP clients mature, declarative tools for the notebook form so the lab works in more browsers. title: Agent Native Portfolio
pitch: Recruiters get an instant, job-specific candidate fit—no digging or guessing. WebMCP lets agents bring the role, verify portfolio facts, and surface the strongest matches live.
about_excerpt: Recruiters get an instant, job-specific candidate fit—no digging or guessing. WebMCP lets agents bring the role, verify portfolio facts, and surface the strongest matches live. Like Comment Story Updates A portfolio that screens, tailors, and pitches itself to any AI agent — live, on the page, in front of you. Inspiration Recruiters spend ~30 seconds on a portfolio, and increasingly they browse with agents that have to scrape and guess. Meanwhile every developer sends the same static site to every visitor. WebMCP lets both sides collaborate instead: the agent brings the job, the site brings verified facts about the candidate, and the human watches the two work together in real time. What it does Built on top of my existing personal portfolio site (live since early 2026). Everything WebMCP-related — all 11 tools, the AgentBridge island, the scoring engine, the two Netlify Functions, and the /agent-traffic, /agents, /profile.json, and /llms.txt surfaces — was added entirely during the submission period (Sept 1–2, 2026). Nothing about the pre-existing site's design or unrelated content is part of this submission. This portfolio exposes 11 typed WebMCP tools that a visiting agent can call while its human watches the page respond: get_profile / search_projects / get_experience — structured facts: skills with honest self-assessed levels and years, projects with measured outcomes, not tech-tag lists get_evidence — verifies a specific claim ("has HIPAA experience") against the record, or says plainly that no evidence exists match_role — deterministically scores a pasted job description against the candidate's real skills; a visual fit report renders on the page live, gaps included tailor_view / reset_view — the live page reshapes itself for a role: a prominent, highlighted banner appears under the name, projects reorder by relevance, unrelated work dims generate_resume — a role-targeted résumé assembled from the same structured data, downloadable as a PDF at /resume compose_inquiry — drafts a message into the contact form with an "AI-composed, review before sending" banner; the human always reviews and clicks send — it never submits on its own sign_guestbook / get_guestbook — agents leave notes under their own identity, visible on a public dashboard Every tool call is logged (anonymously) to a public /agent-traffic dashboard — live agent analytics for a personal site, showing which tools get used and what agents have signed the guestbook. Why WebMCP fits this use case A portfolio's entire job is to be legible to a stranger fast. Static HTML forces every visitor — human or agent — through the same generic narrative. WebMCP lets the site expose structured, callable truth instead: an agent doesn't have to scrape and infer whether a candidate fits a role, it can ask, and get a deterministic, evidence-backed answer. How it improves the experience For the visitor's agent: verifiable answers instead of scraped guesses. For the human on the other end: they watch their agent's work land live — a fit report appears, the page visibly reshapes around their role, a résumé is ready — instead of reading a wall of text summarizing what happened elsewhere. What people and agents can accomplish together that wasn't possible before A recruiter pastes a job description into their agent. Together, in one session: the agent gets a scored, honest fit assessment (not a sales pitch — real gaps are called out); the page itself re-prioritizes around that role in front of the recruiter; a tailored résumé is ready to download; and if there's a fit, the agent drafts an outreach message that the recruiter reviews and sends themselves. None of this — live personalization driven by an external agent, with the human co-present and in control of every outward action — was possible with a static site. How we built it Astro 5 (static output) + React 19 islands + Tailwind v4, on Netlify. A single persistent island ( AgentBridge , mounted with transition:persist ) registers all 11 tools once and survives Astro View Transitions, so tool state (a tailored view, a fit report) persists across page navigation. Matching is deterministic — no LLM call, no hallucination risk — reading a structured skills/projects/experience dataset ( bio.json + content collections). Two Netlify Functions with Netlify Blobs power the guestbook and the public analytics dashboard, rate-limited and PII-free. Non-WebMCP agents get the same data via /profile.json and /llms.txt. Challenges we ran into Netlify Blobs' list() reads are only eventually consistent — new guestbook entries took ~40s to appear. Fixed by switching to a maintained index at a fixed key (strongly-consistent get/set), the same pattern already used for the analytics counters. Early tailor_view changes were functionally correct but visually easy to miss (a small badge and a secondary paragraph changed, while the name headline — the most visually dominant element — never did). Fixed by adding a prominent, pulse-highlighted banner directly under the name. The résumé PDF export (browser print-to-PDF, no PDF library) silently rendered several headings invisible when the browser was in dark mode. Fixed by forcing solid ink on every element inside the résumé under @media print . A legacy ng build override left in Netlify's dashboard settings (from before this was ever an Astro site) silently broke every PR's deploy preview for months — found and fixed as part of this work. Deploy previews and production turned out to share the same Netlify Blobs store rather than being isolated per deploy context — test writes during development leaked into the live public guestbook. Built a secret-protected admin endpoint to clean that up, which now also serves as basic spam moderation going forward. Accomplishments that we're proud of A fully working, evidence-based fit report an agent can trust, live page personalization that's actually visible without scrolling, and an agent-facing guestbook + public analytics dashboard — nobody else appears to have built "agent SEO" analytics for a personal site. What we learned A correct tool isn't the same as a convincing one — tailor_view tool worked perfectly but was almost invisible until we made the change land somewhere a human would actually notice. Trust boundaries need to be designed, not just enforced in code: compose_inquiry tool drafts and discloses, but a human always has to click send. And "agent-native" means building to the open navigator.modelContext standard, not to any one agent's quirks — testing across ChatGPT, Chrome, and a separate coding agent made that concrete fast. What's next for Agent Native Portfolio Extracting the reusable core (context detection, registration manager, generic read tools, deterministic scorer) into a standalone open-source Astro integration package, so any developer can make their own portfolio agent-native by defining one structured data file. title: Nook & Nest
pitch: A cozy 3D apartment planner where you and your AI agent design, furnish, and personalize your future home together—powered by WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A cozy 3D apartment planner where you and your AI agent design, furnish, and personalize your future home together—powered by WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates I started Nook & Nest because a friend of mine was looking for a rental apartment and wanted to figure out how to furnish it. I thought it would be nice to have a website where you could quickly build your floor plan and move furniture around before buying anything or moving in. I wanted it to be useful, but also something you would enjoy spending time in. I really like the cozy miniature look of Tiny Glade, so that inspired the feeling I was going for. Rather than a technical-looking floor planner, I wanted decorating to feel more like a relaxing game. The project grew from there. You can build rooms to real measurements, add floors, walls, doors and windows, and choose furniture, appliances, lighting and decorations. You can change colors and materials, right down to placing books and small decorations on shelves. Getting the furniture looking right took a lot of back and forth. The early models looked like disconnected blobs, and I wasn’t happy with them. We moved toward original Blender models with more recognizable shapes and cleaner textures. Small things like being able to preview furniture before placing it, zoom in close, and easily find items in the library made a big difference too. When I heard about the WebMCP Challenge, I wanted to take it a step further: let an AI agent actually furnish the apartment with you. Not just suggest a sofa in a chat, but look at the apartment, browse the available furniture, and put together an arrangement inside the planner. Through WebMCP, an agent can read the layout and measurements, find furniture, and propose a design. You review the changes first, or you can give it permission to edit directly if you want to let it get creative. You can pause its access and undo an arrangement, so you’re still in control of your space. I built Nook & Nest with help from Codex, using React, TypeScript, Babylon.js and Blender. A lot of the process was trying something, looking at it, and asking what would make it feel better to use. Adding agent support also taught me that the agent needs clear information about the space and clear boundaries around what it can change. There’s still more I want to improve, especially comparing different layouts and expanding the furniture styles. But the idea is still the same as when I started: make it easier to picture your future home and have some fun decorating it. Now you can invite an AI agent to help, or see what it comes up with on its own. title: Urban Planning Copilot
pitch: Helping cities make smarter decisions by pairing planners with an AI collaborator that explores possibilities, reveals trade-offs, and keeps humans in control.
about_excerpt: Helping cities make smarter decisions by pairing planners with an AI collaborator that explores possibilities, reveals trade-offs, and keeps humans in control. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Inspiration This started with a question about how small planning choices can lead to very different outcomes for a city. Shiwani has a university course called Introduction to City , where her instructor teaches urban planning and how these choices can affect the larger system. We started wondering what it would look like if AI could help a planner explore those choices and their consequences. We also worked on Build What, Move India by Varun Mayya, powered by OpenAI, where we explored bringing maps and Records of Rights together. That gave us some experience with combining spatial information and structured records. What it does Urban Planning Copilot is a map-first workspace for exploring urban planning scenarios. For our current case, we use housing in San Francisco. Housing supply and affordability are significant concerns for the city, and its Housing Element targets 82,000 new homes between 2023 and 2031. In the current study, the planner sets a goal of 2,000 homes in Mission and SoMa. The system evaluates potential sites using factors such as transit access, flood risk, parks, schools, zoning, and capacity. The current analysis finds capacity for about 1,098 homes, so the shortfall is visible. The planner can then: Explore and inspect candidate sites. Change constraints and rerun the analysis. Shortlist sites directly on the shared map. Create and compare different scenarios. Why WebMCP matters We wanted the AI to work inside the planning workspace, not just describe what is on the screen. Through WebMCP, the AI can: Run the analysis and inspect candidates. Change planning constraints. Move the shared map to relevant sites. Add candidates to the shortlist. Create and compare scenario branches. Prepare a decision for planner approval. These are planning actions rather than browser actions. The AI works with the same application state as the planner, so when it changes something, the planner sees that change in the workspace too. For consequential actions, the AI prepares the change and the planner approves or rejects it. How we built it We built a shared planning model around projects, scenarios, analysis results, candidates, decisions, and provenance. The spatial analysis uses San Francisco geographic datasets covering parcels, transit, flood areas, parks, and schools. Candidate scoring and capacity calculations are deterministic, while AI suggestions are kept separate from the underlying calculations. The application and WebMCP tools use the same underlying services and state. We also track provenance so it is clear whether something came from source data, a calculation, an AI suggestion, or a planner decision. What we learned Building this changed how we think about the role of AI in planning. AI can investigate, calculate, compare, and prepare options. The planner still brings the context and judgment needed to decide between them. We also found that WebMCP is most useful when its tools represent meaningful actions in the user's workflow, rather than low-level interactions with a website. What's next We want to take the planning side further, but first we want to make sure we are solving the right problems. We are not urban planning domain experts, so the next step is to work with SMEs and practitioners to validate our assumptions, constraints, workflows, and outputs. We'd especially like to learn from people who teach and practice urban planning, including potentially Shiwani's instructor. From there, we want to improve the current workflow, add more real datasets and geographies, and explore planning decisions beyond the current housing use case. title: Job hunt AI
pitch: Autonomous AI career copilot with sub-2ms job matching, resume tailoring, real-world A/B response rate tracking, and voice-driven mock interview coaching.
about_excerpt: Autonomous AI career copilot with sub-2ms job matching, resume tailoring, real-world A/B response rate tracking, and voice-driven mock interview coaching. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for Job hunt AI Inspiration Job hunting today is fundamentally broken, stressful, and opaque. Candidates spend dozens of hours every week manually browsing fragmented job boards (LinkedIn, Indeed, Glassdoor), uploading resumes into automated Applicant Tracking Systems (ATS) without knowing if their keywords align, and receiving silent rejections with zero feedback. Most critically, candidates have no scientific way to A/B test their resumes . When a candidate tweaks their resume, they have no data on whether Version B actually converted better into interviews than Version A. Furthermore, interview practice is often generic and detached from the specific role. We built JobHunt AI to transform the job search from an unmeasured, blind lottery into an empirical, data-driven career acceleration engine. What it does JobHunt AI is an autonomous, full-stack career platform that unifies the entire job search lifecycle: Instant Multi-Source Job Search & Match Engine : Aggregates opportunities across multiple platforms and runs an in-memory scoring algorithm ( scoreJobRelevance ) in under 2 milliseconds, providing a 65%–99% match score with clear explanations. Universal Document Parser & AI Tailoring : Accepts PDF, DOCX, and TXT files. Generates tailored cover letters (250–400 words), extracts candidate profiles, identifies skill gaps, and recommends verified certification courses (Coursera, Udemy, AWS) with duration and difficulty. Scientific Resume A/B Testing : Mode 1 (Comparative ATS Review) : Instant side-by-side comparison scoring ATS keyword density and structure. Mode 2 (Empirical Callback Attribution) : Links applications in PostgreSQL to specific resumeVersionId s to track real response rates, days to response, timeline trends, and statistical sample confidence levels (Low, Moderate, High). Hands-Free Voice AI Mock Interview Coach : Generates 8 role-specific questions (Behavioral, Technical, Culture Fit) with model benchmark answers. Candidates speak out loud using the browser-native Web Speech API , and the AI grades answers on a 0–100 scale using the STAR framework (Situation, Task, Action, Result). Visual 5-Stage Pipeline & Database-Grounded Copilot : Visual Kanban tracker with follow-up deadline alerts and an AI assistant injected with live user database KPIs (total applied, response rate %, upcoming dates) to eliminate hallucinations. Two-Sided Recruiter Hub & 1-Click Email Referrals : Recruiters search candidate talent pools by parsed skills and dispatch branded HTML referral emails via Resend featuring 1-click interactive "Accept Referral" and "Reject" buttons. WebMCP Architecture & Chrome Extension : Exposes 9 core backend tools via document.modelContext.registerTool for browser-native agent interoperability, plus a 1-click Chrome Extension web clipper. How we built it We engineered a decoupled, production-grade cloud architecture: Frontend : Next.js 15 (App Router), React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Lucide React icons, and Recharts for interactive analytics. WebMCP Integration : Registered 9 core tools via document.modelContext.registerTool in app/webmcp-tools.tsx with a live agent activity indicator. Voice Recording : Browser-native Web Speech API ( SpeechRecognition / webkitSpeechRecognition ) for real-time speech-to-text transcription. Authentication & Authorization : Clerk Auth with custom publicMetadata role routing ( candidate vs recruiter ). AI Inference & Resilience : Groq high-speed inference running a 3-tier multi-model fallback chain ( openai/gpt-oss-120b $\rightarrow$ qwen/qwen3.8-27b $\rightarrow$ openai/gpt-oss-20b ), structured with Vercel AI SDK ( generateObject , generateText ) and validated with Zod schemas. Document Processing : unpdf (WASM arrayBuffer page-merging for PDFs) and mammoth (Node buffer extraction for DOCX) with token budgeting and non-printable character sanitization. Database & ORM : PostgreSQL managed with Prisma ORM across 5 relational entities ( User , UserResume , Job , Application , ReferralRequest ). Transactional Email : Resend API for HTML email dispatch with real-time callback webhook endpoints. Deployment : Hosted on Vercel with continuous deployment. Challenges we ran into Sub-Second Job Matching : Calling LLMs for every search query caused noticeable latency. We solved this by designing a deterministic in-memory scoring algorithm ( scoreJobRelevance ) in TypeScript that weighs query tokens (+12), skills (+8), descriptions (+4), and remote tags (+6) in under 2ms. AI Provider Uptime & Rate Limits : Relying on a single AI endpoint risked demo downtime. We implemented an automatic multi-model fallback catch-and-retry mechanism across Groq open-source weights. Cross-Platform Document Extraction : Parsing complex multi-column PDFs without server crashes required moving away from legacy C++ bindings to WebAssembly-based unpdf . Relational A/B Attribution : Designing the database schema so that status updates ( Applied $\rightarrow$ Interviewing $\rightarrow$ Offer ) accurately aggregate back to individual resume versions while calculating statistical sample confidence levels. Accomplishments that we're proud of Building a true closed-loop system where every candidate action feeds into downstream analytics rather than a collection of disconnected features. Implementing browser-native voice interview coaching with real-time transcript streaming and STAR-framework grading without paid external speech APIs. Implementing the emerging WebMCP standard by exposing 9 authenticated backend tools to AI agents through document.modelContext . Designing a two-sided referral loop with transactional email actions that update the database in real time. What we learned How to design zero-downtime AI fallback pipelines using open-source models on high-speed inference engines. How to implement WebMCP browser-level tool registration and handle graceful degradation in standard browsers. The nuances of ATS keyword parsing and WebAssembly document text extraction. How to structure statistical confidence metrics to prevent misleading insights on small data sample sizes. What's next for JobHunt AI 1-Click Application Form Autofill : Enhancing our Chrome Extension to auto-populate job applications across Workday, Greenhouse, and Lever portals. Enterprise ATS Webhooks : Direct integrations with company HR software for automatic application status synchronization. Webcam Video AI Coach : Multi-modal video analysis for eye contact, pacing, and confidence during mock interviews. title: Her Shopping
pitch: Shop alongside your agent. A storefront that redraws itself around your mission.
about_excerpt: Shop alongside your agent. A storefront that redraws itself around your mission. Like 3 Comment Story Updates External Chat action Voice interaction Voice intent understanding Observable actions taken by agent Inspiration Online shopping is still organized around catalogs, but people usually think in outcomes: a trip, an event, a budget, a deadline, and a set of tradeoffs. We wanted to build a storefront where an agent in various interfaces could work with the shopper inside the actual interface, not just chat beside it or click through it. Her as the name of the voice assistant and as a reference to the movie. What it does Her Shopping is an adaptive outdoor storefront that reshapes itself around a shopper’s mission. A user can say something like, “I’m going camping. Keep the total below $700, prioritize warmth and Friday delivery,” and the store reorganizes products into Essential, Useful, and Optional groups. The agent can search products, compare options, change the layout, add items to the cart, open checkout review, and request a demo order. Every change is visible, reversible, and shared with the human. Checkout is simulated and requires explicit human confirmation. How we built it We built the app with React, TypeScript, Vinext, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Base UI, OpenAI Sites, and WebMCP. The site registers 20 typed WebMCP tools using document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Those tools are backed by a shared capability registry, strict JSON Schemas, state-version checks, a single reducer, layout invariants, undo history, and an activity ledger. Voice is powered by the OpenAI Realtime API over WebRTC. The in-page voice agent uses the same validated shopping actions as the WebMCP tools and the human UI. Challenges we ran into The main challenge was making the agent feel powerful without making the user lose control. We had to design tools that were semantic enough for agents, but bounded enough to be safe and predictable. We also had to make agent actions legible on screen. That led to the shared activity ledger, change highlighting, undo support, strict schemas, and a checkout gate that an agent cannot bypass. To find the right balance between human and agent interaction Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that WebMCP is load-bearing in the product. The agent does not just operate the page; it can reshape the storefront’s information architecture around the user’s mission. We are also proud of the shared action layer. Human controls, voice, and WebMCP all mutate the same state through the same validation path, so the experience stays inspectable, deterministic, and reversible. What we learned We learned that WebMCP works best when the website exposes meaningful product-level actions instead of low-level UI clicks. The strongest experience came from treating the page as a shared workspace for both the person and the agent. We also learned that trust depends on visibility. Users need to see what changed, why it changed, and how to undo it before they will comfortably let an agent help with a multi-step task. A WebMCP-powered School ERP that lets educators manage attendance, fees, and records instantly through natural language using AI agents.

 What it does

 What's next for Agent-Native School ERP: Powered by WebMCP 

 Project Story 

 Inspiration
Traditional School ERP systems are notoriously complex, packed with dense menus, multi-step forms, and steep learning curves. We realized that teachers and school administrators spend hours navigating these clunky interfaces instead of focusing on what truly matters: education. When WebMCP was introduced, we saw the perfect opportunity to bridge the gap between complex databases and human intent. We wanted to transform the UX from "navigational" to "conversational," allowing educators to manage an entire school through simple natural language. 

 What it does
Our project is a full-stack, Agent-Native School Management System. It allows AI agents (like ChatGPT) to act as an administrative co-pilot directly within the browser. Once an administrator logs securely into the dashboard, the app exposes 7 powerful WebMCP tools: 

 search_student_records
mark_attendance
check_pending_fees
get_class_summary
get_class_students
generate_invoice
add_student
Instead of clicking through five different screens to find pending fees and generate an invoice, an administrator can simply type: "Find all Grade 3 students with pending fees and generate their invoices." The AI agent automatically chains the WebMCP tools to complete the workflow in seconds. 

 How we built it
We adopted a robust full-stack architecture: 

 Frontend: React and Vite, deployed on Netlify.
Backend: Java Spring Boot, deployed on Render.
Database: PostgreSQL hosted on Supabase.
WebMCP Integration: We used the window.document.modelContext.registerTool API inside a secure, authenticated React useEffect hook. We ensured that tools are strictly exposed only after a successful JWT/Session login. Each tool is equipped with a strict JSON schema for input validation, and the execute function securely passes the user's authentication token/cookies to our Spring Boot backend.
Challenges we ran into
Building a production-ready WebMCP app came with serious hurdles: 

 Supabase Connection Limits: Our Spring Boot's default HikariCP connection pool quickly exhausted the Supabase free tier's 15 concurrent connections limit, causing FATAL: EMAXCONNSESSION errors during deployment. We solved this by strictly limiting the maximum-pool-size and managing idle timeouts.
Cross-Domain Authentication: Because our frontend was on Netlify and backend on Render, the browser blocked our session cookies, throwing 400 Bad Request errors. We had to dive deep into Spring Security to configure Cross-Site cookies using SameSite=None and Secure=true.
Strict CORS Policies: Managing wildcard origins with credentials proved difficult until we upgraded our configuration to use allowedOriginPatterns.
AI Form-Filling Limitations: We learned that headless browsers used by AI agents sometimes struggle with complex SPA login forms, which required us to optimize our DOM structure for agent readability.
Accomplishments that we're proud of
Successfully building and integrating 7 diverse read and write WebMCP tools in a short span of time.
Achieving a secure architecture where AI agents operate strictly within the bounds of human authentication (tools are hidden behind the login screen).
Successfully deploying a complex 3-tier architecture (Netlify + Render + Supabase) that runs seamlessly in the cloud.
What we learned
We gained a profound understanding of the new WebMCP specifications and how the document.modelContext interacts with the browser's DOM. We also learned how to write strict JSON schemas that prevent AI hallucinations, ensuring the agent always sends exactly what the Spring Boot backend expects. 

 What's next for Agent-Native School ERP: Powered by WebMCP
We plan to expand the agent's capabilities by adding WebMCP tools for generating report cards, scheduling parent-teacher meetings, and eventually integrating an automated WhatsApp notification system for parents directly triggered by the AI agent's actions.

title: Together - by Human For AI
pitch: A shared workspace for Human + AI agent to hire a real human - together. Your agent drafts the task on this page through WebMCP tools, and you decide how much rope it gets.
about_excerpt: A shared workspace for Human + AI agent to hire a real human - together. Your agent drafts the task on this page through WebMCP tools, and you decide how much rope it gets. Like Comment Story Updates Process flow: you set the goal, your agent drafts and asks (or acts under Autopilot), a verified human does the work, the result returns. Approval bar: the agent drafted the task on the page and is blocked in await_human, a tool call that only a human click resolves. WebMCP inspector: every tool call logged live with its arguments and result, plus totals: calls, median ms, refusals, stops for the human. Live capability manifest: what each of the 7 tools would do right now (ready, or a coded refusal) and the 4 actions that are never tools. Real run in the ChatGPT desktop app: agent-drafted task, approved on the page, delivered by the verified human operator with a receipt. On a phone: the three lanes stack, the agent drafts and asks for approval, and the live manifest shows what each tool would do right now. The inversion Every WebMCP app in this challenge, is a site an agent can drive for a human. Together is the opposite: a site where the agent is the customer and the human is the service. Human For AI (humanforai.dev) is a live platform where AI agents hire one verified human operator for anything in the real-world. It has served real autonomous agents over REST and MCP since July. WebMCP finally gave it the missing surface: the place where an agent and its own human meet. Why hire a human through an agent? Because an agent hits three walls that no model update removes. It can't walk into a shop and check whether a recalled hair-dryer is still on the shelf (hands). It can't tell you how your headline lands on a stranger in the first three seconds (eyes). And when a judgment call goes wrong, it can't be the one who answers for it (judgment). A human can. But the human who owns the agent shouldn't have to find one, brief one, and chase one - that is precisely the kind of errand they delegated an agent for. So the agent does the hiring, and WebMCP is what puts that hiring on a page the human can see, edit, and approve. The demo video makes this case in the agent's own voice from 0:19 to 0:48; the hair-dryer check is a real delivered task, shown with its signed receipt at the end. Try it in 60 seconds With a WebMCP client (ChatGPT desktop app browser, or Chrome 149+ with WebMCP): open humanforai.dev/together , type a goal, and ask your agent: "Work with me on this page - read my goal and draft the task for my approval." Approve with a click, or flip Autopilot. Any browser : press Simulate an agent . A scripted agent drives the page's real tool objects, gets refused, blocks on your click, and walks a clearly labeled simulated task through the operator lifecycle. Nothing is sent. DevTools : the seven tools are auditable at window.__hfaiTogetherTools , every check in TESTING.md runs from the console in under a minute. What it does /together is a shared workspace with three seats: you , your agent (via WebMCP in ChatGPT's browser or Chrome), and a real human operator on the far end of the API. You type a goal in plain words. Your agent reads it off the page ( read_workspace ) and drafts the formal task on the page ( draft_task ). Every field is tagged with who wrote it last - and you can edit any field directly. One document, two authors. You choose the approval regime. Default: nothing ships without your physical click - the agent calls await_human , a WebMCP tool call that literally blocks until a human presses a button. Or flip Autopilot : grant standing authority with an optional scope note ("UX feedback tasks only, nothing physical"), and your agent submits on its own while you watch. Revocable with one click, the rules text every agent reads rewrites itself the moment you flip it. And if you finished editing the draft yourself, Submit this draft myself sends it without a round-trip through chat: same gate as the agent's submit_approved_task , your click is the approval, and an agent still blocked in await_human is told submitted_by_human with the task ID so it tracks the task instead of submitting it twice. Then the third participant appears. The task pings a real human's phone. The page shows the moment a human sees it ( seen_by_operator_at ), the ETA, the status history, the operator's thread replies - live, for both of you. Delivery carries a signed receipt (EdDSA JWS binding the deliverable's SHA-256 to the task lifecycle, verifiable offline against JWKS). Delegation flowing one way, human-in-the-loop flowing the other - on one page. Why WebMCP is the fit (and not just another API) The REST API and MCP server already serve fully autonomous agents. What they can't do is put the agent and its human in the same room . WebMCP can, because the tool surface lives in a shared browser tab: read_workspace lets the agent read what the human typed on the page - not relayed through chat. draft_task makes the agent's work visible and human-editable in place, with per-field provenance. await_human is only possible in-page: a tool call resolved by a physical click. Try that over HTTP. The Autopilot toggle turns the page into a delegation contract both parties can see. The page degrades gracefully: no WebMCP → fully manual workspace, and a Simulate an agent button that drives the page's real tool objects with a scripted agent - it drafts, gets refused when it tries to submit unapproved, blocks in await_human until you click, then walks a clearly marked simulated task through the operator lifecycle. Nothing is sent. A WebMCP inspector under the lanes logs every tool call, real or simulated, with its exact arguments and result - so judges in any browser can see the protocol, not just read about it. The tools also stay auditable at window.__hfaiTogetherTools . Least authority, made visible A live capability manifest above the inspector shows what each of the seven registered tools would do at this moment - ready , or refuses: not_approved / no_draft / no_reply_address - and lists the four actions that have no tool form at all: approve, reject, grant Autopilot, revoke Autopilot. Those are clicks, and only clicks. The tools stay registered for the whole session and the gates live inside them: a call the state doesn't allow returns a structured refusal ( isError plus an error code and the reason), so an agent learns what to do next rather than finding a tool missing. Every result is bounded to 8,000 serialized characters - long text is shortened with a marker and a truncated note, structure is never dropped - and arguments are accepted as an object or a JSON string. The expected journeys, per-phase refusals, and invariants are encoded machine-readably in evals/together-journey.json , with hand-run results in EVALS.md and console-reproducible checks in TESTING.md . How I built it No framework, no build step. The workspace engine ( together.js ) is a single state object with three writers -human controls, WebMCP tools, and live polling of the operator API - rendered into three lanes and persisted in localStorage (cross-tab safe). The WebMCP layer registers via document.modelContext (W3C draft) with navigator.modelContext fallback, and the site-wide layer mirrors the REST/MCP tools one-to-one, plus declarative toolname attributes on every form. Backend: Firebase Functions - tasks, message threads, signed webhooks, receipts. One interface, three readers: human form, JSON API, in-page tools - same endpoints, same validation. The page is responsive: on a phone the three lanes stack, the banner wraps, and every control keeps a 44px touch target. Challenges I ran into Three writers, one document. Human edits, agent tool calls, and API polling all mutate the same workspace state - and the workspace persists across tabs. A second open tab could silently clobber the agent's draft with stale state, I fixed it by adopting foreign writes via the storage event instead of overwriting. A tool call with a human inside it. await_human deliberately refuses to resolve until a physical click happens. Making that feel natural to the model (and not like a hung tool) took careful result text and rules copy. Autonomy vs. oversight. my whole platform is built on agents acting alone - a mandatory human gate would betray the brand. The Autopilot toggle is the resolution: the human picks the regime, the page rewrites the rules agents read the moment it flips, and the grant is revocable in one click. What's real Everything. There's no fake operator: the Simulate button is labeled as such and never sends anything, while a task actually submitted from the workspace push-notifies a real human, who reviews, accepts, and delivers with a cryptographic receipt. The platform has a public pre-registered experiment where the human operator beat a frontier model on a review task, real commercial tasks from external agents, and listings across the MCP registry, npm, and Smithery under cryptog

pitch: INTENT is a workspace where humans and AI agents can figure out what matters and turn it into a clear direction. With WebMCP, agents can directly inspect with the intent instead of just chatting.\n
about_excerpt:
INTENT is a workspace where humans and AI agents can figure out what matters and turn it into a clear direction. With WebMCP, agents can directly inspect with the intent instead of just chatting.

 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 



 
 Why I Built INTENT 

 I kept coming back to a simple problem: when we use AI, we usually start with a prompt and immediately ask it to do something. But sometimes the hardest part is figuring out what we actually want to do in the first place. 

 That became the idea behind INTENT — a workspace where the human and the AI can work on the intent itself before jumping into execution. 

 How I Built It 

 I built INTENT as a Next.js web app with a structured workspace for an evolving intent. Instead of keeping everything inside a chat, the application keeps track of things like intent nodes, decisions, actions, and open questions. 

 The interesting part for this challenge was connecting that workspace to AI agents through WebMCP. 

 I exposed six tools that let an agent work with the actual application state: 

 
 "inspect_intent" 
 "add_intent_node" 
 "focus_attention" 
 "surface_contradiction" 
 "propose_intent_evolution" 
 "fork_intent" 
 

 These aren't just functions that return text. They are connected to the workspace, so when an agent uses them, the changes can be reflected in the UI. 

 What I Learned 

 The biggest thing I learned was that agent interaction feels different when the agent can actually interact with the application instead of only generating a response. 

 Designing the tools also made me think carefully about what an agent should be allowed to do. I wanted the human to remain in control while still giving the agent enough access to be genuinely useful. 

 I also learned a lot about the practical side of WebMCP — especially tool registration, connecting tools to application state, and testing the experience in the browser. 

 Challenges 

 The main challenge was getting the WebMCP integration working with the current API. My initial implementation used an older registration pattern, which caused the tools to fail during registration. 

 I had to update the implementation to the current "ModelContext" API and make sure the tools were registered correctly without causing repeated registrations during React development and refreshes. 

 Another challenge was making the tools useful enough to represent real actions in the workspace rather than just creating a collection of demo functions. 

 What's Next 

 INTENT is still an early version, but the direction I find interesting is giving agents more meaningful ways to participate in applications while keeping the human in control. 

 For me, WebMCP makes that interaction feel much more direct: the agent doesn't just talk about the workspace — it can actually work with it.
