title: Blnq Studio
pitch: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations.
about_excerpt: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration I built blnq.studio because front-end work had become a pile of tabs: an editor, a dev server, a browser, DevTools, an accessibility checker, a design spec, and now an AI chat window that can't see any of them. Every one of those handoffs is where quality leaks out — especially accessibility, which is the first thing dropped when you're moving fast and the last thing an AI agent notices, because it can't see what it built. I wanted a single tab where the code, the live preview, the audit and the AI all look at the same thing. WebMCP was the missing piece: it lets the editor tab itself become the tool surface an agent uses, so the loop closes without any extra setup. What it does blnq.studio is a browser-based editor purpose-built for front-end: code, preview, ship — all in one tab. Live multi-file editing — Monaco under the hood, real HTML/CSS/JS files with folders and ES module imports, no build step. The preview updates as you type. Accessibility first — every preview refresh runs the pour engine against WCAG 2.0–2.2 A/AA plus best-practice rules. The A11y panel lists each violation with its impact, a plain-English fix and the exact element. Colour-contrast checks are built into the editor, not bolted on afterwards. Multi-device preview — switch viewports, check every breakpoint, see the FPS overlay, all without leaving the tab. Design systems your AI respects — drop a DESIGN.md at the project root and the editor treats it as the source of truth: colour and font literals that drift from your tokens get flagged, so AI-written CSS stays inside the system instead of inventing new values. Baseline compatibility — a built-in tool tab tells you which features you're using aren't yet widely available across browsers. Collaborate and fork — real-time multi-cursor collaboration over Yjs, forks and merge requests, a community showcase. Ship from the editor — push to GitHub, deploy from the menu, or download the whole project as one self-contained HTML file. AI & MCP, on your terms — AI is optional. When you want it, connect Claude Code (or any MCP client) over the built-in MCP server, use the in-editor chat with your own model, or — new for this challenge — turn on WebMCP and let a browser-native agent drive the tab directly. WebMCP: the editor tab is the tool server Click Start WebMCP and blnq registers 30+ tools with the browser via document.modelContext . No MCP ID, no config file, no separate process. An agent running in the browser can then: Read and edit files by line range or find-and-replace, with undo snapshots and live edits landing in the editor and preview See what it built — blnq_screenshot returns a real PNG, plus element inspection, console errors and viewport switching Audit with blnq_check_preview , which returns JS errors, every WCAG violation with its element HTML and fix hint, and any design-token drift Interact — click, type, press keys, wait for elements — so it can tab through a form or open a modal and re-audit the new state Fix and re-audit until the report is clean The key design decision was that WebMCP isn't a separate integration. blnq has one shared tool registry; the MCP server and the WebMCP endpoint are two thin adapters over it. A tool added to the registry appears in both, and edits behave identically — same validation, same undo, same activity toasts, same prompt history — whichever transport the call came in on. How I built it blnq is an Express + Monaco + Yjs app with a plugin system; the MCP server, AI chat, Baseline and spellcheck tools are all plugins. The accessibility engine runs inside the preview iframe and posts results up to the editor, so the panel a human reads and the result an agent reads come from the same run. WebMCP was around 350 lines: a client module that fetches tool descriptors and calls registerTool() for each (with readOnlyHint annotations and MCP-shaped { content } results including images), and a server endpoint that Zod-validates and runs the shared handler. The endpoint is same-origin only and still requires the tab's random bridge ID; the browser handles user consent on its side. What I learned The accessibility audit turned out to be the most valuable thing blnq can hand an agent. A screenshot tells a model roughly what it built; a WCAG report with the offending element and a fix hint tells it exactly what to change. Structured, model-readable audit output beat any amount of prompt engineering. And WebMCP inverts the usual relationship: the page stops being something an agent scrapes and becomes something it calls . Once you have a decent tool registry, the browser becomes the integration layer for free. What's next Structured JSON from blnq_check_preview so agents can diff violations between audits A blnq_fix_a11y tool that applies remedies for common rule classes automatically Focus-order and keyboard-navigation audits driven by key-press sequences Ship the Chrome origin-trial token on blnq.studio so WebMCP works without flags Share a collaboration session with an agent so humans and AI can work on the same project live Built With ai css framework-free html javascript Try it out blnq.studio Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by David Yarham Like Share this project: Updates David Yarham posted an update — Aug 26, 2026 04:58 PM EDT I dont have a youtube or any video of Blnq, it is a live site and no need Log in or sign up for Devpost to join the conversation. title: Sheshat
pitch: Two minds. One shared canvas. The only agentic worksheet builder that checks its own homework.
about_excerpt: Two minds. One shared canvas. The only agentic worksheet builder that checks its own homework. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Worksheets fail for a boring reason: they don't fit. Too long for the period, pitched above the class's reading level, all recall questions and no application, missing half the standard it's supposed to cover. A teacher usually finds this out mid-class, not before printing. I wanted to build something that catches that before the worksheet goes out, not another tool that generates content, but one that keeps checking whether the content actually works, the whole time you're building it. WebMCP made the second half of that idea possible: instead of an AI suggesting text in a chat window, the page itself could hand an agent real, callable tools (check_reading_level, check_time_estimate) and let it act on the actual worksheet directly, alongside the teacher, not instead of them. What it does Sheshat is a worksheet workspace where a teacher and an AI agent build the same document together, live. You start from a photo of an old worksheet, a whiteboard, or pasted notes, and the app drafts real, grounded questions from what's actually there. From then on, four checks stay visible at all times: completion time, reading level, question-type balance, and standards coverage. You can edit the worksheet directly (rewrite, reorder, delete a question by hand) or tell the agent what to change in plain language ("swap the fractions question for something on decimals"), and it calls the exact same tools a direct edit would trigger. Either path updates the same board and reruns all four checks immediately. The worksheet isn't "done" when it has content, it's done when all four checks pass. A dashboard sits in front of the editor: the agent can list your worksheets, filter them, create a new one, and open it, not just edit inside one page, but navigate the whole workspace. In total, the app exposes 24 WebMCP tools across two route-scoped surfaces: 4 on the dashboard, 20 inside the editor. How we built it React + Vite on the frontend, a small Node API with SQLite for persistence, deployed on Vercel. Every constraint check is real, deterministic logic, not a model guess: word/question-count heuristics for time, sentence-complexity heuristics for reading level, straightforward tallying for question mix and standards coverage. The kind of thing that has to stay reliable even if generation has a bad day. WebMCP sits on top of all of it via document.modelContext.registerTool(). Tools are scoped by route: dashboard tools when you're browsing your worksheets, the full editing toolset once you're inside one, so an agent only sees the actions that are actually relevant to where the teacher is. Challenges we ran into The hardest bug wasn't glamorous: an early version of swap_question wrote its own input instruction into the question text instead of a real generated question. The worksheet would silently fill with prompt text instead of usable content. Fixed with real validation guards: reject output that's empty, malformed, or suspiciously identical to the input, and fail visibly instead of committing broken content. A security review also surfaced two real issues: the local API would accept state-changing requests from any website open in another tab (no origin validation), and the image-source tool would happily fetch and render an arbitrary remote URL. Both are fixed now, with strict origin/content-type checks on every mutation endpoint, and image input restricted to inline data only. Accomplishments that we're proud of The four-check system actually does what it claims. I can point to a real before/after: a generated draft opening at 2 of 4 checks satisfied, one direct edit and one agent command later, 4 of 4. Not a mocked demo state, the same recalculation runs every time, from real logic, on real edits. I'm also proud of catching my own bugs before they became someone else's problem (the swap bug, the security findings) by actually testing the exact flows a judge or user would try, not just trusting that generated code worked. What we learned That "AI-powered" is doing a lot of work to hide whether something actually functions. It was tempting more than once to let a claim stand ("it's fixed," "it's dynamic") without re-testing it myself. The moments this project actually got better were the ones where I stopped and checked instead. I also learned the real difference between a chatbot suggesting worksheet text and an agent calling structured tools on a live page: the former can't reliably track question IDs, ordering, or state across a conversation. WebMCP's whole value is that the page, not the chat history, is the source of truth. What's next for Sheshat Real teacher testing. Everything here has been verified by me, not yet by the people it's actually for. Beyond the hackathon scope: accounts, more subjects and grade bands beyond the current Grade 4 to 7 math focus, and eventually making the core "does this fit my class" checking available without requiring a WebMCP-enabled browser, so any teacher can use it, not just ones testing experimental browser flags. title: PrzedWysylka | WebMCP Lab
pitch: A browser-local FA(3) workbench where an agent can prove a repair while approval remains a visible UI decision.
about_excerpt: A browser-local FA(3) workbench where an agent can prove a repair while approval remains a visible UI decision. Like Comment Story Updates 1 The production workbench after WebMCP has staged and validated a two-value repair. Inspiration Invoice XML is boring until one malformed value stops a real workflow. Poland's FA(3) format is strict and large. Inspecting it by eye is difficult. An agent is useful when the fault is two placeholder values buried inside an official template. That does not mean the agent should quietly decide that the repaired document is acceptable. I built PrzedWysylka WebMCP Lab to test a narrower contract. The agent should do the mechanical work against the state already visible in the browser. The reviewer should see the source and proposed bytes. The same screen should show the validation result and final page control. What it does The app opens an official parameterized FA(3) template at Revision 0. The template is intentionally invalid. Its two placeholders fail canonical XSD validation. The page registers exactly six WebMCP tools: get_workspace_status list_official_assets read_official_asset select_official_asset stage_exact_replacements validate_workspace During the demo, the agent selects the template and validates Revision 0. It reads the relevant source lines, then stages two exact replacements. After validating the pending proposal, the page displays its diff and a SHA-256 proof bound to those proposed bytes. There is no WebMCP approval or rejection tool. The review buttons stay in the visible interface. In the demo workflow, I click Approve changes myself. The store creates Revision 1 and runs canonical validation again. An ordinary browser still gets the complete manual workbench. It also gets an honest WebMCP unavailable status instead of a polyfill pretending that the native API exists. Why WebMCP fits this job Without WebMCP, an agent would have to scrape diagnostics from the DOM and infer which file or revision is active. It would then scroll through XML and type into an editor. That is fragile. A remote MCP server would create another copy of state outside the review surface. Here, each tool calls the same asset registry and validator used by the UI. It also uses the page's replacement engine and workspace store. The agent receives bounded structured results. The reviewer watches the same state change in the page. WebMCP is the working interaction contract rather than a decorative endpoint. The missing capabilities matter too. Approval and rejection are not registered as WebMCP tools. Neither are upload, download or submission. The accurate claim is narrow: approval is a visible UI action and is absent from the WebMCP surface. The app does not claim to identify who operates the browser. How I built it The frontend uses React 19 with TypeScript 6 on Vite 8. It feature-detects document.modelContext and registers imperative tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() . The definitions have static descriptions and JSON input schemas. Callback inputs pass through Zod before they reach application state. The callbacks reuse existing application services instead of maintaining an agent-only model. Validation runs in the browser through libxml2 compiled to WebAssembly. The deployed app has no application backend or account system. It also has no analytics and no customer upload path. Every successful tool response is limited to 1,500 serialized characters. Catalog results are paged. Source cursors preserve the locked files' CRLF/LF/bare-CR delimiters. A caller cannot place a cursor inside a UTF-16 surrogate pair. Validation returns the complete finding count with compact summaries and explicit truncation metadata. Proposal proof is owned by the store. validate_workspace hashes the exact content snapshot it checked. The record includes the asset and proposal IDs plus the base revision. It also stores the document generation, validation result and proposed SHA-256. Approval fails closed if any part of that identity is stale. Challenges Registering six functions was the easy part. Keeping async work tied to the same browser state took most of the effort. Cancellation exposed a subtle bug. A dependency could ignore its AbortSignal and resolve late, after the caller had already cancelled. I had to invalidate pending work immediately and check state again after every awaited boundary. A cancelled validation can no longer persist a result or revive an obsolete proof. Byte fidelity caused a different class of failures. Many official files use CRLF, while some contain bare carriage returns. Normalizing line endings made a source excerpt look harmless but broke exact replacement. The reader now slices the original decoded text and returns a recoverable cursor without splitting newline pairs or Unicode surrogate pairs. Evidence also needed a hard boundary. The deterministic Playwright suite uses an injected, standards-shaped harness. That proves callback behavior but not native browser support. A separate production smoke uses Chrome's real document.modelContext ; it records nativeModelContext: true and injectedHarness: false . The report does not pretend that an automated Playwright click was a human approval. Verification The native production smoke registers all six tools and executes every callback. It confirms that the WebMCP surface contains no approval tool. Every proof location resolves to the same value, from proposal preflight through the final applied draft: a41799c158deca1bca74e1a158a0748f401721b0ed4b5731ef1a38cfa087c3f0 The offline corpus gate checks all 55 locked first-party records. Browser WASM validation agrees with an independent xmllint gate on 28 expected-valid and 16 expected-invalid FA(3) records. The committed suite covers shared state and cancellation. It tests proposal gating and the visible approval path as separate boundaries. Other checks exercise the ordinary-browser fallback. Responsive layouts and Axe audits run too. The evidence files are committed under docs/assets/ . They record the exact browser build and production artifact identity used for the smoke instead of relying on a screenshot label. What I learned WebMCP works best when a page exposes capabilities it already owns. Creating a parallel agent backend would have weakened this project because the reviewer and agent could disagree about selection or revision state. I also learned that small protocol details become product behavior very quickly. Output limits and cancellation are not cleanup tasks. Neither are cursor semantics or proof identity. If any one of them is vague, the approval screen can look trustworthy while referring to old or incomplete work. What's next The same approach could support other regulated schemas where an agent prepares a repair but the final review stays visible. User-provided documents would require a separate privacy design and threat model before I add an upload path. The six-tool competition surface will remain narrow. title: SJMaths — WebMCP AI-Ready Curriculum & Tools
pitch: Turning static CBSE Class 10 mathematics into 13 browser-native WebMCP tools so external AI agents can teach with zero backend costs or answer leaks.
about_excerpt: Turning static CBSE Class 10 mathematics into 13 browser-native WebMCP tools so external AI agents can teach with zero backend costs or answer leaks. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration SJMaths is a static educational platform built for CBSE mathematics students. We host structured notes, formulas, and practice problems with zero backend servers. With the rise of AI agents like ChatGPT and Claude that can browse the web, we noticed a major dilemma for static educational websites: Students try using AI to learn from websites , but models usually just read the text, summarize blindly, or blurt out the answer keys immediately when asked for hints. Adding an embedded AI tutor is expensive : Running server-side LLM wrappers requires API keys, ongoing GPU server costs, and constant maintenance. When we discovered the Web Model Context Protocol (WebMCP) , we realized the perfect architecture: Keep the website 100% static, and let the user's external AI agent (ChatGPT, Gemini, etc.) connect via WebMCP directly in the browser. What it does SJMaths WebMCP converts our entire static CBSE Class 10 mathematics curriculum into 13 browser-native WebMCP tools registered in document.modelContext . When any external AI agent visits the site, it instantly gets structured, typed tools to teach the student: Discover Curriculum Structure: Explore 14 chapters, 45 topics, and 85 skills ( get_curriculum_outline , get_chapter_topics ). Diagnose Prerequisite Foundations: Test foundational prerequisite readiness before introducing advanced concepts ( get_prerequisite_check ). Teach with Verified Concepts & Worked Models: Retrieve verified formulas, common math traps, and step-by-step worked examples ( get_topic_concepts , get_worked_examples ). Anti-Leak Assessment Mode: When students practice, the tools automatically strip answer keys from the content on the client side. The external AI evaluates student attempts through evaluate_practice rather than reading raw answers. 3-Tier Progressive Hints: Provide subtle conceptual nudges (Level 1), calculation steps (Level 2), or full solutions (Level 3) only when the student is stuck ( get_hint ). Client-Side State Tracking: Track error streaks and recommend adaptive next steps ( get_next_learning_action , get_learning_progress ). All tools run client-side in memory with sub-millisecond execution (<1.5ms) and zero server costs. How we built it Universal Curriculum Schema: Organized all 14 chapters into a unified JSON format ( cbse-class-10-mathematics.json ). WebMCP Tool Dispatcher: Built webmcp-tools.js to expose 13 standards-compliant tools via document.modelContext and navigator.modelContext . Client-Side Security & State: Created a lightweight in-memory StateStore that prevents solution leakage and tracks student performance locally in the browser. Interactive Visual Inspector: Built a real-time tool inspector in demo/index.html allowing learners and judges to watch live JSON payloads and latency metrics. Edge-Case Test Suite: Authored webmcp-edge-cases.test.mjs with 61 automated assertions across all 45 topics (100% passing). Challenges we ran into Designing clean, anti-leak filters that give external AI agents rich pedagogical context while strictly withholding answers during assessments. Creating a progressive 3-tier hint engine that adapts to error streaks without leaking solutions prematurely. Ensuring WebMCP tool registration works reliably across multiple browser execution environments. Accomplishments that we're proud of 100% static architecture: zero backend servers or LLM API keys required. Full curriculum coverage: all 14 chapters and 45 topics of CBSE Class 10 Mathematics. Blazing performance: sub-1.5ms in-memory execution latency. Rock-solid stability: 61/61 edge-case tests passing. What we learned WebMCP proves that static websites don't need expensive AI backends to be AI-native. By providing clean, typed tools in the browser, any static site can become an interactive learning environment for external AI agents. What's next for SJMaths Expanding the WebMCP tool schemas to CBSE Classes 9, 11, and 12. Canvas-based handwritten math equation evaluation. I architected the 13 browser-native WebMCP tools in document.modelContext, structured the 14-chapter CBSE Class 10 mathematics schema, developed the client-side state tracking engine with anti-leak assessment security, and built the live interactive demo and 61-point automated test suite. title: ShowMe
pitch: Where did they hide that setting? Your agent lights up where to click next, on your own screen. No help article, no guessing, no handing over your account. Next time you won't need to ask.
about_excerpt: Where did they hide that setting? Your agent lights up where to click next, on your own screen. No help article, no guessing, no handing over your account. Next time you won't need to ask. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I'm bad at finding things in apps. Not proud of it, but it's true. Some real ones: Auth0. I needed to change one setting for a login flow and spent way too long clicking around the dashboard before I found it. The docs said "go to Settings". There are a lot of places called Settings. Jira. New team, new board, and a few days in I'm running standup from it in front of everyone, trying to find where you change an issue type or add a column while people wait. Datadog. When I was learning it I couldn't find where to filter logs properly, and later I struggled to find where the RUM integrations live. And that's me, with a technical background. I can only imagine how the websites regular people use every day make people from other backgrounds struggle. These all have the same problem. The answer exists, someone wrote it down, and it still doesn't help, because it's not on your screen. The AI answer to this is "let the agent do it for you". Agents are great, I use them all day. But that answer has two problems. You didn't learn anything, so next month you'll ask again. And the site now has to trust a robot with your login settings or your money. And sometimes you just can't hand it off. You're presenting. You're running standup. You're the one who's supposed to know where it is. Nobody wants to say "hold on, let me ask the agent" in front of the room. So I didn't want an agent that does it for me. I wanted one that points at my screen and says "there", waits for me to click, and next time I don't need it. That's ShowMe. What it does You open a site in a browser that has WebMCP, and you ask your agent something like "how do I turn on international transfers?" Then this happens: The site gives the agent a map of its own interface. Every screen, every menu, every button, with a sentence about each one. The agent works out the path and hands the whole thing to the page in one call. The page lights up the first thing you need to click, with a short message. You click it. The next one lights up. And so on. You don't wait for the model between steps. It's not involved between steps. Click the wrong thing and the page tells the agent, which re-plans. Say "just do it for me" and the site decides. Opening a menu, fine. Pressing Confirm on a transfer, no. The agent tells you why. When you're done, the agent tells you the path in one line so you remember it. I made two sites to show it. Neither has any guide code in it, just the attributes. PeruBank is a fake bank. The switch for international transfers is four levels deep, and the final Confirm is a button I never want an agent pressing. Meridian is a fake team tracker. Board settings behind one three-dots menu, project settings behind another, a type icon nobody realises is a button. Basically the board I struggled with. Who it's for: anyone in an app with hundreds of settings, like developer dashboards and admin consoles. People who should never hand an agent their account, like my parents and their bank. And anyone learning a tool in front of other people. Why WebMCP To show someone where something is, you need three things, and only the page has them: A map of the interface that's actually true right now. A way to wait for a real click and know it happened. A say in what the agent is allowed to do. A screen-reading agent guesses at all three. You could maybe get the map from an accessibility tree. You can't get the other two. WebMCP gives the site one standard way to hand all three to whatever agent the person is using. That's why this works now and didn't before. How I built it One JavaScript file, one stylesheet, no build step. Both sites use the same two files. The site marks its elements: data-guide is the id. data-guide-desc is a sentence about it, written like you'd explain it to a new colleague. data-guide-delegable means an agent may do this step for you. Leave it off and it's yours. data-guide-danger means it can't be undone. Never delegated. data-screen , data-panel , data-dialog , data-menu group things so the agent knows what has to be open first. The map is rebuilt from the live page every time it's asked for, so anything rendered later is in it too. Whether something is open is read from what's actually visible on screen. Five tools, all registered through document.modelContext.registerTool : get_ui_map and get_current_view . Read-only. Flagged untrustedContentHint because they echo text people typed. run_walkthrough . The long one. Takes the whole path, paces you through it on the page, listens for the AbortSignal , and comes back with what you did and where you are now. If it's taking a while it returns in_progress after 40 seconds and the agent calls again. do_step_for_person . Reads the policy from the markup. Refuses anything not marked delegable. end_walkthrough . Only exists while a guide is running. Registered with an AbortController , so when the guide ends the tool disappears and toolchange fires. A Playwright test drives both sites through getTools and executeTool , with Google's polyfill injected so it runs on plain Chrome. Each site also has an Agent activity panel. It shows which bits of the API have actually been used this session, plus a transcript of every call and every click. I added it because the agent's own call log is just two lines, and everything interesting happens inside one of them. Challenges I ran into The first version did one spotlight per tool call. In ChatGPT's browser every round trip was 10 to 20 seconds, so you'd click and then sit there. Handing the whole path to the page in one call fixed that. Then I hit tool timeouts, which is where in_progress came from. Knowing what the person actually did. Clicks are easy. Text fields need Enter or a pause. Checkboxes fire change, not click, if you hit the label. "Clicked somewhere else" needed a listener on the whole document that ignores the overlay, the label around a checkbox, and the panel button. Things that aren't visible yet. If the agent asks for something inside a closed menu, the page has to say what to open first, in a sentence the agent can act on. Annotations. Not every browser accepts every one, so registration retries without the rejected one and the panel says which. The map is big. About 20K characters on the bank, 40K on the tracker. It works, but it's most of the minute the first answer takes. Accomplishments that I'm proud of The first time it worked end to end in ChatGPT's browser. I asked how to turn on international transfers, the profile menu lit up, I clicked, Settings lit up, I clicked, and it kept going all the way to Confirm without me waiting once. Seven steps, planned once. The version before that had a spinner between every click, so that was the moment I knew the design was right. The bank saying no. I asked the agent to press Confirm for me, and instead of doing it, it came back with PeruBank's own words: this is irreversible and an agent never does it. The agent didn't decide that. I didn't put it in a prompt. It's one attribute on one button, and the tool reads it. That's the part I'd show a bank. Getting the wrong click right. I clicked somewhere else on purpose, and instead of the guide silently breaking, the agent got back exactly what I'd clicked, said so, and re-planned from where I actually was. It took a while to teach the page the difference between "clicked the thing", "clicked the label around the thing", "clicked the panel", and "wandered off". A tool that appears and disappears. end_walkthrough only exists while a guide is running. Open Site tools mid-guide and it's there. Finish, and it's gone. Small, but it means the agent's own tool list tells it what state the page is in, and the browser fires toolchange to say so. The whole thing is one file and one stylesheet, and both demo sites run the exact same two. Nothing in PeruBank or Meridian knows about the guide except the attributes. And the one I actually care about. After the guide, I turned the setting back off myself. No agent, no help article. Profile menu, Settings, Transfer limits, Advanced. Four clicks. That's what it was for. What I learned The biggest one: keep the model out of the loop between steps. My first version asked the agent after every click, and every answer took 10 to 20 seconds. Once the agent planned once and the page did the pacing, the whole thing went from painful to instant. The agent is good at reading a map and planning. The page is good at waiting for a click. Let each do its job. Writing the sentence for each element is the real work. It's the same work as writing a help article, one line per button, written for a colleague. The difference is these lines show up on the person's screen at the moment they need them, instead of in a doc nobody finds. U

title: WAYGO — Agent-Native Travel Marketplace for Africa
pitch: AI agents discover, verify and compare African travel packages while travellers retain control of contact, booking and payment.
about_excerpt: AI agents discover, verify and compare African travel packages while travellers retain control of contact, booking and payment. Like 1 Comment Story Updates WAYGO's WebMCP agent searches, verifies and compares Umrah packages, then pauses for human approval before agency contact or payment. Inspiration Across Africa, travel packages are often fragmented across WhatsApp messages, social media posts and disconnected agency websites. Travellers may need to compare incomplete offers manually while also determining whether an agency is trustworthy. Important details—such as flights, accommodation quality, visa support, transfers and cancellation terms—are rarely presented consistently. This inspired me to build WAYGO , an agent-native travel marketplace based on a simple question: How can a traveller delegate difficult travel research to an AI agent without surrendering control of consequential decisions? I did not want to create another generic AI itinerary chatbot. I wanted the website and the agent to work together. The agent should handle repetitive discovery, verification and comparison tasks, while the traveller remains inside a visual marketplace where every action can be reviewed and changed. What it does WAYGO allows travellers to search and compare representative African travel packages manually or ask a compatible browser agent to complete the research through WebMCP. For example, a traveller can ask: I want to perform Umrah from Abuja in October with a budget of ₦2.5 million. Find suitable packages, verify the best agency, compare the strongest two options and shortlist them. Prepare agency contact, but do not book or pay. The agent discovers WAYGO’s structured tools, executes the workflow and updates the same interface the traveller is viewing. Search filters change, packages are selected for comparison, the shortlist count updates and verification evidence is returned. WAYGO exposes five WebMCP tools: search_travel_packages filters packages by origin, budget and trip type. verify_agency returns the available verification evidence for an agency. compare_packages selects up to three packages for comparison. create_shortlist updates the traveller’s visible shortlist. request_agency_contact prepares a contact request but stops for human approval. The final tool deliberately returns human_approval_required . It opens an approval dialog explaining what would be shared and confirms that no booking or payment will be made. How I built it I built WAYGO with React, TypeScript, Vinext, Tailwind CSS, WebMCP and Cloudflare Workers . The challenge prototype contains representative Nigerian Umrah packages with different departure cities, prices, accommodation levels, durations and inclusions. Its current verification evidence is simulated demonstration data rather than live regulatory information. I registered the tools in the top-level page using document.modelContext.registerTool() . Each tool has: A clear name and description A constrained JSON input schema An execution function connected to the application’s React state A structured result that the agent can interpret My most important architectural decision was connecting the WebMCP tools to the same state used by the visual marketplace. The agent is not operating an invisible parallel system. When it searches, compares or shortlists packages, the traveller sees those changes immediately. I also designed WAYGO as a progressive enhancement. When WebMCP is unavailable, the website remains functional through its manual filters, package cards, comparison controls and approval dialog. Challenges I ran into Designing tools around user intentions It would have been easy to expose low-level actions such as “click this button” or “change this field.” Instead, I designed tools around meaningful travel intentions: search, verify, compare, shortlist and prepare contact. This required carefully defining each tool’s responsibility and structured response. Maintaining a shared human-agent workspace The agent’s actions needed to remain visible and understandable. I connected tool execution directly to the marketplace state so users can inspect and modify every result. This makes WAYGO a cooperative workspace rather than a chatbot beside a disconnected website. Establishing a safe autonomy boundary Travel transactions can involve personal information and substantial financial commitments. I prevented the agent from booking or paying. Even the contact workflow stops at a clear approval dialog. The agent prepares the next step, but the human decides whether it should happen. Working with an experimental standard WebMCP is still experimental and is not available in every browser or model configuration. I tested WAYGO in a compatible ChatGPT integrated browser and confirmed that all five tools were discoverable and functional. I retained complete manual controls so the marketplace remains usable in ordinary browsers. Keeping the prototype focused A production marketplace would require live inventory, licensed-agency integrations, evidence-backed verification, identity management and payment infrastructure. For this challenge, I focused on one polished workflow: Search → Verify → Compare → Shortlist → Human approval → Contact preparation Accomplishments I’m proud of Built and deployed a functioning agent-native travel marketplace. Implemented five discoverable WebMCP tools. Synchronized agent actions with the visible human interface. Demonstrated structured agency-verification evidence. Created a budget-aware search, comparison and shortlist workflow. Established a clear human-approval boundary before agency contact. Prevented autonomous booking and payment. Made the application responsive and manually usable without WebMCP. Published the complete source code and implementation documentation. What I learned The biggest lesson I learned was that making a website agent-native involves much more than adding a chatbot. Good agent tools need to represent genuine user goals, use predictable schemas and return structured results. Agent actions should remain visible in the human interface so users understand what changed and why. I also learned that autonomy should be designed in layers. Search and comparison are relatively low-risk tasks that can be delegated confidently. Contact, booking and payment require progressively stronger human confirmation. WebMCP makes it possible to express these boundaries while keeping the agent useful. Most importantly, building WAYGO showed me how agent-native interfaces can address problems that are especially relevant in African markets: fragmented information, inconsistent digital experiences and the need for stronger trust signals. What’s next for WAYGO My next step is to connect WAYGO to licensed Nigerian and African travel agencies, ingest live package availability, verify licences against authoritative sources and support additional departure cities and travel categories. I also plan to add consent-based agency messaging and persistent traveller shortlists. Booking and payment would remain separately confirmed actions. My long-term goal is to make WAYGO trusted infrastructure for human-agent travel collaboration across Africa: agents handle fragmented research, the marketplace provides transparent shared state and people remain in control where it matters. title: Finish Small App — Release Evidence Desk
pitch: Proof, not vibes, for small-app releases.
about_excerpt: Proof, not vibes, for small-app releases. Like Comment Story Updates Midnight control room: five evidence tracks and a release claim dashboard. Agent records a human-supplied observation; supporting proof stays pending human review. Sanitized handoff export removes secrets, private paths, email addresses, and private URLs. Final live dashboard: evidence-derived 2/6 coverage, contradictions, gaps, and operation log. Inspiration Independent developers routinely finish a build and accidentally describe the whole release as complete. But “the source exists,” “the build passed,” “the artifact installed,” “it launched,” “a human completed the journey,” and “the exact version is public” are six different facts. That evidence gap becomes more dangerous when agents help with release work. An agent can summarize logs and record observations, but it cannot honestly claim that a person played a game, that a real device test happened, or that an external store accepted and published a version unless evidence for that exact boundary exists. Release Evidence Desk turns that problem into a visible, shared workspace: proof, not vibes, for small-app releases. What it does A person creates a release project, records exact claims, attaches dated evidence, and sees evidence-derived verdicts across five tracks: Source Build Install / Runtime Human Play External Release The desk separates six release boundaries, highlights contradictions, quarantines unreviewed observations, exposes concrete gaps, generates an ordered verification plan, and exports a privacy-scrubbed handoff. The built-in anonymous demo is intentionally blocked. It has confirmed Source and Build proof, an install note awaiting human review, no confirmed Runtime proof, a contradicted Human Play claim, and no verified External Release status. That honest “2 of 6” is the product’s point. Why WebMCP is essential The most useful context is already in the live page: the active release candidate, exact claim IDs, confirmed evidence, pending review, contradictions, and gaps. A separate chatbot would duplicate or drift from that state. Screen automation would have to infer meaning from visual cards. WebMCP gives the agent a precise contract over the same live page the human is using. A real workflow can run in sequence: Read the current snapshot. Audit every release claim. List the missing evidence. Generate an ordered release plan. Record a human-supplied observation. Export a sanitized handoff. Every state-changing result is immediately visible in the interface and operation log. The write path is deliberately asymmetric. Agent-proposed supporting evidence is always marked pending human review , so it can appear in the UI without upgrading a claim. Contradictions may reduce confidence immediately. Only a human can confirm supporting evidence. WebMCP is therefore not a decorative integration—it is the trust boundary for the product. Human–agent collaboration The human identifies the exact project, target, and release candidate. The agent reads current claim IDs and coverage from the page. The agent separates supported, contradicted, pending, and unknown statements. The agent plans the next checks with explicit developer, tester, and release-owner responsibilities. When the human supplies a new observation, the agent records it and the page updates live. The human confirms or rejects proposed supporting proof. Either side can generate a privacy-safe Markdown or JSON handoff without turning unperformed work into a Pass. How we built it The page uses the real WebMCP imperative API and registers six tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...). Every tool has an exact name, bounded description, strict JSON Schema, additionalProperties disabled, independent runtime validation, corrective errors, annotations, and structured observable output. get_project_snapshot — active project, revision, coverage, evidence tracks, and claim IDs. list_missing_evidence — missing claims, proof gaps, contradictions, and pending review. audit_release_claims — evidence-derived claim verdicts. add_evidence_item — validated live-state mutation with a human-review quarantine. generate_release_plan — ordered verification actions derived from current gaps. export_sanitized_handoff — Markdown or JSON with emails, secrets, private paths, and private URLs scrubbed. React renders the control-room interface. TypeScript owns the proof model and tool contracts. Versioned localStorage keeps projects local-first and reload-safe. Vitest and Playwright test the state invariants, error contracts, keyboard flows, persistence, and responsive UI. Vercel hosts a static production build with no account, backend, paid API, telemetry, or runtime network dependency. Challenges The hardest problem was not registering tools. It was preventing a convenient write tool from becoming a confidence-escalation shortcut. We separated claims from evidence-derived verdicts, separated Install from Runtime within one visual lane, introduced a human-review state for supporting agent observations, and made verdicts pure functions of confirmed evidence. We also created corrective errors for wrong claim IDs, mismatched evidence types, unsupported bounds, and unsafe handoff requests. A second challenge was keeping browser capability claims honest. Ordinary CI Chromium uses a small registration harness to exercise production contracts. Native WebMCP was verified separately in ChatGPT’s in-app browser and in flag-enabled Chrome 151 and 152. The public demo records the actual native getTools() and executeTool(...) workflow. Those proof layers remain explicitly separate. Accomplishments A coherent five-track, six-boundary release evidence model. Six non-trivial WebMCP tools supporting a complete multi-tool workflow. Agent write → visible UI update → pending human review → reload persistence. Empty projects remain 0/6 and incomplete; missing state never becomes a Pass. Positive, invalid-input, empty-data, and state-sync cases for every tool. Responsive desktop and mobile layouts with keyboard access. Privacy-scrubbed Markdown and structured JSON handoffs. A public, audible 2:02 demo showing native discovery, audit, planning, guarded write, persistence, empty-state protection, handoff, and the prior-work boundary. What we learned Agent-ready does not mean agent-controlled. The best collaboration surface gives an agent precise affordances while preserving human authority over evidence the agent cannot physically observe. WebMCP makes that separation explicit in the tool contract, state model, and interface. Prior work disclosure The problem framing was informed by the entrant’s earlier public MIT-licensed project, Culaliya/finish-small-app-v1 . That repository remains a read-only conceptual source and is not this submission. Release Evidence Desk is a clean, independent web application created after the WebMCP Challenge opened. Its UI, data model, state engine, WebMCP implementation, tests, visual assets, documentation, and Git history are new. No source code, assets, or Git history were copied from the earlier project, and the earlier project was not converted into an MCP server. What is next The submitted version will remain frozen throughout judging. A future separate fork could add import adapters for common CI receipts, signed evidence bundles, team review roles, and shareable read-only snapshots while preserving the same evidence boundary. title: Agentready Network
pitch: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it.
about_excerpt: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it. Like Comment Story Updates The problem nobody has budget for Every operations team lives inside sites that will never ship an API for them. Monitoring in Grafana. Customer commitments in Cal.com. Payer portals, vendor consoles, admin dashboards. The person holding the session can see everything and change anything, but their agent can do nothing except screenshot the screen and guess where to click. WebMCP fixes this for sites that adopt it. Today that is roughly none of them. We measured three real open-source products, 522k lines of code, 429 places where a tool obviously belongs, and zero WebMCP registrations. So we asked a different question. What if the user adopts WebMCP for the site? The reframe WebMCP turns the login you already have into an API. A signed-in tab already carries every credential and permission the human has. If that tab registers tools with document.modelContext.registerTool , the agent gets a typed, narrow, inspectable interface to the site, and the vendor never has to ship a line of code. Adoption inverts. It no longer waits on ten thousand vendors. It happens one user, one tab, one reviewed pack at a time. What Agentready Network does Agentready Network is a local-first registry and runtime of reviewed action packs . A pack describes what a site can do, on exactly which origin, with which risk labels. The runtime turns that pack into live WebMCP tools inside the user's own signed-in session, then wraps every call in the safety the vendor never provided: Exact origins. A pack binds to one host and a reviewed fingerprint. Drift fails closed. Declarative, never executable. Manifests are JSON. The registry cannot ship code into your browser. Bounded, untrusted output. Results are allowlist-projected, byte-capped, and labeled contentTrust: "untrusted" . Tool output is content, not instruction. Human authority on consequences. Reads flow. Writes need a preview. Consequential actions need one exact, single-use approval bound to origin, tool, and normalized arguments. Change an argument and the grant is void. Verified closure. After a consequential action an inspector reads authoritative state and issues a receipt with no cookies, secrets, or raw bodies. Unknown outcome is reported as in_doubt , never as success. One concrete job, end to end The demo is not a feature tour. It is one incident. An alert fires in Grafana. Customer bookings in Cal.com are about to be affected. Neither site has WebMCP. The agent discovers the reviewed Grafana and Cal.com packs, installs them for this origin, and reads authoritative state. It never receives a credential. The agent prepares the exact continuity action and states what will change and how it will be inspected. The incident is still investigating . The human grants that exact action once, from a control the agent cannot reach. The agent executes once. The inspector verifies and issues one receipt. The incident is resolved . We poison the fingerprint. The pack refuses to run. We export the recorder draft. Every secret is gone before it can be published. Agents investigate. Humans authorize. Outcomes are verified. That is the whole product. What people and agents can now do together that they could not before Work a real incident across two unrelated vendor sites with no API contract between them. The user is the integration layer. Let an agent read freely and prepare freely, while every consequential step waits for a human decision the agent physically cannot forge. Hand a reviewer a receipt, not a screenshot, as proof of what changed. Teach a site once by observing its own traffic, then reuse that pack every session. Why WebMCP, specifically Screenshot-and-click pays the full cost on every step: a screenshot, a vision pass, a click that misses when the viewport shifts. We measured it. Creating one Grafana data source took nine browser actions and 55 seconds by DOM driving, and one WebMCP tool call in 20 milliseconds. A whole diagramming task took 44 calls versus 5. These are single-trial measurements from our audit work, not a benchmark suite, but the shape is unmistakable. The cost moves from per-action to per-app, and it never comes back. WebMCP also gives us the one thing a bookmarklet never had: a standard discovery surface. Any agent that speaks document.modelContext finds our tools without knowing we exist. How we built it Registry, Pack Lab, and runtime in plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. No framework. Every tool is registered with the current imperative API, document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) , so tools unregister cleanly when a view unmounts. A Chrome MV3 extension injects reviewed read tools into the exact controlled Cal.com and Grafana origins and bridges receipts back to the registry. Reviewed adapters for Cal.com and Grafana were reverse-engineered on the wire, not from source. The recorder wraps fetch and XMLHttpRequest , clusters observed traffic, drafts tools, auto-flags mutating endpoints, and strips secrets before anything is published. Approval, inspection, drift, and redaction are enforced in the shared runtime, so every pack inherits them and no pack can opt out. Node's built-in test runner covers the trust boundaries. All tests pass on the submitted commit. What we deliberately did not claim The public judge path is a deterministic fixture so nobody needs an account. The same runtime drives the real Cal.com and Grafana adapters against controlled localhost instances; the video shows the controlled Grafana and Cal.com state alongside the public lab. The extension checkpoint is read-only. Remembered approvals, arbitrary-site install, generic DOM automation, and automatic rollback are out of scope. Figma taught us the frontier. Its control plane is reachable in-session; its canvas rides a binary WebSocket inside a Worker that no page-context patch can see. We published only what we proved and marked canvas manipulation unsupported. What we learned Discovery is observation, not code reading. Every tool we guessed from source was wrong. Every tool we drafted from the wire worked. Minification cannot rename what crosses the network. Injection inverts the safety burden onto the installer. The vendor never audited these tools, so we had to. That is why approval, inspection, and redaction live in the runtime and not in the pack. What is next Persist packs across sessions in the extension. Chain packs across sites so one agent can read portal A and act in portal B. Generalize the approval contract into a policy layer: read anything, never pay, never cancel, never touch what a human pinned. The first vertical we want to ship is healthcare payer portals, the most session-locked, human-attestation-gated surfaces on the web. Testing instructions for judges No credentials are needed. Open the live site in ChatGPT's browser or in Chrome with the WebMCP flag enabled, follow the 90-second path in the README, and use Reset between runs. Local run: npm test , then python3 -m http.server 8788 and open /site/ . title: Left Out Security - WebMCP Security Lab
pitch: An interactive lab where people and AI agents inspect WebMCP tools, narrow their authority, approve one exact action, and verify the real effect with security receipts.
about_excerpt: An interactive lab where people and AI agents inspect WebMCP tools, narrow their authority, approve one exact action, and verify the real effect with security receipts. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration I started Left Out Security - WebMCP Security Lab because I was trying to understand what WebMCP really changes. The basic idea is powerful: instead of an AI agent looking at a webpage and guessing what buttons or forms mean, a website can expose structured capabilities directly to the agent. That immediately raised a security question for me: How does the human know what the agent is actually being allowed to do? As I dug through documentation, developer discussions, forum posts, security conversations, and other early WebMCP material, I kept seeing the same gap. There are really three different surfaces involved: Presented Surface — what the website tells the human. Declared Agent Surface — what the WebMCP tool tells the agent. Effective Surface — what the code actually does when the tool runs. Those three things can match. They do not have to. That became the core idea behind the lab. I did not want to write another article explaining that agent tools could create security problems. I wanted to build a place where someone could actually inspect the problem, approve a capability, invoke it, and then verify what really happened. What it does WebMCP Security Lab is a synthetic security test range for WebMCP. The lab walks a person and an AI agent through deliberately vulnerable examples where the user can compare what was promised, what was declared, what was authorized, and what actually occurred. The basic path is: Public URL → native Site Tool → human review → narrow approval → one invocation → verified receipt The current lessons explore problems such as: A supposedly read-only tool that changes state An input schema that asks for more authority than the task requires Tool output shaped like instructions A vague confirmation around a mutating action A site making compatibility claims it cannot actually support One lesson uses a synthetic eligibility check for TRAINING-1042 . The point is not whether the eligibility check succeeds. The point is whether the user and the agent can prove that the capability they approved is the capability that actually ran. How people and agents work together The human determines intent. The agent invokes the capability. The application verifies the result. I wanted those responsibilities to stay visibly separate. With ordinary browser automation, the agent often has to infer intent from the DOM, buttons, labels, and forms. The user sees the webpage, but usually does not see a clean representation of the authority being exercised by the agent. WebMCP improves that by allowing sites to declare structured tools directly. But a declaration is still a claim. A tool can be named like a harmless lookup and still mutate state. An annotation can say something is read-only without technically enforcing that behavior. A schema can be technically valid and still request far more information than the visible task requires. So the lab keeps asking three questions: What did the site promise? What did the agent receive? What actually happened? How I built it This project is also an experiment in how far I could get using almost nothing except ChatGPT and GitHub . The concepts and security model are mine, informed by the documentation, forums, developer conversations, and security discussions I was following while learning WebMCP. The implementation was almost completely vibe coded using Daybreak Blue across the ChatGPT product surface: ChatGPT Chat ChatGPT Work ChatGPT Sites Codex GitHub for the repository and source control There was no traditional development team. I would work through the security idea in ChatGPT, turn it into a concrete lesson or control, build and modify the application through ChatGPT and Codex, test the behavior, find where my assumptions were wrong, and iterate again. The public application registers structured capabilities through WebMCP using: document.modelContext.registerTool() One of the design decisions I cared about most was keeping approval separate from execution . A broad teaching capability can be inspected first. After the user approves an exact task, the application can replace that broad capability with a generated, narrow capability that is: Bound to the approved task Zero-input One-use Consumed after execution Not intended to be retried Approving it does not execute it. The agent still has to invoke the capability. After invocation, the lab generates a receipt describing things such as: Result Before state After state Side effects Invocation count Remaining authority That receipt is important because I did not want the lab to end with a green checkmark that simply says everything worked. I wanted evidence. Challenges This project is still actively moving. I am still grinding on it, so some implementation details are changing even while the submission is being prepared. The biggest design challenge was separating: Registration Discovery Review Approval Invocation Verification It would have been much easier to collapse those into a single flow. But doing that would hide the exact trust boundaries the project is supposed to teach. Another challenge has been browser-side execution. I have been working with a local extension path for some of the more advanced testing, and that integration has been giving me trouble. Rather than pretend that path is finished, I am moving that work into the advanced path while keeping the public native Site Tool experience focused and reproducible. That separation turned out to be useful anyway. The public experience can demonstrate the core security model cleanly, while the advanced path can continue exploring deeper browser-side instrumentation and local execution. There were also a lot of less glamorous implementation problems. Stale tool registrations could accumulate while moving between lessons. Capabilities had to be registered, replaced, consumed, and invalidated correctly. State had to remain understandable to both the human and the agent. Those problems are not exciting to describe, but they matter if the lesson is supposed to prove something instead of simply looking like it works. What I learned The biggest lesson is that a tool's name is not a security control . Neither is an annotation. They are useful metadata, but they are still statements made by the tool provider. Security has to look at the complete interaction: Human intent Declared schema Granted authority Mutation language Tool output Runtime behavior Observed effect The verification step became especially important. A lot of systems focus heavily on whether an agent should be allowed to perform an action. Much less attention is paid to proving what actually happened after the action ran. That is why the receipt became part of the design. Another thing I learned I also learned something about the development process itself. This project became an exploration of what one person can build using essentially: ChatGPT + GitHub The security architecture, UI, code, debugging, documentation, testing ideas, lesson design, and submission work have all moved through the same AI-assisted workflow. That does not mean ChatGPT invented the project. The concepts, threat model, decisions, and direction came from me. What surprised me was how far I could push the implementation by treating ChatGPT not as a chatbot sitting beside the project, but as the development environment surrounding it. Chat for thinking. Work for organizing. Sites for publishing. Codex for building and debugging. GitHub for the actual repository. That became a second experiment running underneath the WebMCP experiment. What's next The project is still evolving. Near-term work includes: More adversarial WebMCP lessons Additional conformance fixtures Accessibility testing Better declared-versus-observed comparisons Privacy-reviewed evidence workflows Advanced browser-side instrumentation Continued work on the local extension and advanced testing path The larger goal is to turn WebMCP Security Lab into a reusable place for understanding and testing agent-facing web capabilities. WebMCP gives websites a new way to expose functionality directly to AI agents. I want people to have an equally good way to ask: What did I actually authorize, what did the agent actually receive, and what actually happened? And, somewhat accidentally, I am also finding out how much of that can be built with just ChatGPT and GitHub. Apparently, quite a lot. title: ArenaMCP
pitch: A game engine that facilitates training-data collection from human–agent interactions. You can design games, play them with your agent & collect structured data for machine & reinforcement learning.
about_excerpt: A game engine that facilitates training-data collection from human–agent interactions. You can design games, play them with your agent & collect structured data for machine & reinforcement learning. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I recently participated in a public Kaggle simulation competition for a collectible-card game — The Pokémon Company, PTCG AI Battle Challenge Simulation . From my experience as a data scientist, I can see that the competition was born out of a training problem in machine learning / deep learning : a finite-horizon, partially observable , competitive , multi-agent , sequential decision process. In particular, card-trading games often involve hidden information, a large combinatorial action space, and an opponent — often a human — who is also learning. This makes the dynamics messy and non-stationary, unlike in more conventional reinforcement learning settings. The organizers' answer to that mess was to open an arena . Independently written agents share one simulator, receive a structured observation, return an action, and play against each other on a ladder. That is a good design for agent-versus-agent evaluation. However, it is a poor design for the kind of data that modern game-agent research actually starves for. This is because humans and agents do not share an interface. A human wants a board and an interface they can see and interact with. An agent wants a typed observation, a legal-action mask, and a step . This made me think that this is such a great use case for WebMCP, where the agent communicates through WebMCP tools while the human interacts through the web browser. My idea is ArenaMCP, a gym-style environment where humans and agents can design games, share them with others, play them, and collect training data from human-versus-agent interactions. Why human-versus-agent game design is a strong fit for WebMCP Problem. Data collection for a partially observable, competitive, human-versus-agent, sequential decision-making problem. Game-agent research needs diverse interactive trajectories, but humans and agents require fundamentally different interfaces, so human-versus-agent data is always among the most challenging and expensive to collect. An environment includes 5 functions: init(seed) -> state legal_actions(state, player) -> string[] observe(state, player) -> observation step(state, action) -> { state, rewards, terminal } render(observation) -> { html, css } observe is the fair-play boundary. legal_actions is the action mask. render is the human board. The agent never clicks that board — it calls get_observation , take_action , wait_for_turn . Both seats write the same JSONL: episode { match_id, environment, seed, seats, returns, length } step { observation, legal_actions, action, reward, terminal, latency_ms, … } Each step records which interface took the action ( human_ui or webmcp ), so a click and a tool call stay distinguishable. Optional rationale and confidence ride on the agent seat. A Python loader ( arena_dataset.py ) yields (obs, legal, action, reward, next_obs, done) . This only works if they share one live page and one match state . A server MCP could write environment files in the dark. A screenshot agent could guess at buttons. Neither gives the agent a legal-action mask, a per-seat observation, or the board the person is looking at. WebMCP does: the tools run in the page, against the same step() the clicks use, and export_episodes hands back the schema, a sample row, and a download link. The surface is the whole loop — author, verify, play, export — registered on document.modelContext . Every write repaints the table before it returns , so the agent's next observation matches what the human sees. Every play tool returns enough state — observation, legal actions, whose turn, whether the game ended — for the agent to choose the next call. Authored markup is treated as hostile ( untrustedContentHint ); the sandbox iframe has no same-origin access and no network, so a game cannot reach document.modelContext . How it creates a better user experience The person never leaves the page, and they never have to become an RL engineer to get a dataset. They speak; a playable table appears. Ask the agent to design a game. It writes the five functions, the checks run, and the board lands on their screen. No gym wrapper, no separate frontend, no "now export this to a notebook." They play the board they asked for. Clicks are ordinary UI. The agent sits in the other seat through tools. The trajectory panel fills in as they play — observation , mask, action, reward, latency. They can see whether the game is fair. Publishing shows an information-flow matrix: which state fields each seat can observe. A leak ("seat 0 can see seat 1's private cards") is a failed check, not a footnote. The person confirms the matrix before the environment is shared. The agent can look at the table the way a person does. preview_view / inspect_view collapse the painted board into a character grid with real colours and list every control. The agent can tell a blank render() from a working one without reading raw HTML. The download is the point of the session, not homework after. JSONL from the play panel or GET /api/episodes?match_id=…&format=jsonl . Same bytes the agent already described with describe_dataset . Without WebMCP the person would watch an agent edit files they cannot play, or play a game an agent cannot legally sit in. The better experience is that those are the same session. What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before Author a new environment, verify it, and play it, in one sitting. Before, that was three projects: a simulator, a UI, an agent API. A person could describe Kuhn poker in a chat and get code. They could not immediately sit across from the thing that wrote it, on a board that hides the other seat's card, and download a trajectory that names which side was human. Collect human-versus-agent data without a custom integration. Agent-versus-agent ladders (the Kaggle pattern) produce volume. They do not produce a person thinking across the table. Browser-use agents produce clicks. They do not produce a typed observation and a legal mask. Arena records both seats against the same step() , tagged by interface, with optional agent rationale. Enforce the observation boundary in front of both of them. observe(state, player) is checked by perturbing state fields and seeing which seats' views change. If a private field leaks, publish is blocked and the agent gets repair text. A person and an agent can argue about fairness against a generated matrix instead of trust. Let the agent repair what it can see. The agent is not scoring its own HTML. preview_view says what painted; validation says what is broken ( step threw, the game never ends, the markup ignores the observation) and names the seed. trace_episode walks that seed so the agent can see the state at the break. The person watches the table change as the agent patches one function at a time. None of that is possible if the agent is in a file tree and the person is on a different website. It needs one page, two interfaces, shared state — which is what WebMCP is for. How I implemented WebMCP Imperative registration on the live document, from a client component ( ArenaTools ). Feature-detect both names; abort on unmount because there is no unregisterTool() . Each tool has a title for the browser UI, a description, and a JSON Schema whose properties are described in English. execute receives the run's AbortSignal and threads it into every fetch, so a cancelled call does not leave work running: const model = document.modelContext ?? navigator.modelContext; if (!model?.registerTool) return; const controller = new AbortController(); await model.registerTool( { name: "take_action", title: "Play a move", description: "Play one legal action. Quote expected_revision from the last observation.", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { action: { type: "string", description: "One id copied from legal_actions." }, expected_revision: { type: "integer" }, rationale: { type: "string" }, confidence: { type: "integer", minimum: 1, maximum: 5 }, }, required: ["action", "expected_revision"], }, annotations: { untrustedContentHint: true }, execute: async (input, { signal }) => { const result = await play(input, { signal }); await refreshView(); // table updates before the agent reads the reply return result; }, }, { signal: controller.signal }, ); The agent has access to a suite of 18 WebMCP tools: Stage Tools Author get_authoring_guide , list_environments , get_environment , create_environment , fork_environment , update_environment See preview_view , inspect_view — the agent cannot trust its own HTML, so these describe what actually painted Verify validate_environment (V0–V8), trace_episode , describe_dataset Share publish_environment , open_environment Play start_match , get_observation , take_action , wait_for_turn Keep

title: Sky to Porch
pitch: Turn official environmental observations into shared, inspectable evidence for people and AI agents.
about_excerpt: Turn official environmental observations into shared, inspectable evidence for people and AI agents. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Ambiguous place? The Agent asks, the page shows the same choices, and the map waits for the person to decide. Official NYC air-quality evidence becomes a plain-English answer with sources and limitations beside the map. The Missions view traces Las Vegas drought evidence to the NASA and U.S. Drought Monitor products behind it. The Houston Beryl result shows validated NOAA wind observations, storm context, citations, and property-level limitations. The About view explains Sky to Porch’s evidence model, coverage, safety boundaries, and independent attribution. The catalog shows which NASA, NOAA, and regional satellite products are live, candidate, or require credentials. Inspiration After a wildfire or a storm, people ask whether smoke was recorded near their family that day. The records exist, but the hard part is tying a place and a date to what was actually observed. What it does Sky to Porch is a map-based evidence workspace where a person and an AI Agent investigate the same question on the same screen. The person gives a place, a completed date or range, a hazard, a radius, and a concern. The strongest supported assessment comes first, then the observations with times, official citations, confidence, limitations, and source status. Seven hazard families are covered, and a broad question runs related ones together. Fire & Smoke brings Air Quality. Extreme Heat brings Drought & Land. Earth & Volcanoes brings Air Quality and Extreme Heat. A plain storm question runs Wind & Storm and Flood & Heavy Rain. Naming one hazard keeps it focused. Chains never merge. Rainfall is not proof of wind damage, and a regional observation is not a verdict on one house or one person. Why WebMCP fits Sky to Porch WebMCP lets the person skip that setup and ask the question they actually have. "What environmental evidence was recorded near Los Angeles during the wildfire?" The Agent picks the tools, runs the Fire & Smoke and Air Quality chains, and summarizes in plain English what they support. Real questions also need cross-checking. A storm question means wind readings, rain totals, flood extent, and gauge levels from different agencies, on the same day, for the same area. A person doing that by hand runs each path and compares the results one at a time. An Agent is good at exactly this. It runs every relevant chain, reads all of them, and tells the person where the sources agree, where they differ, and what is still missing. This is collaboration, not hand-off. Human queries and Agent calls use one analysis service and update the same map, Meaning panel, and Evidence panel. The person can take over at any point, change the radius or the date, pick a different hazard, or click into a source. The person can also keep asking. "Which source failed?" or "Show me the exact gust reading" gets answered from the result already on screen, without rerunning anything. Every chain keeps its own button, so the Agent cannot hide a result, and the final judgment stays with the person. How I built it The stack is Next.js, React, TypeScript, and MapLibre GL. Adapters for NASA, NOAA, USGS, and EPA sources feed one deterministic analysis service that owns validation, retrieval, calculations, freshness, provenance, confidence, limitations, and safe display. The model chooses tools and explains validated results. It cannot invent an observation. The page registers eight WebMCP tools, covering hazard analysis, two-scenario comparison, active-result inspection without a rerun, source coverage, help and demos, a storm claim checklist, place lookup, and map layers. The Agent comes from a WebMCP-compatible browser. The site holds no model API key. Challenges I ran into Ambiguity. "Houston" matches several places, so the place tool lists up to five candidates with stable IDs and waits. The pick resumes the run with the original date, hazard, radius, and concern intact. Size. A result gets about 2,400 characters, so compaction drops optional detail first and keeps the strongest observations, provenance, limitations, and links to the visible result. Real Agent behavior. A valid schema does not mean the Agent picks the right tool or runs every chain, so I added live-source checks and model-scored evaluations of tool selection, ambiguity recovery, comparisons, and summaries. Accomplishments that I'm proud of User-specified locations, dates, and radii stay authoritative. Every result separates a valid observation from no observation returned, source failure, unsupported coverage, stale data, and inconclusive evidence. The Agent can answer a follow-up from the active result without rerunning it. The same experience works on desktop and mobile. The current build passes typecheck, lint, 1,617 unit tests, 133 integration tests, a 14-page production build, and the full desktop and mobile Playwright suite. What I learned Exposing tools is the easy part. The collaboration has to be visible on the screen. "No observation returned" is not the same as "no hazard," and a source failure must never disappear inside a confident summary. What's next I want more official-source coverage, portable evidence summaries, and contextual follow-up tools across the whole hazard catalog. Prior work and Challenge contribution Sky to Porch existed before the OpenAI WebMCP Challenge. The map, the human query interface, the source adapters, and the evidence contracts are prior work. Everything Agent-facing above is the Challenge contribution, along with more evidence for all hazards and the WebMCP testing. I built it solo with AI coding assistance. PRIOR_WORK.md in the repo documents the boundary. This was my first time working with WebMCP, and I led the product direction, UX, safety boundaries, and final review.
