title: Verified Giving Protocol | Agent-readable Donate pages
pitch: A standard JSON for donate pages built for agents. The problem: A nonprofit's donate button is JavaScript and a hero image. PayPal Giving Fund has an API and will route agents to their pipes.
about_excerpt: A standard JSON for donate pages built for agents. The problem: A nonprofit's donate button is JavaScript and a hero image. PayPal Giving Fund has an API and will route agents to their pipes. Like 1 Comment Story Updates donate page of powerpoetry.org with info about webmcp Generate a file based on standards verify a page Inspiration A nonprofit should decide where its own donations go. This is going to matter as AI Agents begin to take over web actions like donating. Tell an AI agent "donate $50 to this nonprofit" and it routes to whatever it can parse. That is structurally almost never the nonprofit's own donation page. It's an aggregator, an outdated page, or a third-party fundraising page set up on the organization's behalf without its knowledge. Those pathways can hold funds for weeks before disbursing — some intermediaries take up to 90 days — introducing float, intermediary risk, and a donor record the nonprofit never sees. The organization gets the money once and loses the relationship. Two trends are making this worse at the same time: Agents are being locked out. Cloudflare challenges, bot rules, and hardened forms mean the legitimate path is often the hardest one for an agent to complete — so it takes the easy path, which is somebody else's page. Donation forms are unreadable by design. Most are cross-origin iframes. An agent looking at a real nonprofit donate page cannot see the amount, the frequency, or who receives the money. It's a black box, so it guesses. The result is an agent doing the reasonable thing with bad information. We wanted the nonprofit to be able to state, in a way a machine can act on, this is where our money may go — and have that statement come from the one domain nobody else controls. What it does The Verified Giving Protocol lets a nonprofit publish a machine-readable declaration at https://their-domain.org/giving.json naming the giving destinations it authorizes — and exposes that to AI agents as WebMCP tools. The protocol turns on one distinction: Statement Who makes it Authorizes? benefits — "proceeds go to Organization X" anyone no confirmed — "evidence consistently identifies this destination" a discovery process no authorized — "we declare this an approved destination" the organization yes No amount of evidence converts confirmed into authorized . A human at the nonprofit types a fixed affirmation verbatim , and that's the only route in. It's enforced as a const in the JSON Schema, in the Python approval script, and in the WebMCP tools — not as a UI check. A paraphrase is refused. The nonprofit's own page then registers four WebMCP tools built entirely from that declaration: giving_verify , giving_options , giving_designations , and giving_prepare . An agent asks instead of scrapes. The reference implementation is live. Power Poetry ( https://www.powerpoetry.org/donate ) publishes a declaration naming To Be Heard Foundation Inc, EIN 13-3648963, verified against the IRS Business Master File. An agent starting from the donate page alone can determine who legally receives the money, that the organization authorized it, and construct a working prefilled donation URL. How we built it The standard — a specification, a JSON Schema, and a stdlib-only Python validator and approval script. No dependencies, so a nonprofit can run the tooling without a toolchain. The WebMCP layer — giving-tools.js , generated from a reviewed template by generate_webmcp.py and byte-compared against a fresh generation in CI. The tools cannot drift from the template, and hand-editing them to say something the declaration doesn't is caught by the test suite. The site — verifiedgiving.ai, an Astro build with an in-browser generator and a live validator. The site pins the standard as a git submodule and renders the specification and publishes the JSON Schema from it at build time, so no copy can drift from the source. The discovery agent — vgpify , a Claude skill that crawls a nonprofit's site, extracts organization identity and giving pathways, flags conflicts, and produces an evidence-backed review document. It proposes ; it cannot publish. 54 tests , and most of them assert refusals rather than successes. Challenges we ran into There is no payment API to route to. We assumed one existed. Givebutter — the processor behind our reference implementation — publishes 42 API endpoints and none of them creates a checkout session, payment intent, charge, or token . POST /v1/transactions requires a past timestamp and has no payment-instrument field: it records a gift that already happened. The capability exists one layer down (Givebutter settles through Stripe), but no nonprofit-facing platform exposes it. We're now in conversation with people interested in changing that, and published an open request ( https://verifiedgiving.ai/providers ) describing exactly what we'd need and — importantly — what we would not ask a processor to take on. Publishing is not discovery. We deployed a correct declaration, at the correct path, with the correct media type, plus the link relation and the WebMCP script — then pointed ChatGPT at the page. It found almost nothing. Every discovery mechanism we'd built required the world to have already adopted VGP: nobody probes /giving.json , nothing parses rel="giving" , and ChatGPT's browser provides no document.modelContext so the tools never register. That five-minute test reshaped the project. The cold start. VGP has one adopter and zero consumers . A standard nobody consumes is invisible, and a nonprofit that does everything right and sees no effect concludes the standard doesn't work. That's the likeliest way this dies, and we'd rather say so than imply an ecosystem that doesn't exist. Platform documentation isn't platform behaviour. Givebutter documents frequency=quarterly ; it's not enabled on our campaign and is silently ignored. once works and is undocumented. Amounts over 999 are silently dropped from prefill. Every one of those was found by testing the live widget, and each would have failed in the worst place — a donor believing they'd set up a monthly gift that wasn't. Accomplishments that we're proud of The tools fail closed, and it's provable. If a declaration is missing, unapproved, or wrongly served, the page registers no giving tools at all . An agent is told "this site exposes no authorized giving pathway" rather than handed a plausible form. Flip one boolean and watch it happen: node --test webmcp/harness.test.mjs . Authorization cannot be faked, and you can check in ten seconds. In the live generator, type a paraphrase of the affirmation — authorized_destinations stays empty. Type it exactly — the destination is authorized. A live reference implementation , end-to-end verified: an agent derives the receiving legal entity, its EIN, the authorization record, and a prefilled donation URL that drives the real payment widget to the right state. giving_prepare never charges. It returns payment_completed: false and requires_human_payment_authorization: true . VGP routes; the donor authorizes; the nonprofit's existing processor charges. We shipped the honest version. The site states its own adoption position rather than implying consumers exist. What we learned Absence of a tool is safer than presence of an ambiguous one. The most valuable thing our WebMCP integration does is decline to appear. Infrastructure ahead of its consumers is invisible, not broken — and the escape is to speak a vocabulary that already has consumers while the new one accumulates them. We added schema.org ( legalName , taxID , nonprofitStatus , DonateAction with an EntryPoint.urlTemplate ) and a plain visible link to the declaration. That turned "a couple more details" into an agent that could name the receiving entity and build a working donation URL — with no change to the underlying declaration. Rank discovery mechanisms by how little the world must change: a visible link needs nothing; schema.org needs a vocabulary that already has consumers; llms.txt needs a spreading convention; your own new mechanism needs adoption. Ship them in that order. The declaration belongs at the document root, not /.well-known/ . /.well-known/ is for protocol metadata; the root is for owner policy — robots.txt , sitemap.xml , ads.txt . VGP is the second kind, and ads.txt is the near-exact analogue: a domain owner naming who may act on their behalf, published to defeat unauthorized intermediaries. The test is what absence means. Declare, never infer. Every platform parameter is declared by the organization with an explicit vocabulary and bounds. A guessed parameter fails silently where it costs most. What's next for Verified Giving Protocol A payment endpoint worth declaring. We've specified what we'd need from processors: a checkout session an agent can create, a required idempotency key (agents retry, and a dropped response on a donation charges someone twice), published amount and currency rules, status and receipt — and explicitly

title: Credsutra
pitch: CredSutra brings credit-card intelligence to AI with WebMCP—review, compare, discover news, calculate rewards & lounge benefits, and get personalized card recommendations based on your spending.
about_excerpt:
CredSutra brings credit-card intelligence to AI with WebMCP—review, compare, discover news, calculate rewards & lounge benefits, and get personalized card recommendations based on your spending.

 1 2 3 



 
 About the Project 

 I’ve always wanted to build a website that brings together useful, practical information about credit cards. 

 When I started earning, choosing the right credit card was surprisingly difficult. There were limited sources of information, information was scattered across different websites, and it wasn’t always easy to figure out which card actually made sense for my spending habits. I had the idea of building something that could solve this problem, but like many side projects, I never found the time to actually build it. 

 AI changed that. 

 With the rise of AI-powered experiences, I thought: why not finally give it a shot? That idea eventually became CredSutra — a platform designed to help people understand, compare, and choose credit cards based on how they actually spend. 

 For the OpenAI WebMCP Challenge, I took CredSutra one step further. Instead of making users navigate through pages and manually search for information, I exposed CredSutra's capabilities through WebMCP. The website currently provides six tools that an AI agent can interact with: 

 
 Card Review — get detailed information and insights about a credit card. 
 Card Comparison — compare cards and understand their differences. 
 Credit Card News — discover relevant and recent card-related updates. 
 Reward Calculator — estimate rewards based on spending. 
 Lounge Calculator — determine lounge eligibility and benefits. 
 Card Recommendation — find cards that fit specific spending criteria. 
 

 The interesting part for me was seeing how a website can evolve from being a destination that users browse into a capability that AI agents can interact with . 

 What I Learned 

 Building this project taught me that WebMCP is more than just exposing APIs. The real challenge is thinking about how an AI agent will understand and use your tools. 

 I had to think carefully about tool descriptions, inputs, outputs, and how to structure the capabilities so that an agent can make meaningful decisions instead of simply calling an endpoint. 

 It also made me rethink the traditional website experience. A user might ask an AI something like: 

 
 "I spend ₹50,000 a month on travel and dining. Which credit card would give me the best rewards?" 
 

 Instead of the user learning how CredSutra works first, an AI agent can use CredSutra's tools to find the relevant cards, calculate potential rewards, and provide an answer. 

 Challenges 

 The biggest challenge was deciding what should become a tool and what should remain part of the website experience. 

 I also had to make the tools useful independently while ensuring they could work together as part of a larger AI-driven workflow. Designing clear inputs and outputs and making the tools predictable for an agent required more thought than I initially expected. 

 And, of course, building a real product while learning and experimenting with a relatively new technology comes with plenty of iterations and debugging. 

 What's Next? 

 CredSutra is still very much a beginning. 

 There are many more features I want to add, more credit-card data to bring together, and many ways I can make the recommendations smarter and more personalized. 

 What started as an idea I had years ago but never got around to building has finally become something real — and WebMCP has given me an exciting new direction for it. 

 This is just the beginning.

title: YOZZ: Zero-knowledge webmail
pitch: 🗿 Browser decrypt; server no key. WebMCP only way for 🤖. Server MCP cannot 🙅‍♀️.
about_excerpt: 🗿 Browser decrypt; server no key. WebMCP only way for 🤖. Server MCP cannot 🙅‍♀️. Like 1 Comment Story Updates YOZZ's three-pane inbox with multiple email addresses and a message open Inspiration YOZZ started with a personal problem. For years, I relied on Gmail’s “Send as” feature to send emails from my custom domains. When Google announced it was discontinuing the feature , I went looking for an alternative. After days of searching, I was unable to find anything that satisfied the privacy, aesthetics, and convenience that I was after. That is why I built YOZZ: a zero-knowledge, modern-looking webmail client that is private by design, clean to use, and accessible anywhere in the browser. Zero-knowledge password managers were the main inspiration for YOZZ: secrets are decrypted on the user’s device while the servers only handle data it cannot understand. What if I apply the same idea to webmail? Modern email interfaces and zero-knowledge cryptography were well-established and easy to learn from existing solutions. The real challenge lay in the networking: client-side JavaScript cannot open raw TCP sockets, so a direct connection to mail servers via IMAP/SMTP is impossible. Moving the connection to a backend server would defeat the whole zero-knowledge premise. The entire feasibility of YOZZ came down to whether I could solve that one fundamental constraint. Having previously built a zero-dependency ACME client in TypeScript, I knew low-level cryptographic handshakes were viable in pure JS. The missing link was the transport layer. The breakthrough was a Cloudflare Worker acting as a relay: tunneling WebSocket traffic from the browser into raw TCP connections to the mail servers, while ensuring TLS terminated exclusively between the JS in the browser and the mail servers. The worker sees only encrypted bytes. Once that proof-of-concept held up, I knew the architecture was sound. YOZZ has since become the daily driver for all my custom-domain email. The biggest capability YOZZ lacked was AI assistance. Moving my daily email workflow from Gmail to YOZZ made that clear: I had grown used to Gemini inside Gmail and to ChatGPT’s Gmail connector for more complex tasks spanning my other connected services. I first considered connecting YOZZ to ChatGPT through a conventional connector or server-side MCP. But YOZZ’s service has no readable access to mailbox credentials or mail, and giving it that access would break the product’s zero-knowledge premise. I also tested local models through Transformers.js, but the models I tried were either not reliable enough for work as sensitive as email or too slow and resource-hungry on my hardware. When this challenge introduced me to WebMCP, I realised that a capable external agent could instead work through the user’s active YOZZ client. What it does YOZZ is a zero-knowledge webmail client for supported IMAP and SMTP accounts you already own. Its server-side infrastructure receives no plaintext mailbox credentials or messages. Received mail remains with the existing provider and is cached only on the user’s device. Credentials, drafts and any sent-mail copies stored on the server are encrypted by the web app before reaching D1. YOZZ’s web app and the mail provider are the TLS endpoints. Since browser APIs cannot open the required TCP connections to mail servers, the relay simply forwards the ciphertext between them. It never receives the TLS session keys, mailbox passwords or plaintext messages, so YOZZ’s server-side infrastructure cannot decrypt the traffic it carries. This boundary is deliberately narrow. The existing mail provider retains its access, and an external agent can read mail returned through WebMCP. The user chooses which agent receives that mail; YOZZ’s servers gain no readable access in either case. YOZZ does retain limited operational metadata. “Zero-knowledge” here applies to stored vault contents and traffic crossing the relay. It does not make email end-to-end encrypted or protect against malicious client code delivered to the browser. After the user logs in, YOZZ registers six focused WebMCP tools: get_addresses : list the configured addresses. get_threads : search and read conversations without marking them as read. update_threads : mark conversations read or unread, star them, archive them or move them to Trash. save_draft : create a message, prepare a reply or update an existing draft. delete_draft : discard a draft, recoverable for 30 days. navigate : open a conversation or draft in the interface. Opening an unread conversation marks it read, just like the user’s own click. navigate is the only tool that changes what the user is currently looking at. The other tools work in the background without taking the user away from their current task. Before WebMCP, every multi-message task had to be completed manually inside YOZZ. Now the user and agent can divide the work: the agent can summarise unread mail across every configured address, find messages about a trip or purchase, clean up selected low-value threads and prepare a reply. The resulting draft can be opened inside YOZZ for review, but no WebMCP tool can send mail . Sending is a separate action in YOZZ's visible composer. A browser-capable agent may offer to perform that action, but only after surfacing the draft and requesting the user's confirmation. Why WebMCP belongs here For these workflows, a conventional server-side MCP integration would require moving readable mailbox access from the web app into server-side infrastructure, breaking YOZZ’s zero-knowledge premise. It would need mailbox credentials, an equivalent authorisation token or a server-terminated mail session. Any of those would give YOZZ’s infrastructure readable mailbox access it deliberately does not have. WebMCP instead uses the capabilities already present in the user’s logged-in web app, allowing an agent chosen by the user to work with mail without giving YOZZ’s servers new access. The immediate audience is people who already use custom-domain email or other IMAP and SMTP accounts and want webmail without entrusting another client operator with their credentials. YOZZ supports multiple inbound and send-only addresses, and Google’s upcoming change gives some of these users a concrete reason to seek another client. How I built it YOZZ is a deployed TypeScript application whose server-side infrastructure runs on Cloudflare Workers. Its web app implements TLS 1.3, X.509 certificate validation, IMAP, SMTP and MIME message handling. The API Worker handles three things: User authentication. Storing and updating ciphertext vault records in D1, including records for mailbox credentials, drafts and sent-mail copies. All are encrypted by the web app before reaching the Worker. The WebSocket-to-TCP relay. I initially considered making YOZZ accountless, with users connecting their IMAP and SMTP accounts directly in the web app. That would work on one device, but I wanted to access the same mailbox configuration across multiple devices. I therefore introduced authentication and an encrypted vault. The user’s password or a PRF-capable passkey provides the client-side material needed to unlock the vault. YOZZ’s server stores the wrapped data-encryption key and ciphertext vault records alongside the authentication and operational metadata described above. This provides multi-device access without giving the server the key needed to decrypt mailbox credentials, drafts or settings. The WebMCP tools call the same application services as the user interface. Tool actions immediately appear in the product and follow the same state rules as user actions. I started working on YOZZ on August 16, 2026. The challenge began on August 25, and the first WebMCP implementation was committed on August 26. Before the challenge, YOZZ was already a deployed mail client but had no agent tools. During the challenge, I added the six-tool WebMCP layer, defined the WebMCP no-send and untrusted-content boundaries, added behavioural tests and built the judge infrastructure. The existing TLS, X.509, IMAP, SMTP and MIME implementation is the foundation this extension works through, not challenge-period work. YOZZ lives alongside dozens of other projects in my private monorepo. That private repository contains YOZZ’s original development history and is the source of the dates above. video_title: YOZZ: zero-knowledge webmail your AI agent can use (WebMCP demo)
video_transcript_excerpt: Hello, I'm Jason. I built a zero-knowledge webmail client called Yoz. Zero-knowledge roughly means the servers can't see your stuff. So, how is Yoz zero-knowledge? When you save sensitive data, your browser encrypts it right there on your machine before sending it off. Yoz's servers only ever store and return scrambled unreadable ciphertext. We don't hold the key and we can't see what's inside. For example, this API response contains my saved mail account, but the actual details are returned as ciphertext. Only the unlocked web app can turn that ciphertext back into something meaningful, in this case, the email address you see here. Mail traffic follows the same principle. The TLS connection runs between the Yoz web app in your browser and the mail server you use. Yoz's relay only transports encrypted traffic. The session keys exist at those two endpoints, so the relay cannot decrypt what passes through it. In short, Yoz's servers are blind. We cannot read your mail. So, how can Yoz connect with AI agents? A traditional server-side MCP is impossible because Yoz's servers are blind, cannot read mail. So, we need something that works purely on the client side that also connects to AI. Wait a second. Isn't this exactly what web MCP's for? Let's see this in action now. Here, I have Yoz open in ChatGPT desktop. Yoz registers six web MCP tools directly with the page. I give ChatGPT a simple request to summarize the inbox. ChatGPT gives me a clear summary of the mailbox. Notice how it also flags the suspicious confirm your mailbox email. Yoz marks tools that return mail as carrying untrusted content. This tells the agent to treat what it reads with caution. By design, every tool except one works in the background. So, you can use Yoz while the agent is working. The one exception is the navigate tool, which is used when the agent needs to show you something for review. Let's ask ChatGPT to reply to Sam about the lunch. It saves the reply as a draft, then uses the navigate tool to open the draft editor in Yoz. Now, I can review the message and press send myself. Together, these tools let your agents read, organize, and draft mail through the unlocked web app without giving Yoz's servers any new access. That is how Yoz brings capable AI to your mailbox without giving up its zero knowledge design.

 Inspiration 

 Recreating a beat usually involves repeatedly changing the music, listening again, and deciding what to fix. We wanted to see if an AI agent could handle that loop directly inside a music-making website. 

 What it does 

 The user gives the agent a reference beat. The agent writes a Strudel program, tests it, compares the result with the original, and tries again. Every attempt is saved so users can inspect earlier versions or continue from them. 

 How we built it 

 We built a browser-based Strudel editor with React and TypeScript. The website gives the agent six tools for reading and changing the program, testing attempts, and managing saved versions. It records each result, compares its first ten seconds with the reference, and saves everything in the browser. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Connecting the agent to a live music editor was the biggest challenge. We also had to capture Strudel’s audio reliably, compare recordings of different lengths, preserve attempts after reloading, and handle experimental browser support for WebMCP. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 The agent can complete several attempts from one prompt without needing the user to tell it to continue. Every attempt has its own code, score, feedback, and connection to the previous version. The project also works as a live deployed website. 

 What we learned 

 Clear feedback matters more than simply giving the agent a score. The agent made better decisions when it received both measurements and a short explanation of what sounded different. We also learned that matching audio requires more than comparing volume and energy.

title: Agent Market: agents negotiate, you confirm
pitch: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order.
about_excerpt: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order. Like Comment Story Updates negotiation between seller and buyer interface Inspiration People delegate the boring parts of shopping, but the boring part that a plain API integration can never capture is the haggle . A price is one number; a real deal is price times quantity, which freebie the seller throws in, whether shipping is waived, and which coupon stacks on top. We wanted the shopper's browser agent to work that whole space on the site the user is already looking at, and still leave the final yes/no to a human. What it does Agent Market is a multi-vendor storefront with 95k+ real products. Every page registers storefront tools on document.modelContext (WebMCP): search, product details, cart, add-ons, coupons, and a full negotiation set. A buyer's agent opens a negotiation and haggles a multi-dimensional deal against the store's agent over several rounds. When they settle, the page shows a Confirm dialog and nothing is bought until the human confirms the price . The same tools work in a WebMCP browser (ChatGPT's in-app browser, Chrome with the flag) or drive an in-page agent loop that needs no API key from the user. How we built it Frontend: Next.js 15 / React 19 / TypeScript on Vercel. StorefrontTools registers every tool on document.modelContext ; lib/agent-loop.ts is a tool-agnostic agent harness that discovers tools from the registry and runs a hand-rolled chat-completions loop. Backend: Spring Boot (Java) on Render, Azure SQL, Flyway, Hibernate. One mutation path: every state change (buyer, seller, or the server-side auto-negotiator) goes through OffersService.applyTurn , a pure function that is the only code allowed to decide a negotiation transition. It enforces the two hard economic limits (buyer total <= budget, seller net >= floor); which freebie and how much to concede is agent judgment. Human gate: accepting mints an HMAC confirm token; the order is placed only when the human clicks Confirm. Model: Google Gemini through the OpenAI-compatible endpoint, key server-side only. Challenges we ran into Gemini "thinking" models and tool history. Gemini 3.x rejects a multi-turn tool conversation unless each function call's thought_signature is echoed back. The OpenAI-compat shim dropped it, so turn 2 always 400'd. We now capture tool_calls[].extra_content on the way in and replay it on the way out. Small models stall on long tool loops. Asking a fast model to drive search then offer then counter then counter then accept meant it derailed a turn later every time. We collapsed the buyer's negotiation into a single deterministic negotiate tool: the server plays both sides of the haggle, persists every round so the transcript is real, and returns a confirm token. The agent's job is now two calls, and reaching the confirm step no longer depends on the model finishing a loop. Optimistic concurrency vs agent reliability. A strict round guard made the agent stall forever when its round number drifted. We made the guard opt-in for proposals and mandatory only for the binding accept. What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part to the server and leave the model the judgment call. What's next Seller-side takeover controls, agent-negotiated bundles across multiple sellers, and a browser-vs-browser two-agent mode for a fully agentic negotiation. title: EMR WebMCP: LabLatch
pitch: A safe agent hunt for unowned abnormal labs inside OpenMRS, with human-confirmed follow-up.
about_excerpt: A safe agent hunt for unowned abnormal labs inside OpenMRS, with human-confirmed follow-up. Like Comment Story Updates Why I am building this I am Dr. Sithira Ambepitiya, a doctor and the Head of AI at AIGP Health. At AIGP Health, I work on Anzu, an agentic clinical platform built in Singapore. Anzu is HSA Class A approved, and we are building the wider system toward an agent-native EMR. Working on Anzu has shown me what is possible when a new clinical system is designed around agents from day one. That is exciting, but a new EMR is obviously not the answer for everyone. Most clinics cannot throw away the medical record they already use. Large health programs have years of data, workflows, training, and infrastructure tied to existing systems. Open source EMRs like OpenMRS are already being used by real clinics and large populations, especially in places where budgets, staff, and infrastructure are limited. That is why I wanted to build this. The real opportunity is not only creating new agent-native medical records. It is also making the systems people already depend on understandable and usable by agents. The medical record already has most of the information a clinic needs. The painful part is the work around it. Someone still has to search through screens, open several charts, check whether an abnormal result was followed up, work out who owns the next step, and make sure nothing important has disappeared into a queue. When people talk about medical AI, they often jump straight to diagnosis. I do not think an agent has to start there to be useful. There is a huge amount of repetitive operational work that pulls clinicians away from patients. It is structured enough for an agent to help with, but important enough that it needs proper safety boundaries. What EMR WebMCP does EMR WebMCP gives an existing medical record a small set of structured tools that an agent can understand and use. Instead of handing the agent unrestricted browser control or a generic API key, the OpenMRS page exposes specific actions through WebMCP. The tools available at any moment depend on the current page, the logged-in user, their permissions, and what that OpenMRS installation supports. A clinician can ask, "Prepare tomorrow's diabetes clinic. Show me unresolved abnormal results, missing follow-up, and overdue tasks." The agent can find the appointments, assemble a focused brief for each patient, identify recorded gaps, prepare follow-up drafts, and take the clinician to the right native screen. One workflow is called LabLatch. It finds abnormal results that do not have an active follow-up owner. It gathers the relevant context and prepares a task for review, so an important result does not quietly disappear into the record. The important word is prepare. The agent does not make the final clinical action. How it works I did not want to fork OpenMRS or build a fake medical record just for a hackathon demo. The whole point is to show that an existing system can become agent accessible without being replaced. The project is a TypeScript monorepo. A shared core defines the tool contracts, safety rules, result format, lifecycle, and privacy-aware telemetry. The OpenMRS adapter connects those contracts to O3, FHIR R4, REST data, routes, permissions, and native workspaces. Reusable workflow packages contain the clinic preparation and follow-up logic. An O3 frontend module registers twelve bounded tools through document.modelContext. Some tools read a limited amount of existing information. Some open a known screen. Some prepare a temporary draft inside the browser. There is no tool for arbitrary REST calls, unrestricted FHIR queries, SQL, code execution, or free-form DOM manipulation. The demo uses synthetic patients and a simulated clinic backlog. It does not need real patient data. The safety boundary The hardest part was not connecting an agent to an API. The hard part was deciding exactly what the agent should not be allowed to do. I split every action into four classes: read, navigate, draft, and commit. The agent can read, navigate, and draft. It cannot commit. Before anything is written, OpenMRS shows the patient, the source evidence, the proposed action, the assignee, the priority, and the due date. The clinician can edit it, confirm it, or discard it. Only that visible confirmation creates a durable task. The agent cannot prescribe, sign a note, discharge a patient, change clinical facts, contact a patient, or quietly mark work as complete. It also cannot bypass the current user's permissions. There is no shared superuser token behind the demo. What was difficult The easy version would have been one generic tool that could call any EMR endpoint. It would look powerful, but it would miss the point of WebMCP and create a dangerous interface. The better version required small tools with clear meanings, bounded inputs, predictable outputs, and visible confirmation points. OpenMRS also spans frontend context, FHIR resources, REST metadata, routes, permissions, and task workspaces. Keeping those details inside one adapter while keeping the workflows reusable was a real architecture challenge. I also had to treat stale screens, patient changes, duplicate follow-ups, expired drafts, authorization failures, and logout as normal safety cases, not rare edge cases. What I am proud of The part I am most proud of is not the number of tools. It is the boundary. The agent can do enough preparation to make a real difference, while OpenMRS remains the system of record. The existing EMR still controls identity, permissions, clinical evidence, and the final write. This is also what makes the idea larger than one OpenMRS demo. A different EMR can implement the same workflow contracts through its own adapter, using its own API, terminology, routes, and confirmation screens. What I learned WebMCP is much more interesting than simply turning a webpage into another API. A good WebMCP surface lets an application explain what actions are meaningful, what data is needed, what the current user is allowed to do, and where a human decision is still required. For healthcare, that is the difference between an agent that clicks faster and an agent that can actually fit into clinical work. What comes next OpenMRS is the first proof point. I am not claiming that EMR WebMCP already works with every medical record. The next test is a second adapter that passes the same contracts without changing the workflow packages. After that, the same approach could support referrals, patient recall, documentation drafts, inventory, and discharge readiness. I also want to compare the same tasks across normal manual use, ordinary browser automation, and WebMCP. The goal is to measure whether the structured agent path saves time while preserving the clinical safety gates. title: InfraPilot WebMCP
pitch: Agent-native control plane orchestrating distributed LLM inference clusters directly via WebMCP tool calls.
about_excerpt:
Agent-native control plane orchestrating distributed LLM inference clusters directly via WebMCP tool calls.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 💡 Inspiration 

 As large language models scale and multi-model inference pipelines (vLLM, SGLang, DeepSeek, Qwen) become the backbone of modern AI infrastructure, operating and orchestrating these distributed clusters has become increasingly complex. 

 Traditional DevOps observability relies heavily on human-centric graphical user interfaces—complex dashboards, nested SVG node graphs, and dropdown menus. When autonomous AI agents are tasked with managing or triaging cluster incidents via raw DOM scraping or vision models, they frequently suffer from hallucinations, missed metrics, or misclicks. 

 InfraPilot was born to bridge this fundamental gap using OpenAI's emerging WebMCP standard ( document.modelContext.registerTool ). Instead of forcing models to guess through UI pixels, InfraPilot transforms the web control plane into an agent-native environment where models directly discover and execute structured cluster management tools. 

 

 🚀 What It Does 

 InfraPilot provides a real-time, agent-native control plane for distributed LLM inference clusters. It registers four core atomic tools directly on the browser's document.modelContext : 

 
 get_cluster_topology : Exposes the complete topology of active inference engines, gateways, prefix KV caches, and vector databases in clean, structured JSON. 
 scale_service_replicas : Allows an autonomous agent or human operator to dynamically scale inference pods (e.g., DeepSeek-R1 or Qwen2.5) during sudden traffic surges. 
 optimize_gpu_memory : Triggers immediate eviction of stale prefix KV caches and reclaims fragmented GPU VRAM across nodes. 
 run_inference_benchmark : Automatically executes concurrent throughput stress tests to verify cluster latency and throughput post-optimization. 
 

 Every single tool execution is transparently recorded in a real-time Execution Audit Log , giving operators full observability with exact millisecond duration, input parameters, and structured outputs. 

 

 🛠️ How We Built It 

 
 Frontend Architecture : Built with React 19 , TypeScript , and Vite with a responsive Linear-inspired design. 
 WebMCP Integration : Native registration against browser-level document.modelContext.registerTool with a development fallback bridge ensuring seamless evaluation across standard browsers, ChatGPT In-App Browser, and WebMCP-enabled Chrome. 
 Hosting & Edge Delivery : Deployed globally on Cloudflare Pages for sub-millisecond edge response times. 
 Styling : Styled using Tailwind CSS v4 with zero-compromise accessibility and dark-mode aesthetics. 
 

 

 🧠 Challenges We Ran Into 

 
 State Synchronization & Zero-Latency Feedback : Ensuring that agent-driven WebMCP tool executions seamlessly update the React visual topology and the streaming execution audit log without UI lag or race conditions. 
 Standard Protocol Compliance : Carefully designing the JSON Schema for tool inputs/outputs to guarantee maximum discovery reliability across both ChatGPT's in-app browser and Chrome's WebMCP experimental runtime. 
 

 

 🏆 Accomplishments We're Proud Of 

 
 True Agent-Native UX : The cluster can be fully managed through natural language prompts via ChatGPT in-app browser (e.g., "DeepSeek latency is high, scale it to 4 replicas and free stale KV memory" ). 
 Sub-Second Recovery Loop : Demonstrating how WebMCP enables autonomous closed-loop cluster healing (triage → scale → optimize → benchmark) in under 2 seconds without a human touching a mouse. 
 

 

 📚 What We Learned 

 WebMCP represents a paradigm shift in web development. Web applications are no longer just human-to-computer interfaces; they are becoming shared collaborative workspaces for both humans and AI agents. Building with WebMCP taught us the immense power of declaring structured API capabilities directly at the document level. 

 

 🔮 What's Next for InfraPilot 

 
 Adding dynamic multi-cluster federation support (AWS, CoreWeave, Lambda Labs). 
 Integrating autonomous anomaly-detection background triggers that proactively invoke WebMCP optimization tools before SLA breaches occur.

title: CareWeave
pitch: CareWeave gives older and disabled people one calm place to coordinate daily care with loved ones and WebMCP agents, reducing complexity while protecting independence, privacy, and human control.
about_excerpt: CareWeave gives older and disabled people one calm place to coordinate daily care with loved ones and WebMCP agents, reducing complexity while protecting independence, privacy, and human control. Like Comment Story Updates Summary Careweave - Functionality Careweave - Overview Inspiration An appointment reminder arrives by email. The journey depends on the weather. A carer is visiting that morning. A son can help, but should not need access to private messages. None of these facts is difficult on its own. Keeping them aligned is. For many older and disabled people, daily life is spread across inboxes, calendars, maps, notes, and several people's memories. A small uncertainty can become a missed appointment, a wasted journey, an empty fridge, or another phone call asking someone else to check. The result is not just inconvenience. It is time, energy, confidence, and independence gradually lost to administration. Most planning tools assume that someone can scan a crowded calendar, remember where each detail lives, notice every change, and recover when information conflicts. Those assumptions become barriers for people managing fatigue, pain, reduced mobility, sensory loss, memory changes, or recovery. Support can also come with a hidden trade. To receive help, a person is often expected to hand over more privacy or control than the task requires. CareWeave began with a belief that independence does not mean doing everything alone. It means deciding how help happens. We wanted to build one calm place where a person, the people they trust, and an agent could work from the same understanding. The technology should carry the complexity. The person should keep the authority. What it does CareWeave turns the scattered work of daily care into one accessible dayboard. It brings together appointments, care visits, food, shopping, reminders, travel, weather, and important messages, then answers three human questions: What is happening today? Is there anything I need to decide or prepare? Can you help me deal with it safely? Instead of a dense monthly calendar, CareWeave begins with a clear day. It shows what matters now, what needs attention, and whether the pace feels calm or rushed. Large controls, readable text, high contrast, written alternatives to speech, and generous touch targets reduce the effort needed to use it. WebMCP makes CareWeave a genuinely shared workspace. A compatible agent can understand structured household information instead of guessing from pixels. It can explain the day, check the surrounding week, focus the visible board on an appointment, calculate when to leave, and open the route on the same screen the person is viewing. The clearest example is a clinic appointment. A person can ask: What matters today, and is tomorrow rushed? CareWeave returns confirmed plans, preparation, travel, and unresolved attention items. The person can then ask: Show me tomorrow and the route to Dr Patel. The dayboard moves to tomorrow and displays the route with a safe departure time. The conversation and the interface stay in sync. If the day feels too demanding, the person can ask: Prepare a request to move the appointment to a calm morning. CareWeave finds suitable options and prepares the exact recipient, subject, and message. It presents an expiring review plan before anything progresses. The original appointment remains confirmed until the clinic verifies a new time. A suggestion is not a draft, a draft is not a sent request, and a request is not a confirmation. Trusted supporters have a deliberately limited view. They can offer practical help without reading private messages, medical notes, or detailed care records. The person receiving support can accept, decline, undo, or revoke access. The agent handles coordination. The person keeps the decision. How we built it CareWeave is an installable SvelteKit progressive web app built with Svelte 5, TypeScript, and Vite. We started with the domain model rather than the interface. Confirmed commitments, untrusted attention items, reminders, support offers, data freshness, and action plans are separate objects. This prevents proposed actions from being mistaken for real outcomes. The application registers 32 imperative WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . They cover understanding the day, checking pace, finding options, changing shared visual focus, showing routes, managing reminders, offering support, reviewing mailbox information, preparing actions, and applying verified confirmations. All tool inputs are validated again when they run. Read-only, untrusted-content, and consequential annotations expose the relevant safety boundaries to compatible agents. State revisions prevent an old action plan from being approved after the household information changes. If tool registration fails, CareWeave rolls back the attempted set instead of claiming a partial connection is ready. The touch interface, voice experience, and WebMCP tools call the same domain functions. There is one state for the person and the agent, not separate implementations that can quietly disagree. We used Leaflet and OpenStreetMap for routes, Open-Meteo for privacy-conscious forecasts, browser speech features, and an optional OpenAI Realtime voice path. An optional server-side Gmail connection reads bounded previews and creates drafts, but it cannot send email. The challenge experience uses deterministic fictional data stored on the device. It needs no account, credentials, API key, or private information. Unit tests, Playwright interaction and accessibility tests, and a browser-based WebMCP evaluation cover the core workflows. The production-host smoke run completed all 10 expected tool steps across six journeys. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was making the interface tell the truth about real world state. In ordinary software, "requested," "drafted," and "confirmed" can blur together. In care coordination, that ambiguity matters. Someone could leave at the wrong time or believe help is arranged when it is not. We created an explicit appointment lifecycle and made every consequential action pass through a frozen, expiring review plan. We also had to find the right boundary for agency. A single powerful tool would have been easier to demonstrate, but harder for a person to understand or interrupt. We chose narrow tools that can be inspected, combined, and stopped at meaningful human decision points. The next challenge was keeping a broad care story visually calm. Every extra status, button, and warning adds cognitive work. We reduced density, enlarged targets, revealed details progressively, tested tablet and phone layouts, and kept spoken information available as text. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that WebMCP changes the actual CareWeave experience. The agent does not merely describe the page. It understands structured care context, reasons across it, and brings the person to the same date, appointment, or route being discussed. We built an end-to-end appointment workflow that remains truthful at every step. CareWeave can interpret an attention item, assess the week, find calmer options, prepare the exact clinic request, show it for review, and record the result without silently changing the confirmed appointment. We are equally proud of the social model. Supporters can be useful without becoming supervisors. Privacy is limited by purpose, help can be revoked, and the person at the centre retains the final say. The working build exposes 32 validated WebMCP tools, shares domain logic across touch and agent interactions, protects changes with revisions, and passed all 10 steps in our production-host smoke evaluation. It also supports large text, high contrast, keyboard navigation, reduced motion, and responsive tablet and phone layouts. What we learned We learned that autonomy is not a permission checkbox. It is the visible difference between offering help and taking over. We also learned that truthful state is part of accessibility. People should not need technical knowledge to know whether an appointment has changed, a message has been sent, or a relative has accepted a task. Structured tools help an agent understand a website. Shared visual focus helps a person understand the agent. CareWeave needs both. If the answer remains only in chat, the person still has to find the appointment, route, or reminder afterwards. Finally, calmness has to be engineered. Every new capability carries a cognitive cost. The best interface is not the one that shows everything. It is the one that helps someone answer the next question with the least effort. What's next for CareWeave The next step is to develop CareWeave with the people it is intended to support. We want to test the core experience with older and disabled people, unpaid family supporters, and professional carers, then adapt it to their language, routines, and access needs. Before CareWeave handles real household or care

title: WebMCP Video by AgentCDN
pitch: Ask a video a question. WebMCP Video finds the right moment, explains what happens, and prepares the official player at that time.
about_excerpt: Ask a video a question. WebMCP Video finds the right moment, explains what happens, and prepares the official player at that time. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Ask a video a question. The page helps AI find the exact moment, explain it, and prepare the official player there. Use this tool only to search the videos and moments available on this page. It returns moment_ref values for context or playback. Use this tool only to inspect transcript, visual, rights, and link details for a moment_ref from this page. Use this tool only after the user asks to play, show, cue, or jump to a moment on this page. ChatGPT with WebMCP Video would be able to efficiently search videos, find moments and play back right inside ChatGPT. This repository is a reference implementation. Why I built it Ask AI about a video and the answer often stops at text or a link to the beginning. I built WebMCP Video so ChatGPT can find the exact scene, explain it, and prepare the site's official player at that moment. Video takes a huge share of our attention. EMARKETER forecasts that video will account for just under half of US digital media time in 2026 . DataReportal reports that online adults say they spend 11 hours and 39 minutes with online video each week, 14% more than television, including streaming TV . For creators and media brands, much of their most valuable knowledge now lives inside video. If I ask what a motorized exoskeleton looks like, I should see that moment. If I ask about robotic massage, I should not have to scrub through the video to find it. Multimodal models can analyze video. Repeating that work for every agent visit is slow and costly. The agent may need to fetch the video, transcribe it, inspect the frames, and still return only a summary. AgentCDN prepares the transcript, visual context, and timing once. WebMCP gives the open page a standard way to share that prepared understanding with an agent. The agent finds and explains the right moment. The page checks current permission and prepares its official player. The person decides when playback starts. What it does WebMCP Video gives ChatGPT three tools from the page: search_this_catalog finds the best matching video moment. get_moment_context returns what was said and what appeared on screen. play_moment prepares the official player at the requested time. The person asks a normal question. ChatGPT uses the page tools. The page updates the same player the person can see. The person presses play when ready. In the demo, ChatGPT finds a motorized exoskeleton at 46 seconds. On my founder site, it finds robotic massage at 53 seconds. Both results use the official YouTube player already controlled by the page. Why WebMCP fits WebMCP connects the agent's answer to the live page and its real player. Without WebMCP, a viewer must install a separate MCP connection or plugin for each video provider, wait while an agent processes the video again, or open a link and search the timeline manually. With WebMCP, the capability travels with the page. ChatGPT can use the tools that the open site provides. The site keeps control of its catalog, permission checks, player, and visible state. People and agents now do different parts of the same task: The person asks. The agent finds and explains. The page prepares the official player. The person chooses when to watch. How I built it The public demo uses TypeScript, document.modelContext , and the YouTube IFrame API. It registers the three tools directly in the browser. It has no backend, model calls, secrets, or bundled media. Search returns an exact start and end time plus a short-lived moment_ref . Context and playback must use that same reference. The reference is tied to the page and expires after five minutes. Playback reports only what the browser can prove: cued means the correct video and time are ready. sought means the loaded player reached the requested time. fallback means the page could not confirm either result. None of these states claim that playback started. I also shipped the same three WebMCP tools on AgentCDN's production watch page. That version searches a live catalog, checks current permission before playback, delivers an audit outcome, and never returns a raw stream URL. I then added the tools to the video page on my founder site. The site controls its official player. AgentCDN handles search, context, permission, and the audit outcome. The public repository contains the complete standalone example, a replaceable YouTube adapter, setup instructions, adversarial browser tests, CI, and an Apache 2.0 license. What was hard The hard part was making a WebMCP result match the visible page honestly. Tool discovery had to work in the supported browser. The descriptions had to guide ChatGPT through search, context, and play in the correct order. Every later call had to use the exact short-lived reference returned by search. The YouTube player is asynchronous. Accepting a command does not prove that the player selected the correct video or reached the requested time. I added bounded checks for the video ID, requested time, and player state. The page reports cued or sought only after stable browser evidence. Permission can also change between search and playback. The production version checks it again before acting. Expired, altered, cross-page, and denied references fail closed. Finally, the agent and the person must see the same result. Each tool updates structured output for ChatGPT and visible state on the page. This made browser testing as important as API testing. What I learned WebMCP works best when tools describe useful user actions, not internal API endpoints. The agent should understand the question and select a moment. The page should control the player, check current permission, and report what actually happened. For video, a valid data response is not enough. The visible player is part of the result. What is next First, I will add adapters for more official players, content management systems, and video platforms, including WordPress and Brightcove. The public tool can remain play_moment while AgentCDN translates the request for each supported player. Next, I plan to add controlled video editing tools through WebMCP. An agent could draft a clip, adjust its timing, add captions, and render a preview. AgentCDN would keep permissions, attribution, and version history attached. Longer term, this could support personalized video experiences with agent as an editor and host assembling video content based on individual interests, while keeping the original source and attribution attached, so original authors get credited. These are roadmap items. This submission proves exact search, prepared transcript and visual context, current permission checks, and official YouTube player preparation. title: Resident
pitch: A human-agent record store where an agent digs, plays and curates in full view—while the listener stays in control.
about_excerpt: A human-agent record store where an agent digs, plays and curates in full view—while the listener stays in control. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Desktop Interface with Agent Mode Enabled + WebMCP Tool Plugin Sidebar Desktop Interface with Agent Mode Enabled Desktop Interface with Agent Mode Playing Music Mobile Interface with Agent Mode Enabled (Light Mode) Mobile Interface with Agent Mode Enabled (Light Mode) Inspiration Most browser-agent experiences happen behind the scenes. A user asks for something, waits, and receives a result without seeing what the agent searched, what it considered, or when control changed. Resident explores a different model: the agent joins the music interface instead of operating behind it. What we built Resident grew out of my existing 3D digital record crate at https://sephmartin.com/ . For the WebMCP Challenge, I extended that same environment rather than building a separate demo. The original experience remains at https://sephmartin.com/ , while the challenge build lives at https://demo.sephmartin.com/ . The result is a meaningful page-level WebMCP extension, not a separate wrapper. The agent can orient over the catalog, search and rank releases using conservative metadata-only Song DNA, focus and inspect records, play and navigate previews, move between tracks and releases, manage a reversible local My Crate, and prepare checkout. The interface makes the agent's work legible. Agent Mode, Thinking, Digging, Listening, Returning and Human Mode are visible states; the orb mirrors the active release and operation; and the crate, player and detail panel update together. The same page remains usable by a person through pointer, keyboard and touch input. How WebMCP is implemented The adapter feature-detects document.modelContext and keeps a compatibility fallback for navigator.modelContext. It registers narrow tools with explicit schemas and read-only or UI-mutation annotations. The tools call a small page facade exposed by the existing crate runtime rather than reaching into arbitrary DOM nodes. A local browser diagnostic log records the tool sequence, visible state and failures so the interaction can be inspected during a demo. The Song DNA layer is evidence-bound: it uses catalog fields such as tags, descriptions and track titles, labels text-derived matches, and reports unavailable audio analysis instead of inventing BPM, key or texture. Stable record IDs keep agent actions reliable across sorting and browsing. Human control and safety The human remains in the loop. A pointer, keyboard or touch gesture can reclaim the page immediately and return it to Human Mode. Crate changes are reversible. Checkout is intentionally split into review and confirmation: the on-site challenge simulator records no real payment, and the final download step ends at a copyright-safe DEMO COMPLETE boundary rather than delivering an original audio file. What I learned I don’t come from traditional software engineering; I come from music, where experience, rhythm and emotion matter as much as functionality. AI gave me a medium for turning that perspective into software. I didn’t get into AI to write code. I got into it to build experiences that didn’t exist before. I built Resident iteratively with coding agents on a standard ChatGPT Plus subscription. I brought the product vision, music knowledge and interaction design; the agents helped me test, break and refine the implementation until it matched what I had imagined. The original 3D crate was already a long-running creative project. The challenge gave me the spark to extend it into a shared human-agent space. WebMCP is valuable here beyond button automation: it lets an agent operate inside a stateful, visual application while the person can see, interrupt and review the work. The strongest interaction is not a one-shot recommendation; it is the visible loop from natural-language intent to digging, focus, playback, curation and human handoff. Try it Open the live demo in ChatGPT's in-app browser, ask the agent to start the curator session, request a late-night disco or house selection, play and inspect a result, add it to My Crate, and prepare checkout. The purchase is a no-payment demo flow. If audio does not start immediately, click or tap the page once: browser autoplay policies require a user gesture before sound can play. A human gesture during Agent Mode demonstrates immediate priority. title: Signoff - the agent proposes, you decide
pitch: A refund-approval queue where the agent proposes decisions with written reasons - and the tool that applies one doesn't exist until a human approves it.
about_excerpt: A refund-approval queue where the agent proposes decisions with written reasons - and the tool that applies one doesn't exist until a human approves it. Like Comment Story Updates The refund queue: risk signals and proposals Tool console: get_policy called live via WebMCP WebMCP surface: the apply_proposal tool doesn't exist in the registry until a human approves the agent's proposal - enforcement lives in tool existence , not a runtime permission check. Inspiration Working a refund queue is judgment sandwiched between drudgery: read the ticket, weigh the amount against the risk, write a defensible reason, repeat forty times. The judgment is the human's job. The reading, weighing, and drafting shouldn't be. What it does The agent reads a written refund policy and every request's evidence, proposes approve / deny / partial decisions with a written reason each, and stages them as cards next to the requests they concern. Nothing applies until a human clicks Approve - and apply_proposal , the tool that actually applies a decision, is registered only while at least one approved-but-unapplied proposal exists. Approve nothing, and the tool to apply anything simply isn't in the agent's list. How we built it One file, vanilla JavaScript, no framework. Every tool and every UI button call the same mutation through one invoke() chokepoint that also writes the shared activity log. apply_proposal dynamically registers/unregisters via an AbortController tied to whether a pending approved proposal exists - a permission boundary expressed as which tools exist, not as an instruction a model could ignore. Challenges we ran into Two rounds of adversarial testing against real Chrome (not headless mocks) found two distinct bugs in that dynamic-registration path: first, a self-abort race where the tool's own disarm logic cancelled the very call it was running under; then, after fixing that with a deferred abort, a second race where a fast Approve → Revoke → re-Approve cycle could silently desync the tool from Chrome's real registry - no error, but the tool had actually vanished. Root-caused via page.mouse.click() (real coordinate clicks reproduced it 12/15 times; Playwright's polling clicks never did), then fixed by tracking and synchronously draining any stale pending abort before re-arming. Accomplishments that we're proud of An approval boundary enforced by the browser's own tool registry, not by prompt instructions - and proven against the actual WebMCP bridge under adversarial, rapid-clicking conditions, not just the happy path. What we learned "It passed headless Playwright" and "it's correct against real Chrome" are different claims. The riskiest bugs in a dynamic-tool-registration pattern only show up under real, synchronous, same-tick timing. What's next A written audit trail export per decision, and richer risk-signal explanations sourced from order history across the whole account, not just the single request. Part of a seven-app portfolio Each entry proves a different WebMCP capability: Tablemap (dynamic tool registration), Paperwork (structurally human-only fields), Shortlist (a tool schema generated live from the catalog), Jhola (genuinely cancellable long-running tools), Almari (quarantined untrusted content), Dhwani (declarative, no-JavaScript tools). title: ORPHEUS: A Case You and Your Agent Can't Crack Alone
pitch: A detective game where your agent reads every byte of the evidence and sees none of it. 25 WebMCP tools, no screenshot tool, and a case that only closes when the human and the agent both look.
about_excerpt: A detective game where your agent reads every byte of the evidence and sees none of it. 25 WebMCP tools, no screenshot tool, and a case that only closes when the human and the agent both look. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Thumbnail Verification Panel Inspiration Co-op games need a second person. That is why I never play them. Every agent demo I have seen has done the same thing: the agent screenshots the page, clicks the button, and the human watches. The human is a spectator to their own software. I wanted the reverse. An agent that is genuinely powerful and genuinely incomplete, where I am the half it cannot replace. So I asked myself a question: what if the agent could read everything on the page, and see nothing? What it does Orpheus is a co-op detective game you play alone, because your agent is player two. A physicist is dead. His workstation was seized intact. Files, mail, messages, photos, a browser, a terminal, a system log. Every application on that desk is also a tool your agent can call. Twenty-five of them. Your agent can search every file, read every email, and filter fifty-one log entries down to the six that matter. What it cannot do is see. I gave it no screenshot tool, no vision tool, and no pixel access anywhere in the registry. It gets the filename, the camera, the timestamps, and not one pixel. So when the case turns on what is visible in a photograph, it opens the image on your screen and asks you what is in it. You describe. It searches what you described. The case will not unlock until a correlation has run through a tool and you have done your own looking. How I built it I built it using Next.js and React, fully client side. No backend, no database and no sign-up. I set one rule and it carried the whole build: if the human can do it and the agent can do it, the logic exists once. My register.ts declares 25 tools and implements none of them. Each delegates to the same service functions the UI calls, so the agent can never reach state a human could not. I added a static check that fails the build if the tool layer ever imports a data module directly. On top of that, 4 declarative HTML forms using the WebMCP declarative API. Then I added some guardrails: a 1500 character output budget, untrustedContentHint on every tool returning prose the agent did not author, and a nine verb terminal allowlist that refuses rm , chaining, and injection. Challenges I ran into The agent solved the whole case in one turn. It made forty tool calls, then handed me a finished report. I have to say it was correct, but completely against the point. Asking a model to slow down is like asking it not to delete a file. It might comply. It might delete the file anyway. So I put it in the tool layer: after five reads with no human action, read tools stop answering and tell the agent to hand back. I left actuation ungated, because putting a document on my screen is the behaviour I want. My hints made a blind agent sound sighted. They described photo contents to help the player along, so the agent just told the player everything right away. I rewrote every hint to give a location and a question. "The window glass, lower half. Tell me what is there." A tool result silently ate my rules. The output budget trims by halving the longest array, which was the protocol array in the briefing. A model asking for the rules of play was getting one rule of seven, with no sign the rest existed. I found it by measuring the payload instead of trusting it. Accomplishments that I'm proud of The blindness is a mechanic, not a disclaimer. A prompt asking a model not to look is only advice, and it will look anyway if it decides it needs to. Withholding the capability from the registry is a rule. The page audits itself. If you want to test it yourself, open the LINK console and press QUICK VERIFY. 15 checks run against the tool registry in front of you, in your own browser. And it generalises, which I proved instead of claiming. I built a second instance at /apollo13 running the same 25 tools over the real Apollo 13 accident record: the Review Board report, the Mission Report, five voice loop threads, nine NASA photographs with real byte sizes and SHA-256 prefixes you can check yourself. I invented nothing. Where the primary sources contradict each other, I left the contradictions in. A corpus that resolves its own conflicts cannot teach you to find one. Same engine, same tool layer, one data file and a route. All of it is public domain. What I learned Withholding a capability is a design tool, and an underused one. The interesting question is not what else I can let an agent do. It is what it should have to ask me for. And a prompt is not a mechanic. Anything I wanted to actually be true had to live in the tool layer. What's next for ORPHEUS: A Case You and Your Agent Can't Crack Alone My corpus is a single interface, so any archive fits: a leaked document dump, a codebase post-mortem, a medical file, a legal discovery set. The version I want to build next is not fiction. It is the archive where letting an agent click freely is exactly what you cannot allow, and where the person reviewing it needs a partner that can hold fifty thousand files and no judgment at all. title: Tourbrick
pitch: Tourbrick is a voice OS for tour operators to create tours using voice commands
about_excerpt: Tourbrick is a voice OS for tour operators to create tours using voice commands Like Comment Story Updates Torubrick: The AI operating system for tourism professionals Tourbrick — About the project Tagline A shared WebMCP workplace where tour operators, travellers, and their AI agents co-create trips together. Inspiration I am a tour guide and tour operator. A good private trip depends on hundreds of details that do not fit neatly into a booking form: relationships with suppliers, scenic roads, seasonal nuances, great meals, rooms with a view, and my professional experience. Much of this knowledge still lives in documents, messages, and people’s heads. Traditional back-office software can store records, but it struggles to create interesting, inspiring trips with local specifics. General AI can suggest a generic itinerary, but it does not know what the tour company can actually provide, and it should not make silent changes to operational records. That's why we create Tourbrick — a space where professional tour operators and AI agents can work together. What it does Our demonstration begins with a real kind of request that is difficult to serve from a catalogue: a couple wants to spend five days travelling around Estonia and experience the sauna culture. The company has no pre-designed tour for that. First, ChatGPT uses Tourbrick’s WebMCP tools to read the original message and turn it into a structured brief. Then, ChatGPT can search Tourbrick’s inventory: individual experiences, suppliers, accommodation options, transfers, etc. From those records, it can assemble a custom trip around four sauna experiences grounded in the real-world services that we work with. Tourbrick turns the selected records into a five-day itinerary with a stored road route and a timetable for every day. The manager can open day three and see breakfast, the drive south, lunch, the Mooska smoke-sauna experience, the hotel, and dinner in chronological order. Each item remains connected to its supplier record, rate, duration, and conditions. Costs are grouped into accommodation, experiences, transportation, and meals, with every line behind the total. Nothing is silently committed. Tourbrick first creates a no-write preview. The manager can inspect, edit, or reject it; accepting saves exactly the reviewed version. It does not book a supplier, send a message, or take payment. Once reviewed, the same trip becomes a customer presentation. For this prototype, we created a sauna-led presentation to give it a personal feeling instead of the fixed website template. The customer page is also WebMCP-enabled. Travellers can open it with their own ChatGPT, focus a specific day, and prepare feedback such as: “Could we replace day two’s spa with a quieter countryside sauna?” Why WebMCP A conventional MCP server can expose a database or service even when no webpage is open. That is useful, but it is not the experience we wanted to create. With WebMCP, the webpage itself becomes the integration and the shared workspace. ChatGPT discovers the tools offered by the page the person is currently viewing and works in the same live context. The manager and the agent can look at the same request, map, timetable, and cost review. When the traveller opens the public proposal, their ChatGPT discovers a separate, customer-safe set of tools without requiring access to the operator’s workspace or a separately configured Tourbrick MCP connection. Before this, an operator had to manually reconcile records across spreadsheets and back-office screens, or copy incomplete context into a chat. Customer feedback arrived separately and then had to be matched back to the right trip and day. With Tourbrick, both agents work against the relevant structured version while people see and control the decisions on the page. What we built during the hackathon Tourbrick builds on an existing tour-operations product direction and domain model. During the WebMCP Challenge, we created the agent collaboration layer and the complete end-to-end experience demonstrated in the video: Tour operator tools for reading customer requests, publishing grounded briefs, searching inventory, previewing and creating custom trips, inspecting saved versions, and opening exact itinerary days. A visible operator journey from an ordinary customer message to a mapped, costed, day-by-day and hour-by-hour private trip. Preview-before-write controls, explicit approval, content hashes, immutable versions, idempotency protection, and loud rejection of stale data. Persisted Mapbox routes that are calculated when a new connection is needed and then reused rather than recalculated on every view. A separate customer presentation with three public, customer-safe WebMCP tools for reading the shared proposal, focusing a day, and drafting an unsent change request. Live deployments for both operator and customer experiences, plus the public source repository, setup instructions, and automated tests. How we built it The operator and customer interfaces use React, TypeScript, Vite, and Tailwind CSS. Each top-level page registers typed tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) , including a clear name, description, JSON input schema, execution handler, and read/write annotations. The application API is built with FastAPI and Pydantic, with PostgreSQL storing inventory, requests, immutable trip versions, customer presentations, and reusable route geometry. Mapbox provides road routing. The customer presentation runs against a separate public-only backend that does not expose manager routes, API documentation, or the operator MCP surface. The most difficult part was making agent work operationally trustworthy. A proposal can combine many records and prices, so approval is bound to the exact preview the manager saw. We also had to keep route legs connected to real timetable transfers so the map and itinerary describe the same journey. The finished workflow was tested end to end using ChatGPT’s in-app browser. The public repository’s 209 frontend tests and 203 backend tests cover tool registration, validation, approvals, versioning, routing, customer isolation, and the visible workflows. What we learned The important change about WebMCP is that the human interface and the agent interface no longer need to be separate products. The page can expose precise actions while still giving the person a map, itinerary, evidence, costs, and a clear approval boundary. We also learned that different people should not receive the same tools. The operator can search inventory and create a trip; the traveller can read the shared proposal and prepare feedback. Both collaborate with AI around the same journey, but Tourbrick preserves the responsibilities and access of each participant. What’s next The sauna presentation demonstrates a larger direction: customer proposals do not have to be forced into one fixed website template. An agent could compose the presentation around what matters to that particular traveller — saunas for this trip, wildlife, food, architecture, or accessibility for another — while the underlying itinerary remains structured and reviewable. The next product steps are live supplier availability, contracted rates, richer operator permissions, and turning confirmed customer feedback into a manager-reviewed itinerary revision. For my business — and for more than a million tour operators like me — WebMCP moves AI out of a separate chat window and into the work itself.
