title: Accessible Action Mode — Returns & Exchanges
pitch: A shopper-controlled WebMCP workflow for conditional multi-item returns and exchanges.
about_excerpt: A shopper-controlled WebMCP workflow for conditional multi-item returns and exchanges. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for Accessible Action Mode — Returns & Exchanges Inspiration People often describe a multi-item return as one outcome: “refund the jacket, exchange the shoes only if it is free, keep the coffee maker, and use a free drop-off.” Conventional returns interfaces split that intent across policy pages, item selectors, fee screens, and irreversible actions. An agent that merely clicks through those controls must guess what the merchant allows and when a real consequence will occur. We wanted a safer, more accessible model: the agent prepares a precise plan from merchant-authoritative data, the page explains it in plain language, and the shopper keeps visible control over approval. What it does Accessible Action Mode — Returns & Exchanges lets a shopper state the desired outcome once. A compatible browser agent uses five explicit WebMCP tools to: Read the current order. Read authoritative return and exchange options. Stage one exact, reviewable resolution plan with no business side effect. Read the same plan displayed on the page. Apply it only after the shopper approves that exact plan using the ordinary page. Approval, rejection, reset, and test-state controls deliberately remain page actions. There is no agent-facing approval or rejection tool. Demonstrated workflow The fictional test order AAM-2048 contains three items: Midnight Field Jacket — $74.00 refund. Stone Running Shoes — exchange from size 8.5 to size 9 at $0.00. Matte Countertop Coffee Maker — keep. Free QR drop-off. Total refund — $74.00. Additional cost — $0.00. Before approval, the page clearly says NOT SUBMITTED. Applying early returns APPROVAL_REQUIRED. After page approval, the plan applies exactly once in the local simulation; a repeat attempt returns DUPLICATE_EXECUTION without a second effect. Why WebMCP is essential Without WebMCP, an agent has to infer intent and policy from page-specific widgets, labels, disabled controls, and prose. WebMCP lets the page expose merchant-intended action contracts, constrained inputs, authoritative state, and side-effect boundaries directly. The five registered tools are: get_order get_return_exchange_options stage_resolution_plan get_resolution_plan apply_approved_resolution The agent and shopper share one server-backed plan, so they do not drift into separate interpretations of the return. How we built it The application uses TypeScript, React/Vinext, Cloudflare D1, Drizzle, deterministic policy functions, and document.modelContext.registerTool(...). Each authenticated principal receives an isolated workspace. Plans capture order, item, policy, and plan versions; expire automatically; record approval attribution; enforce idempotency; and emit ordered audit events. The ordinary page remains fully usable when WebMCP is unavailable. It supports keyboard navigation, visible focus, labeled controls, live-region errors, responsive reflow, reduced-motion preferences, and the same review and page-approval journey. ChatGPT served as the browser-agent client. Codex supported the specification, implementation, testing, accessibility work, deployment preparation, and evidence review. Human review set the safety boundaries and retained control over credentials, publication, and approval. Challenges The hardest part was preserving a clear authority boundary while keeping the experience useful. We had to make staging helpful but consequence-free, bind approval to the exact plan and versions the shopper reviewed, reject stale or expired state atomically, and guarantee that retries cannot create duplicate effects. We also separated the Shopify proof from the execution claim. The authorized development-store path demonstrates read-only order, returnability, and calculation evidence. Staging and apply remain an isolated local D1 simulation. The project performs no real return, refund, payment, fulfillment, inventory, label, carrier, or merchant mutation. Accomplishments Exactly five focused WebMCP tools and no approval tool. A coherent shopper-and-agent workflow rather than a technical-only demo. 109 passing unit/integration tests and two Playwright journeys. Verified authentication, tenant isolation, stale-state, expiry, rejection, atomicity, and duplicate-execution guards. Keyboard and responsive accessibility coverage with zero reported axe violations in the verified browser run. Public live site, Apache-2.0 source repository, and a public 2:48 narrated demo. What we learned WebMCP is strongest when it exposes a domain workflow instead of wrapping arbitrary UI automation. Structured tools make the agent more accurate, but they do not replace ordinary accessibility or human authority. For consequential commerce actions, the most useful collaboration is: agent reads and prepares, page enforces policy, human approves, and the server revalidates everything. What's next A production Shopify product would add shop-scoped installation and OAuth, encrypted per-shop credentials, customer authentication, compliance webhooks, generalized policy mapping, reconciliation, monitoring, support, and a reviewed distribution path. This challenge build intentionally stops at a safe synthetic and read-only provider boundary; it does not claim App Store readiness or live Shopify return processing. title: Concord — an agent that cannot overpromise
pitch: WebMCP tells an agent what a site can do. Nothing tells it what a site can take back. Concord is that missing layer: it computes what it can honestly promise across sites before contacting any.
about_excerpt: WebMCP tells an agent what a site can do. Nothing tells it what a site can take back. Concord is that missing layer: it computes what it can honestly promise across sites before contacting any. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration An agent books your flight on one site and your hotel on another. Halfway through, the hotel fails. Ask what happens next and no part of the web can answer. inputSchema describes a tool's shape . readOnlyHint describes whether it has an effect . Nothing anywhere describes whether that effect can be reversed — which is the one fact an agent needs to plan across sites rather than to act and hope. So today that gap is filled by a marketplace: an intermediary both businesses have a contract with, which is why one sits between almost every pair of businesses an agent might transact with, taking 15–30% to stand there. The tax is not for the booking. It is for the guarantee. The failure mode of agentic commerce is not the booking going wrong. It is the agent telling you it went fine. What it does Concord is a convention over WebMCP by which any site declares its commitment surface — one of three rungs: Rung Meaning Example reservable hold it, release it, nothing happened an airline seat compensable undoable, but it leaves a mark a hotel charge and refund irreversible it cannot be taken back a government fee …and an in-browser coordinator that computes the strongest honest guarantee across several such sites before contacting any of them — then refuses when the honest answer is that atomicity is not available at any price. Three things to try on the live URL, in ninety seconds: Ask for a flight, a hotel and the visa fee. The agent reads back what it can promise, which step is the point of no return, and which charge becomes briefly real before being reversed. Only then does a Go ahead button exist. Ask for a flight, the visa fee and the entry permit — two things nobody can take back. It says it cannot do that as one commitment, and that nothing has been contacted. There is no button on that answer. Kill the coordinator mid-commitment. Reload. It asks every vendor what actually happened and puts back what can be put back. Why WebMCP, specifically This needs exactly the thing WebMCP uniquely provides and nothing else does: two mutually distrusting origins' authenticated, typed capabilities present in one execution context, under the user's authority, with consent enforced on both sides by the browser. That is not scraping and it is not an API partnership. A participant grants with registerTool 's exposedTo . The embedder grants with allow="tools" . The coordinator must ask by name with getTools({ fromOrigins }) . Three separate grants, none forgeable by any party, and none requiring the participants to have heard of each other. No server anywhere is in the commitment path. How WebMCP is implemented The permission model is registerTool itself. This is the idea the whole project rests on: concord_commit does not exist until a person accepts the exact guarantee they were shown. Not disabled. Not registered. Four read-only tools at boot. concord_explain_guarantee appears once something is proposed. Explaining is not consent, so the surface does not change when the agent reads the guarantee out. A human clicks Accept on the page — registerTool puts concord_commit on the surface. The commitment begins — an AbortController takes it away again, so a second call arriving mid-flight finds nothing to call. toolchange fires on every one of those transitions, and you can watch it in the tool inspector. There is no tool that grants that permission, and there will not be one. An agent has every door; none of them opens this one. The rest of the surface actually used: exposedTo — each participant exposes its tools only to the coordinator's origin, so cross-origin consent is explicit on the participant's side. allow="tools" + Permissions-Policy: tools=(self "…") — the embedder's half of the same consent, verified on every deployed origin. Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 — required for cross-document tool access; without it getTools() returns empty with no error . getTools({ fromOrigins }) — discovery, opt-in on both sides, asked one origin at a time. executeTool(tool, jsonString) — arguments as a JSON string, per Chrome's imperative API. annotations.readOnlyHint — used honestly: true on the two tools that perform nothing, and on nothing that acts. AbortSignal — a deadline on every call, enforced by the coordinator too, which does not assume a participant honours cancellation. modelContext.requestUserInteraction — feature-detected. Chrome 151 does not implement it, so we measure that and use it wherever it exists: a second door onto the same accept, deliberately not a lock. A test hands it a host that approves every request and requires the surface to stay exactly as it was. If asking for attention could produce consent, the central claim would be false. And it fills a gap in the standard rather than decorating it. SPEC §19 proposes the missing annotation upstream: annotations: { readOnlyHint: false, commitment: 'reservable' | 'compensable' | 'irreversible', reverses: 'release_seat', ttlSeconds: 900, } The receipt Every commitment produces an RFC 6962 Merkle receipt in which every statement is signed by the counterparty that made it , with per-vendor ECDSA P-256 keys resolved from each vendor's own origin over TLS — never from a map the coordinator writes. The outcome is derived from the statements, never read off the receipt , because that field is the one thing no vendor signs. Check one on an origin we do not run, or with npx concord-verify receipt.json , and nothing of ours executes. How we built it, and what broke Zero dependencies, on purpose. Node's own test runner, a ~100-line property-testing kit, and Chrome. An audit found the receipt was forgeable. Seven of fourteen forgeries verified clean: a coordinator could delete a charge, relabel the outcome "Committed", and the receipt passed, because verifyReceipt gated its strictness on a string nobody signed. Fixed by deriving the outcome from the entries and by provable silence — a vendor that did nothing signs that it did nothing, so an absence is distinguishable from a deletion. You can fire all fourteen at our own verifier from the live site. Running on the real API found two defects a polyfill can never surface. The coordinator was not delegating tools to the origins it embeds, so every participant registered and none was discoverable. And Chrome returns inputSchema as a JSON string where the polyfill returns an object. Both worked flawlessly under the shim — which is the argument for never trusting one. getTools({ fromOrigins }) rejects for the whole call when any one origin is unreachable. One dead site produced "0 of 6 answered" and a failure screen with five participants healthy. Discovery now asks one origin at a time. What we learned That a sampled mutation score is not a score. We reported 92%. It came from 60 mutants taken every-Nth from a list sorted by file and by operator — a stratified sample of a sorted population. Running all 116 gave 87% . Closing what that exposed took it to 97% (112/116) , and the four survivors are documented as equivalent with the reasoning attached, not hidden. That a property test which cannot fail passes loudest. Our first reference-model test registered the commit tool in 1% of the states it checked, and its unwind-ordering property was vacuous in 95% of runs because the fixture had one participant of each rung — so reversing and not reversing produced identical output. Mutation testing found it. Every property now asserts how much of the interesting space it reached and fails rather than going green faster. That the measuring instrument needs measuring too. Our mutation runner's timeout killed the npm wrapper but not the test process beneath it; two orphans took throughput from ten mutants a minute to ten every three — and a loaded machine turns survivors into false kills, silently inflating the score. Challenges Refusing well is harder than committing. Anyone can run a saga. The hard part is computing, from declarations alone and before contact, that no honest promise exists — and then having no button on that answer. Proving a negative in a browser. "The commit tool does not exist yet" is only worth something if you can watch it not exist. So the claim is checked through the same getTools() an agent calls, state by state, against the live deployment. Not overclaiming about our own proof. We ship a formal model — 855 reachable states, 9 safety invariants, breadth-first so a violation reports the shortest trace. spec/Concord.tla is generated from the same declaration the checker executes, so it cannot drift. But TLC has not been run against it, and the README says so in those words rather than letting a .tla file imply a proof nobody ran. What it can't do — said before you ask A vendor can lie about being compensable. One does, on purp

Before it contacts anybody, it works out what it can honestly promise across sites that have never heard of each other. This panel is the live output of get tools. Five read-only tools. The commit tool is not disabled. It is not registered. title: SafeShare
pitch: Redact sensitive PDFs and images locally with privacy-preserving WebMCP assistance.
about_excerpt: Redact sensitive PDFs and images locally with privacy-preserving WebMCP assistance. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Sharing a document often means choosing between speed and privacy. Existing redaction workflows are either manual, destructive, or built around uploading a sensitive file to another service. At the same time, giving an AI agent unrestricted access to document contents creates a new disclosure risk. SafeShare explores a narrower, more useful contract: the browser handles the private document locally, while WebMCP gives the agent structured access to the redaction workflow. The agent can help manage masks and verify readiness without tool responses containing the document text, file name, image, or detected private values. What it does SafeShare opens PDFs and images directly in the browser, detects likely sensitive information, and immediately draws editable masks. People can move, resize, delete, or draw masks directly on the page. Preview opacity can be adjusted without weakening the final redaction. When the review is finished, SafeShare creates a flattened PDF or PNG in which every visible mask is permanently fused into the pixels. The original file remains unchanged. A supported browser can also hand the finished copy to the operating system's native share sheet, but only after a human click. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Redaction is not a background automation task; it is a shared visual decision. The person and the agent need the same live page, the same selected mask, and the same reversible history. WebMCP makes that collaboration explicit. SafeShare exposes nine narrow tools. An agent can read a privacy-filtered editor summary, list safe mask metadata, focus a mask, explain generic detection signals, add or delete a visible mask, undo a change, run the export safety check, and prepare the final download. The agent cannot download or share the file. The final export remains a deliberate human action. This is substantially better than scraping buttons from the interface: tool inputs are constrained, side effects are described, results are verifiable in the page, and the application can enforce a clear privacy boundary around tool output. What people and agents can do together A person can ask the agent to inventory every mask, focus the least confident detection, explain why it was created, make a reversible correction, and verify the final export — while watching each change happen on the document. Before WebMCP, that required fragile visual automation or a separate integration disconnected from the live editing session. The human contributes contextual judgment and final consent. The agent contributes structured navigation, consistency checks, and reversible execution. Neither replaces the other. How we built it SafeShare is a React and TypeScript application built with Vite. PDF.js renders PDFs, Tesseract.js performs local French and English OCR, and deterministic pattern checks detect common personal data. Every detected region is converted to normalized page coordinates so the same geometry works for display, editing, WebMCP actions, and export. The application feature-detects document.modelContext.registerTool() and registers nine imperative tools from the top-level page. The tools reuse the editor's existing state, validation, undo history, and safety report. Registrations share an AbortSignal for page-lifecycle cleanup. PDF-lib and Canvas produce the final rasterized document. The opacity slider affects only the editor preview; exported masks are always solid. The Web Share API is progressively enabled only when the browser confirms it can share the generated file. Challenges we ran into The main challenge was designing useful agent actions without turning WebMCP into a data-extraction channel. SafeShare's tool results intentionally return categories, IDs, pages, confidence levels and outcomes — not raw values, file names, images, document text, or mask coordinates. We also had to keep coordinates accurate across PDF text extraction, OCR output, responsive zoom, direct pointer editing and final raster export. A single normalized geometry model now drives all of those paths. Finally, native file sharing requires a direct human gesture. SafeShare prepares the current flattened file locally after edits so the operating system share sheet can open immediately from the user's click. Accomplishments that we're proud of A complete redaction product rather than a WebMCP proof of concept. Nine working tools with visible, reversible effects and privacy-filtered results. A human-only final export boundary. Local PDF/image processing with no SafeShare application server. English and French interfaces selected from the browser language. Direct drawing, moving, resizing, deleting, undo/redo, preview opacity and zoom. Flattened PDF and PNG output plus progressive native sharing. Automated tests for privacy boundaries, geometry, detection, history, localization, file validation and sharing. What we learned WebMCP is most powerful when it exposes the semantic operations of a live interface rather than recreating an application's backend API. The best tools are small, observable and honest about side effects. We also learned that privacy is not achieved by calling a tool “read-only”; it comes from deliberately limiting both inputs and outputs and preserving human control over consequential actions. What's next for SafeShare Next steps include more OCR languages, stronger local entity detection, reusable redaction presets, better keyboard editing, and an optional fully local model for document-specific suggestions. The core principle will remain unchanged: document processing belongs in the browser, agent actions should be inspectable, and export should stay under human control. title: LightningPricePilot
pitch: Agentic Price Discovery and Negotiation - LightningPricePilot is a WebMCP-enabled laptop marketplace.
about_excerpt: Agentic Price Discovery and Negotiation - LightningPricePilot is a WebMCP-enabled laptop marketplace. Like Comment Story Updates App Landing Page Shopper Page Merchant Page Shopper joining buying group after ChatGPT negotiated a group price for the laptop Shopper placing order after ChatGPT negotiated a good price for the laptop Two-sided bargain loop diagram Architecture diagram Actors diagram Use case diagram Inspiration The app's idea was inspired by my recent coffee brewing kettle buying experience. It wasn't a great experience trying to find a reasonable price after spending a couple of hours checking on Amazon and coffee equipment websites, only to realize the bargain price kettle I want in Amazon has target delivery date next year 2027 on the very final order payment page. My intent is to get it as soon as possible. Hence, it inspired me to create LightningPricePilot - a Two-sided Intent Market so that shopper can better communicate their intent to the merchant. What it does LightningPricePilot is a two-sided intent marketplace where shoppers and merchants use AI agents to discover fairer laptop prices. Instead of scraping product cards, a shopper’s agent uses structured WebMCP tools to search laptops, compare new and refurbished prices, negotiate within merchant-defined guardrails, join group buys, subscribe to target-price bargains, receive notifications, and prepare a mock checkout. On the other side, a merchant’s agent can analyze aggregate demand, review offer activity, adjust private pricing policies, and publish limited bargains to matching shoppers. The experience keeps people in control: commitments, policy changes, bargain publication, and checkout require visible human approval. Merchant price floors remain private, shopper targets are shown only in aggregate, and the demo never collects payment or personal information. Why your use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Product discovery and pricing depend on live website state: condition-specific inventory, current and group-buy prices, group progress, active bargains, offer expiry, and merchant pricing policies. These details are difficult for an agent to understand reliably by reading page text or clicking through filters. WebMCP turns that state into precise, discoverable actions. On the shopper page, an agent can search the laptop catalogue, compare condition, group, and bargain price paths, request a rule-bound offer, join a group buy, save a target-price subscription, read bargain notifications, and prepare a mock checkout. On the merchant page, a different agent can review aggregate demand and offer activity, update private pricing guardrails, and publish or close limited bargains. Each page registers only the tools appropriate to its role, with the room code already bound to every call. Both roles use the same validated room backend, so a shopper action can change aggregate demand and a merchant action can create a qualifying shopper notification without exposing the merchant’s private floor through the shopper tool surface. This transforms the storefront from a static catalogue into a structured negotiation space for people, shopper agents, and merchant agents. How it creates a better user experience The shopper describes the outcome once: “Find me a lightweight laptop under $900. Excellent refurbished condition is acceptable. Compare every available price path and negotiate toward $800 if sensible.” The agent can then present understandable options instead of another long list of products: Buy at the current price for the selected condition Join a group buy and show how many more commitments would unlock its next discount Use an active, inventory-limited merchant bargain Request a ten-minute offer or transparent counteroffer within the merchant’s private guardrails Save the product, acceptable condition, and target price for a future bargain Every price path states why it is available, whether it is currently unlocked, and what the shopper must do next. Offers include their rationale and expiry. Joining a group, saving a subscription, and placing the fictional mock order pause for visible human approval. The shopper no longer needs to repeatedly search the catalogue, compare product conditions, monitor group progress, or refresh the page looking for a relevant bargain. Matching merchant bargains create persisted in-app notifications, while server-sent events update the open room live. Merchants gain a complementary experience: they can see group commitments, subscriber counts, average target prices, and offer volume; tune the private floor and discount limits; and publish limited bargains that are matched against saved shopper intent. They do this without receiving a list of individual shopper budgets. Describe what people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before People remain responsible for the important trade-offs: Which laptop condition is acceptable What target price is worthwhile Whether to join a non-binding group buy Whether to save buying intent in the room Whether to complete a fictional checkout On the merchant side, whether to change pricing policy or publish or close a bargain Agents handle the structured, repetitive work: Search products by need, use case, condition, and budget Compare current condition, unlocked group, and active bargain prices Request an accepted offer or explain a policy-bound counteroffer Retrieve relevant bargain notifications Summarize aggregate demand and recent offer outcomes Turn a demand signal into a proposed limited bargain For example, the merchant agent can see that a product has five group commitments, three bargain subscribers, an aggregate average target, and recent offer activity. It can propose a price, condition, inventory allocation, expiry, and shopper-facing message. The merchant reviews the action before publication; matching subscribers then receive an in-app notification that the shopper agent can retrieve and explain. This creates something that was previously difficult: asynchronous negotiation around durable buyer intent . A shopper can save a condition and target price, leave the original search, and return to a persisted notification after a merchant publishes a qualifying bargain. Demand is used to unlock lower group prices and guide shared bargains—not to secretly calculate a different price for each shopper. Briefly explain how you implemented WebMCP LightningPricePilot implements two role-specific WebMCP surfaces with document.modelContext.registerTool . The shopper page registers seven tools: search_products — find up to five laptops by plain-language query, use case, condition, or maximum budget get_price_options — compare the current condition price, group-buy path, and any active bargain for one laptop request_offer — create a non-binding ten-minute accepted offer or counteroffer within merchant guardrails join_group_buy — record the shopper’s non-binding group commitment and unlock a tier when its threshold is reached subscribe_bargains — save a product, acceptable condition, and target price in the demo room get_notifications — retrieve persisted bargain notifications, treating merchant-authored messages as untrusted content prepare_mock_checkout — place a human-approved fictional order from a valid offer and decrement demo inventory The merchant page registers five tools: get_demand_summary — return group commitments, subscriber counts, aggregate average targets, and offer counts get_offer_activity — return recent accepted, countered, expired, and checked-out offers set_pricing_policy — update the private floor, maximum instant discount, and five- and ten-buyer discounts publish_bargain — publish a condition-specific, inventory-limited, expiring bargain and notify matching subscribers close_bargain — stop an active bargain while preserving its notification and audit history Each tool posts its role, action, and structured input to the room action API. The server validates the room, role-specific action allowlist, and input schema before running shared domain logic against the room’s persisted state. The deterministic pricing service enforces condition inventory, merchant floors, instant-discount limits, five- and ten-buyer group tiers, bargain inventory, and expiry. How we built it We built LightningPricePilot with Next.js 16, React, and TypeScript. The shopper and merchant pages register 12 role-specific tools using document.modelContext.registerTool: seven shopper tools and five merchant tools. The app intentionally contains no embedded model or OpenAI API key—the intelligence comes from the WebMCP-capable browser agent. Every tool calls a shared, validated room API backed by Zod schemas and deterministic pricing logic. That pricing engine handles condition-based inventory, private merchant floors, instant-discount limits, group-buy tiers, expiring offers, and inventory-limited bargains. title: Pathfinder
pitch: The vast amount of data on the internet makes analysis paralysis all too real. Pathfinder allows an agent to assist with one of the major decisions of many people's lives, where to go to college.
about_excerpt: The vast amount of data on the internet makes analysis paralysis all too real. Pathfinder allows an agent to assist with one of the major decisions of many people's lives, where to go to college. Like Comment Story Updates Pathfinder helps students turn overwhelming engineering-college research into a choice they can understand and explain. Start with a question in your own words. The agent researches the facts and organizes the decision visually. The agent narrows 75 sourced colleges into a focused shortlist shaped around the student’s actual priorities. Compare the differences that matter, including published cost, career outcomes, and engineering-program strength. Explore climate, walkability, campus scale, and nearby communities to understand what daily life could feel like. Open any school for a focused view of its program, costs, outcomes, admissions context, and surrounding area. Compare exact-major degree counts alongside clearly separated broader-field earnings, debt, and career context. Inspiration College research is not suffering from a lack of information. Students and parents already have access to costs, programs, outcomes, admissions data, weather, and campus-life details. The difficult part is organizing all of it into a decision they can understand and explain. I built Pathfinder to explore whether an agent could help with that actual decision, not just answer another isolated college question. What it does Pathfinder is an agent-first decision space for choosing an engineering school. A student can start with an imperfect question like: I’m interested in mechanical engineering. Show me a few reasonably priced schools with good career outcomes, and I don’t want somewhere brutally cold. The agent can search Pathfinder’s catalog of 75 colleges and 20 engineering majors, inspect supporting evidence, build a focused shortlist, and compose the website around the student’s question. Instead of returning a wall of text, the agent can create a visual comparison, explore campus life, open a focused school profile, or test a temporary “what if” scenario. The student supplies the priorities and judgment; the agent handles the research and organization. Why WebMCP WebMCP turns Pathfinder from a website beside a conversation into a workspace shared with the agent. Pathfinder exposes fifteen purpose-built tools for reading the student’s decision, searching colleges and programs, retrieving evidence, updating preferences, managing schools, creating temporary scenarios, and changing the visual workspace. The agent does not need to scrape the page or guess where to click. The student does not need to learn a complicated filtering system. Both work with the same decision state and see the same result. This also makes interactions possible that are difficult in either a traditional website or a standalone chat. A student can ask a natural follow-up, have the agent reorganize the relevant evidence visually, and continue refining the decision without starting over. How I built it I built Pathfinder iteratively with Codex. I would test realistic student scenarios, identify where the agent lacked the right tool or where the interface became confusing, and then work with Codex to redesign, implement, test, and refine the next version. The application uses React, TypeScript, Next.js, Vite, Tailwind CSS, MapLibre GL, and OpenAI Sites. Its bundled catalog draws from public sources including College Scorecard, NCES IPEDS, NOAA, EPA, Census, and the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Visitors need no account or API key, and their personal decision stays in their browser. The hardest architectural problem was separating three kinds of state: The student’s saved decision A temporary what-if scenario The visual workspace currently being shown That separation lets the agent reorganize the page or explore a hypothetical situation without silently changing what the student has actually decided. What I learned The central lesson was that agent experiences are stronger when they are designed as shared environments. A chat response can explain a comparison. A WebMCP workspace can also preserve it, visualize it, expose the evidence, and support the student’s next question. Pathfinder is not meant to declare one objectively “best” college. It helps students reduce an overwhelming field of information into a focused choice they understand and can confidently explain. title: CountryLab
pitch: A shared economic laboratory where humans and AI agents investigate, manipulate, explain, and test the same visible country through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A shared economic laboratory where humans and AI agents investigate, manipulate, explain, and test the same visible country through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most web agents still have to infer what a page means from pixels, text, and UI controls. That works for simple interactions, but it becomes brittle when the application has domain state, history, causality, and actions with different safety implications. CountryLab explores a different model: the webpage itself exposes the semantic operations an agent actually needs. What it does CountryLab is an interactive miniature country with a deterministic economy. A human can inspect regions and metrics, change interest rates, taxes, spending, and tariffs, trigger shocks such as floods or oil shocks, and advance the simulation through time. The same application exposes 17 semantic WebMCP tools to an agent. Instead of scraping charts or clicking blindly, the agent can: read the exact current country state; inspect regions and sectors; query event, metric, and causal history; make explicitly requested live policy or event changes; run isolated counterfactual experiments without overwriting the live country; and visibly focus the map, WHY inspector, or scenario comparison so the human sees the same evidence. The flagship workflow is: A human floods the port and advances the simulation. The agent observes the changed world through WebMCP. It investigates event, region, metric, and causal history. It traces a chain such as flood → trade/import disruption → supply pressure → inflation . The human asks the agent to prove the claim without changing the live country. CountryLab creates an isolated alternate timeline that removes only the selected flood and replays later interventions at their original points in time. The agent compares both timelines and opens the result in the webpage. The original live country remains unchanged. Why WebMCP is a strong fit CountryLab depends on domain semantics that are difficult and unreliable to recover through ordinary browser automation. An agent should not have to infer numeric state from charts, reconstruct chronology from visual labels, or guess whether an action mutates the live simulation or runs a safe experiment. WebMCP gives the agent structured access to: exact simulation state instead of visual inference; stable region, sector, event, snapshot, and scenario identifiers; bounded metric and event history; deterministic causal provenance; explicit live-world actions; isolated counterfactual experimentation; and visible UI-focus tools that return the agent's reasoning to the human interface. This turns the webpage into a shared experimental instrument rather than a collection of buttons for an agent to automate. How it improves the user experience Without WebMCP, an agent would need to infer values and chronology indirectly, reconstruct causal relationships from presentation, and simulate UI clicks to manipulate the country. That is brittle and loses the important distinction between observation, live mutation, and isolated experimentation. With WebMCP, the agent can begin read-only, understand exactly what the human changed, gather deterministic evidence, run a safe alternate timeline, compare outcomes, and visibly show the proof. Human actions are immediately visible to subsequent agent reads, and agent live actions immediately update the same interface because both use the same application-service and shared-state layer. What humans and agents can do together A human can create a disaster or policy situation visually and ask open-ended questions such as: “Something changed. Investigate what happened.” “Why did inflation rise? Show me the chain.” “Prove the flood caused the increase, but do not change my live country.” The agent can independently gather evidence, identify the relevant event and metrics, retrieve deterministic causal provenance, formulate a counterfactual test, run the alternate timeline, compare outcomes, and open the visible comparison for the human. The human can intervene again at any time, and the next WebMCP read observes the same updated world. How WebMCP was implemented CountryLab uses the imperative document.modelContext.registerTool(...) API with capability detection and registration-scoped AbortSignal cleanup. The 17 tools are grouped into four categories: Observation: country state, region/sector inspection, metric history, event history, causal history. Explicit live mutations: policy changes, shocks, emergency response, time advancement, snapshots. Isolated experiments: counterfactual runs and scenario comparison. Visible explanation: region highlighting, metric focus, causal-chain display, and scenario-comparison display. Tool schemas use strict object shapes, enums, numeric bounds, and additionalProperties: false . Read-only tools carry readOnlyHint: true . Live mutation tools explicitly describe their effects. The WebMCP layer does not contain economic formulas. Both the React/Phaser human interface and WebMCP actions use the same application service and Zustand state over the deterministic economy engine. Counterfactual event removal branches from saved event-time checkpoints and replays subsequent recorded live interventions into both branches. That allows the comparison to mean “same later history, except this event,” while keeping the live world untouched. Testing CountryLab has been tested with ChatGPT's WebMCP-capable agent browser. The deployed app exposes exactly 17 CountryLab tools and the human UI continues to work normally when WebMCP is unavailable. A recommended judge flow is: Open the live site. Trigger Flood · Port and advance six months. Ask: “Something changed. Investigate what happened.” Ask: “Why did inflation rise? Show me the chain.” Ask: “Prove the flood caused the increase, but do not change my live country.” Confirm the scenario comparison opens and the live world remains unchanged. Built with React, Phaser, TypeScript, Zustand, Vite, WebMCP, and a deterministic in-browser economy/counterfactual engine. Accuracy note CountryLab is an educational toy causal model. It demonstrates transparent directional relationships and deterministic experimentation; it is not a real-world economic forecasting or policy-advice system. title: Once Upon
pitch: A living manuscript where every discovery changes what AI can do.
about_excerpt: A living manuscript where every discovery changes what AI can do. Like Comment Story Updates Notes (Clues) Inspector for Debugging Manuscript Inspiration Interactive fiction is most exciting when players can try anything, but its most memorable mysteries still depend on deliberate reveals and consequences. Players should not have to choose between a rigid action menu and an AI story that can improvise past the clues that make discovery matter. We wanted each discovery in the story to become a new capability for the agent. WebMCP made that relationship explicit and inspectable. What it does Once Upon is a living manuscript played through natural-language actions. Each player action becomes the next chapter on the page, while authored discoveries open new ways to interact with the story. The first release centers on one complete authored mystery, The Last Manuscript . It begins in a correction room with a handleless door. Finding a pencil, following a memory, and reading a hidden manuscript do more than change the prose: each discovery gives the agent a new WebMCP action through the page. There are no character sheets, dice, fixed choices, or turn limits. Why it matters Most websites present a fixed interface and leave agents to guess how to operate it. Purely generated stories have the opposite problem: they can respond to anything, but they struggle to protect a carefully timed mystery. Once Upon uses WebMCP to connect free-form play with authored causality. The human supplies intent and makes every meaningful choice. The agent turns those choices into a responsive narrative. The page protects secrets, commits consequences, and reveals new structured verbs when the story earns them. None of the three participants can create the complete experience alone. This turns agent capability into a visible narrative mechanic rather than a hidden automation layer. The result is an agent-native experience that would be difficult to build reliably through UI guessing, DOM scraping, or an unconstrained model prompt. How it works The running product does not call a hosted model or require a specific provider. It works with whichever WebMCP-capable agent is already accompanying the player, so there is no app-owned model API key or provider lock-in. Before every turn, the agent reads the page's structured story state. It then uses a currently allowed action and commits one to three short paragraphs back to the manuscript. The page types the chapter at reading speed, and the agent leaves the prose on the page instead of repeating it in chat. Three stable core tools coordinate the story. Story-object tools are registered only after authored prerequisites are satisfied, remain registered until used, and retire after their one-shot interaction. Using an object changes the page before the next chapter is written; that commit must reference the same effect and every fact it revealed. The page — not the model — owns session state, revision checks, authored discoveries, sealed facts, interaction rules, and completion order. Every mutation checks the active session and revision, while operation IDs make same-page retries idempotent. The agent remains free to improvise characters and consequences without inventing executable tools or revealing protected facts early. Gameplay state remains in the current page and is not uploaded during play. After finishing the story, the player may explicitly create an anonymous, unlisted, read-only manuscript link. Only that completed reader copy is stored as story content, and it expires after 30 days. How we built it Codex was the primary coding agent throughout the project. It helped inspect and refactor the repository, shape the WebMCP protocol, implement the narrative state machine and interface, turn runtime edge cases into validation rules, add regression tests, and prepare the deployment. Claude Code was also used as a supporting coding tool during development. Architecture Once Upon is a TypeScript application built with React 19 and Vinext, deployed on ChatGPT Sites through a Cloudflare Workers-compatible runtime. The in-memory story engine owns narrative state and validation; the WebMCP bridge derives the live tool surface from that state; and Cloudflare D1 stores only completed manuscripts that a player explicitly chooses to share. Testing No account, API key, or credentials are required. Playing requires ChatGPT's in-app browser with an agent attached, or Google Chrome with WebMCP enabled. Open the public demo in a supported browser with an agent attached. Ask: “Play The Last Manuscript with me through this page. I look around the room before answering the speaker.” Verify that the player's move appears on the sheet and that the committed chapter is typed at reading speed instead of repeated in chat. Continue choosing actions. When a story object becomes available, explicitly ask the agent to use it and verify that the page changes before the next chapter is written. Enable Settings → Tool inspector to inspect the active tools and the prerequisites, registration, invocation, and retirement lifecycle. Choose Start over or reload to confirm that a fresh manuscript begins at the prologue. Follow the Pencil → Memory → Last Manuscript progression. After completion, choose Create a link to open the anonymous, read-only manuscript reader; the link expires after 30 days. The repository passes strict TypeScript checks, linting, the Drizzle schema check, 90 unit tests, a production build, and 22 Playwright end-to-end tests. Challenges and accomplishments The hardest part was keeping free-form narration and authored causality in sync. The player can attempt anything, but an agent still has to recover cleanly from an interrupted turn, avoid revealing a secret early, and finish the exact page change caused by a story object. We turned stale sessions, duplicate operations, interrupted turns, premature discoveries, and early completion into explicit validation rules and regression tests. The finished experience keeps the player's action, the agent's prose, and the page's evolving capabilities synchronized and inspectable from the prologue through the final passage. What's next More stories can be added through the same declarative experience definitions. Next, we want manuscripts to persist across visits. We also plan to expand agent compatibility testing from the evaluation scenarios already documented in the repository.
